stem: Which statement about the facebow is true?
choices: An arbitrary facebow puts the hinge axis within about 2-5 mm of the patient's
A facebow transfer mounts the mandibular cast to the hinge axis
A kinematic facebow relies on average ear-canal points rather than locating the exact hinge axis
The Slidematic's anterior point is marked 43 mm above tooth #24
ex: The facebow mounts the maxillary cast only, using the ear canals and one anterior point (the Slidematic: 43 mm above #7). An arbitrary facebow is within about 2-5 mm of the hinge axis; a kinematic facebow finds the exact axis.
why: An arbitrary facebow uses average points and lands within about 2-5 mm of the true hinge axis.
The facebow mounts the maxillary cast; the mandibular cast is mounted to it with a CR record.
A kinematic facebow locates the exact hinge axis; the ear-canal version is the arbitrary one.
The Slidematic's anterior point is 43 mm above #7, a maxillary tooth.

stem: Which statement about articulators is false?
choices: In an arcon articulator, the condylar element is on the upper member
A non-adjustable articulator is accurate only in MICP
The Bennett angle setting is the one least needed on a semi-adjustable articulator
An articulator is most useful when it is about the size of the patient
ex: Arcon: condyle on the lower member, fossa on the upper. Non-adjustable: accurate in MICP only. Semi-adjustable: SCI and Bennett angle, the Bennett angle least needed. Best value: an articulator about the patient's size, about 110 mm between condyles.
why: This is the false one: in an arcon articulator the condyle is on the lower member and the fossa on the upper, as in the skull.
This is true: any other position, or a record that separates the teeth, adds error.
This is true: Dr. Givan would leave it off first, because the average values are close.
This is true: about 110 mm (4 inches) between the condyles.

stem: Which statement about CR records is false?
choices: A CR record should be made with the teeth lightly touching
Wax is often preferred for a CR record
MIP differs from CO in about 90 percent of people
On a fully adjustable articulator, the CR record's thickness doesn't affect accuracy
ex: A CR record: no tooth contact, minimal opening (or at the treatment VDO), usually wax. MIP and CO differ in about 90 percent of people. On a fully adjustable articulator, mounted on the exact axis, record thickness doesn't matter.
why: This is the false one: a CR record is made with no tooth contact, so the teeth can't deflect the mandible.
This is true: wax is the usual material for a CR record.
This is true: in about 90 percent, the teeth close from CO into a different MIP.
This is true: with the exact hinge axis, opening and closing on the articulator follows the patient's arc.

stem: Which statement about occlusal splints is true?
choices: A mandibular splint interferes less with speech, so it suits daytime wear
A repositioning splint is a reversible treatment, like a stabilization splint
A maxillary splint is ideally suited to a Class III relationship
A maxillary stabilization splint has deep cusp indentations instead of a flat plane
ex: Maxillary stabilization splint: flat plane plus an anterior ramp, sturdy, worn at night, ideal for Class II division 1. Mandibular splint: less speech interference, for daytime. A repositioning splint is irreversible.
why: Less speech interference is why the mandibular splint is the daytime choice.
The slides class a repositioning splint as irreversible; the flat plane stabilization splint is the reversible one.
The maxillary splint is ideally suited to Class II division 1.
A stabilization splint has a flat plane with an anterior ramp, so the teeth aren't locked into one position.

stem: Which statement about tooth mobility is false?
choices: Tooth mobility is greatest late in the day, after a day of function
A healthy tooth moves about 28 µm vertically under load and needs about 4 hours to recover
An implant moves only about 2-3 µm vertically
About 150 µm is the limit of physiologic horizontal mobility
ex: Vertical: about 28 µm, about 4 hours to recover; an implant 2-3 µm. Horizontal: 56-108 µm, limit 150 µm. Mobility is worst on waking. Adapted mobility is stable (monitor); traumatic mobility is increasing (splint).
why: This is the false one: mobility is greatest on waking, after a night of parafunction.
This is true: about 28 µm, with full recovery taking about 4 hours.
This is true: with no PDL, an implant moves only about 2-3 µm.
This is true: normal horizontal movement is 56-108 µm, with 150 µm the limit.

stem: Which statement about occlusion and TMD is false?
choices: Existing posterior interferences are much more common in symptomatic patients
Muscle problems make up about 50 percent of TMDs and joint problems about 35 percent
Reversible and irreversible treatments report similar success, so conservative care comes first
Bruxism is centrally driven and is not started by occlusal contacts
ex: TMD: muscles about 50 percent, joints about 35 percent. Existing interferences are equal in symptomatic and asymptomatic people, so don't equilibrate to prevent TMD, but don't add new ones. Reversible and irreversible care both report 50-90 percent success. Bruxism is CNS-driven.
why: This is the false one: existing interferences are found about equally in symptomatic and asymptomatic people.
This is true: about half are muscle problems and about a third are joint problems.
This is true: both report 50-90 percent success, so start conservative.
This is true: bruxism is a CNS event tied to arousal, not to the occlusion.

stem: Which statement about support, retention and stability is true?
choices: Stability, resistance to horizontal forces, is the most important property
Support is the resistance to forces that pull the denture away from the tissue
Retention is the resistance to horizontal forces that slide the denture
The ridge crests are the best areas to take a denture's support
ex: Support: resistance to vertical force toward the tissue (buccal shelf, retromolar pad, palate). Retention: resistance to dislodgement. Stability: resistance to horizontal force, the most important, and what implants help most.
why: When stability fails, biting hurts; it is also what implants improve most.
Resistance to dislodgement is retention; support resists vertical force toward the tissue.
Resistance to horizontal force is stability; retention resists dislodgement.
Support is taken on the buccal shelf, the retromolar pad and the palate, not the ridges.

stem: Which statement about lingualized denture occlusion is false?
choices: Lingualized occlusion puts a long mandibular buccal cusp into a flat maxillary fossa
Lingualized occlusion can be set either balanced or non-balanced, depending on the patient
Lingualized occlusion directs the force over the ridge crest
Wear and loss of VDO are drawbacks of lingualized occlusion
ex: Lingualized: a long maxillary lingual cusp on a flat or wide mandibular fossa, like a mortar and pestle. It can be balanced or not, has no anterior contact, directs force over the crest, and can wear and lose VDO.
why: This is the false one: it is the long maxillary lingual cusp that sits on a flat or wide mandibular fossa.
This is true: lingualized can be set either way.
This is true: force over the crest is among its advantages.
This is true: the slides list wear and VDO loss as its disadvantages.

stem: Which statement about how complete dentures contact is false?
choices: Dentures are built in MIP, with the joints free to find their own position
Anterior denture teeth are kept out of contact in centric occlusion
Each denture moves as one piece, so it acts like one upper and one lower tooth
Setting the posterior teeth in crossbite is acceptable after resorption
ex: Denture occlusion is built in centric occlusion with the joints seated (no MIP), with posterior contacts and the anteriors out of contact. Each denture is one piece. After resorption, a crossbite setup is acceptable.
why: This is the false one: dentures are built in centric occlusion, with the joints seated; MIP isn't used.
This is true: the contacts are posterior, because the premaxilla is weak.
This is true: a force anywhere on it moves the whole denture.
This is true: the mandible resorbs down and out and the maxilla up and in, so a crossbite is fine.

stem: How does occlusion differ from articulation?
choices: Occlusion is static contact; articulation adds the dynamic contact of function
Occlusion includes jaw movement; articulation is only the static contact in MIP
Occlusion describes the joints; articulation describes the teeth
They are synonyms, so either word is correct on an exam
ex: Occlusion is the static relationship of the incising or masticating surfaces (or tooth analogs). Articulation is the static AND dynamic contact relationship during function. Dr. Givan: people use them interchangeably, "but they're not quite the same," and an educated professional knows the difference. The reversed pair (occlusion = movement) is the trap.
why: Occlusion is the static relationship of the teeth; articulation is static plus dynamic contact during function.
This reverses the two terms. Occlusion is the static contact; articulation is the one that adds movement.
Both terms describe tooth contact relationships, not the joints. The joint is the TMJ.
Dr. Givan stresses they are not quite the same: articulation adds the dynamic contact of function.

stem: The neutral zone is best defined as:
choices: The potential space where the forces of the tongue and of the lips and cheeks are equal
The space between the teeth when the mandible is at physiologic rest
The area of the occlusal table between the buccal and lingual cusp tips of the posterior teeth
The zone of the articular disc that carries no load in function
ex: The neutral zone is the potential space between the lips and cheeks on one side and the tongue on the other, where their forces balance. It is thought to guide where teeth develop. The space between the teeth at rest is the freeway (interocclusal rest) space, a different idea.
why: The neutral zone is the potential space where tongue force and lip and cheek force balance, and it guides where teeth sit.
The space between the teeth at physiologic rest is the freeway (interocclusal rest) space, not the neutral zone.
That describes the occlusal table, the area between buccal and lingual cusp tips.
The neutral zone is about soft-tissue forces around the dental arch, not a region of the articular disc.

stem: A crown is contoured well outside the patient's neutral zone. What does Dr. Givan expect to happen?
choices: Tongue and lip forces push against it, so it is unlikely to be successful
It stays stable because the PDL adapts and the surrounding bone remodels to the new position
It improves lip support with no functional cost
It only matters for complete dentures, not natural teeth
ex: Restored or orthodontically positioned teeth should be within the neutral zone. "You put something in their way, they'll just sort of knock it out of the way." The muscles win: teeth or restorations outside the zone are pushed, displaced or fail.
why: A restoration in the way of the tongue, lips and cheeks gets pushed on; the muscles win and it tends to fail.
The muscles win, not the tooth: a crown outside the neutral zone is pushed and displaced rather than accepted.
Overcontouring outside the neutral zone has a functional cost: the soft-tissue forces push against it.
Restored and orthodontically moved natural teeth should also be within the neutral zone, not just dentures.

stem: The occlusal plane is:
choices: The planar mean of the curvature of the incisal and occlusal surfaces, not truly flat
A flat plane through the buccal cusp tips of the mandibular teeth
The plane passing through both condyles and the mandibular incisal point (Bonwill's triangle)
The curve from the mandibular canine tip through the condyle
ex: The occlusal plane (older term: plane of occlusion) is the average plane established by the incisal and occlusal surfaces. "Generally, it is not a plane but represents the planar mean of the curvature of these surfaces." The canine-to-condyle curve is the curve of Spee; the condyle-condyle-incisor plane is Bonwill's triangle.
why: The occlusal plane is the average plane of the incisal and occlusal surfaces; it is really the planar mean of a curved surface.
The occlusal plane is not truly flat and is not defined by the mandibular buccal cusp tips alone.
Condyle to condyle to incisal point is Bonwill's triangle, not the occlusal plane.
The curve from the mandibular canine tip back to the condyle is the curve of Spee.

stem: The curve of Spee begins at the ___ and ends at the anterior-most portion of the mandibular condyle.
choices: Cusp tip of the mandibular canine
Incisal edge of the mandibular central incisor
Buccal cusp tip of the mandibular first premolar
Mesiobuccal cusp tip of the mandibular first molar
ex: Curve of Spee: an anatomic curve in the median (sagittal) plane, from the mandibular canine cusp tip along the buccal cusp tips of the premolars and molars, through the anterior border of the ramus, ending at the anterior-most part of the condyle (Ferdinand Graf Spee, 1890).
cue: Spee starts at the canine, Sees the sagittal side.
why: The curve of Spee starts at the mandibular canine cusp tip and runs along the buccal cusp tips back to the condyle.
The curve of Spee begins at the canine cusp tip, not the central incisor's incisal edge.
The first premolar buccal cusp is along the curve, but the curve starts one tooth forward at the canine tip.
The first molar MB cusp lies along the curve of Spee; the curve starts at the mandibular canine cusp tip.

stem: From which view do you see the curve of Spee, and from which the curve of Wilson?
choices: Spee from the sagittal view; Wilson from the frontal view
Spee from the frontal view; Wilson from the sagittal view
Both from the sagittal view
Spee from the horizontal view; Wilson from the frontal view
ex: Spee is the anteroposterior curve (side view, median plane). Wilson is the mediolateral curve (front view, frontal plane), following the buccal-out maxillary and lingual-in mandibular inclination of the posterior teeth.
why: Spee is the anteroposterior curve seen from the side (sagittal); Wilson is the mediolateral curve seen from the front.
This swaps the two. Spee is seen from the side; Wilson, the side-to-side curve, is seen from the front.
Only Spee is sagittal. Wilson follows the buccolingual tilt of the posterior teeth, so it is seen in the frontal view.
Spee is seen in the sagittal (side) view, not the horizontal plane.

stem: Viewed in the frontal plane, the curve of Wilson in the mandibular arch is:
choices: Concave
Convex
Flat
Reverse in Class III only
ex: Curve of Wilson: in the mandibular arch it is concave, in the maxillary arch convex. It follows the lingual inclination of the mandibular posterior teeth (they erupt angled in) and the buccal inclination of the maxillary posterior teeth (angled out).
why: The mandibular curve of Wilson is concave, following the lingual inclination of the mandibular posterior teeth.
Convex describes the maxillary curve of Wilson, where the posterior teeth tilt buccally.
The curve of Wilson is a real curve created by the inclination of the posterior teeth, not a flat line.
The curve of Wilson is not defined by Angle class; it is concave in the mandibular arch.

stem: When artificial denture teeth are set, the combined anteroposterior and mediolateral curvature used to create balanced occlusion is called the:
choices: Compensating curve
Curve of Spee
Sphere of Monson
Bonwill triangle
ex: Dr. Givan: "Curve of Spee is specific for teeth." For artificial teeth the term is the compensating curve, which covers both the Spee-like and Wilson-like curvature because you set both at once. It is one of the five factors of denture (balanced) occlusion.
why: For artificial teeth, the combined Spee-like and Wilson-like curvature is called the compensating curve.
The curve of Spee is specific to natural teeth and is only the anteroposterior curve.
The sphere of Monson is a theory that cusps conform to a 4-inch sphere, not the term for a denture setup curve.
Bonwill's triangle is the equilateral triangle from condyle to condyle to the mandibular incisal point.

stem: The sphere of Monson proposes that each cusp conforms to an imaginary sphere with a radius of about:
choices: 4 inches, centered near the glabella
4 inches, centered on the condyles
110 mm, centered on the mandibular symphysis
6 inches, centered on the coronoid processes
ex: Monson's spherical theory (1916): each cusp conforms to an imaginary sphere of about 4-inch radius centered in the region of the glabella. The 4-inch (110 mm) number also appears in Bonwill's equilateral triangle, which is condyle to condyle to symphysis, not a sphere.
why: Monson proposed a sphere of about a 4-inch radius centered in the region of the glabella.
The radius is about 4 inches, but the center is near the glabella, not the condyles.
110 mm (4 inches) and the symphysis belong to Bonwill's triangle, which is a triangle, not a sphere.
The radius is about 4 inches, centered near the glabella, not 6 inches at the coronoid processes.

stem: In a normal buccolingual relationship, which cusps occlude in the opposing central fossa line?
choices: Maxillary lingual cusps and mandibular buccal cusps
Maxillary buccal cusps and mandibular lingual cusps
Maxillary buccal cusps and mandibular buccal cusps
Maxillary lingual cusps and mandibular lingual cusps
ex: Normal: maxillary LINGUAL (palatal) cusps sit in the mandibular central fossa line and mandibular BUCCAL cusps sit in the maxillary central fossa line. These are the centric (supporting, holding, "stamp") cusps. The reverse pair (maxillary buccal + mandibular lingual) is a crossbite.
cue: Centric cusps are the ones toward the tongue on top and toward the cheek on the bottom: "upper lingual, lower buccal."
why: In a normal relationship the maxillary lingual and mandibular buccal cusps are the centric cusps sitting in the opposing central fossa lines.
Maxillary buccal and mandibular lingual cusps in the opposing fossae is a posterior crossbite.
Maxillary buccal cusps are non-centric in a normal relationship; they overlap the mandibular teeth on the outside.
Mandibular lingual cusps are non-centric in a normal relationship; only the maxillary lingual cusps are centric here.

stem: In reverse articulation (posterior crossbite), which cusps sit in the opposing central fossae?
choices: Maxillary buccal cusps and mandibular lingual cusps
Maxillary lingual cusps and mandibular buccal cusps
Only the mandibular buccal cusps
Only the maxillary lingual cusps
ex: Crossbite flips the buccolingual relationship: maxillary buccal cusps go into the mandibular central fossae and mandibular lingual cusps into the maxillary central fossae. It comes from a discrepancy in arch size or eruption pattern.
why: Crossbite flips the relationship: maxillary buccal cusps go into mandibular fossae and mandibular lingual cusps into maxillary fossae.
Maxillary lingual and mandibular buccal cusps in the opposing fossae is the normal relationship, not a crossbite.
In a crossbite the mandibular buccal cusps are no longer the centric cusps; the lingual ones take their place.
In a crossbite the maxillary buccal cusps, not the lingual ones, sit in the opposing central fossae.

stem: How did Dr. Givan describe posterior crossbite (reverse articulation)?
choices: It is functionally fine; implant crowns often must be built in crossbite
It always needs orthodontic correction before any posterior restoration is placed
It causes TMD and should be equilibrated
It only occurs in Class III patients
ex: "There is absolutely functionally no problem with this." It reflects growth and arch size. After bone loss, most posterior implant restorations have to be made in crossbite, "otherwise we end up with weird-shaped crowns that are not functional." Design matters, though: in a crossbite area it is easy to catch the cheek.
why: Dr. Givan says crossbite is functionally fine, and after bone loss posterior implant crowns often must be made in crossbite.
Crossbite reflects growth and arch size and is functionally fine; it does not need orthodontics before restoring.
Crossbite is not described as a cause of TMD or a reason for equilibration; it is functionally no problem.
Posterior crossbite comes from arch size or eruption differences and is not limited to Class III patients.

stem: Average arch lengths quoted in lecture were about:
choices: Maxillary 128 mm, mandibular 126 mm
Maxillary 126 mm, mandibular 128 mm
Maxillary 110 mm, mandibular 100 mm
Maxillary 140 mm, mandibular 120 mm
ex: Maxillary arch length and width are greater than mandibular (about 128 vs 126 mm, with great variation). Arch length runs from the distal of the last tooth on one side to the distal of the last tooth on the other, through the contact areas. The point: the difference is small.
why: Maxillary arch length is slightly greater than mandibular, about 128 vs 126 mm, with a lot of variation.
This reverses them. The maxillary arch is the larger one, about 128 mm vs 126 mm.
These numbers are too small and the gap too large; the two arches differ by only about 2 mm.
These overstate the difference; the lecture figures are about 128 and 126 mm.

stem: Arch length is measured:
choices: From the distal of the last tooth on one side to the distal of the last tooth on the other, through the contact areas
From the mesial of one first molar to the mesial of the other, across the palate
From the incisal point straight back to a line joining the distal surfaces of the second molars on each side of the arch
Around the buccal cusp tips from one canine to the other
ex: Arch length: distal of the last tooth on one side, through the contact areas, to the distal of the last tooth on the other side. Arch width is the distance across the arch. Both are greater in the maxilla.
why: Arch length runs from the distal of the last tooth on one side, through the contacts, to the distal of the last tooth on the other.
Arch length includes all the teeth, running distal to distal, not mesial of one first molar to the other across the palate.
A straight line back from the incisal point is a depth measurement, not arch length, which follows the contacts around the arch.
Arch length includes all the teeth to the last molar, not just canine to canine around the cusp tips.

stem: The occlusal table (between the buccal and lingual cusp tips) makes up about what share of a posterior tooth's buccolingual width?
ex: The occlusal table is about 50-60% of the buccolingual extension, where most of the chewing work happens. 1/3 is the width of a centric cusp; 1/6 the width of a non-centric cusp.
why: The occlusal table is about 50-60% of the buccolingual width, where most chewing work happens.
20-30% is too small; the occlusal table is about half or more of the buccolingual width.
One-third is the width of a centric cusp, not the occlusal table.
75-85% is too large; the occlusal table is about 50-60% of the buccolingual width.

stem: Posterior proximal contacts sit buccal to the central fossa line. What does that do for chewing?
choices: Lingual embrasures are larger, so food is preferentially returned toward the tongue
Buccal embrasures are larger, so food is pushed out into the vestibule for the cheek to clear
It keeps the marginal ridges level for cusp-fossa contact
It lets the non-centric cusps carry the vertical dimension
ex: Because contacts are buccal to the CF line, lingual embrasures are larger than buccal ones. Food falls back toward the tongue, "where you want it to go." The tongue sweeps food that goes buccal back onto the table, working with the buccinator.
why: Contacts sit buccal to the central fossa line, so lingual embrasures are larger and food returns toward the tongue.
The buccal embrasures are the smaller ones, because the contacts sit buccal to the central fossa line.
Embrasure size affects where food goes, not the level of the marginal ridges.
Vertical dimension is held by the centric cusps, and this has nothing to do with embrasure size.

stem: Compared with non-centric cusps, centric cusps are:
choices: Broad and rounded, about 1/3 of the buccolingual width
Sharp with definite tips, about 1/6 of the buccolingual width
Shorter, so they avoid eccentric interferences
Responsible mainly for keeping the cheek out of the way
ex: Centric (supporting) cusps are broad and rounded, about 1/3 of the B-L width; they maintain the vertical dimension of occlusion and do the final grinding contact. Non-centric cusps are sharper, about 1/6 of the width, about "half the size."
why: Centric cusps are broad and rounded, about 1/3 of the buccolingual width, and hold the vertical dimension.
Sharp cusps about 1/6 of the width describe the non-centric cusps.
Centric cusps are the broad supporting cusps; being shorter to avoid interferences is not what defines them.
Keeping the cheek and tongue out of the way is a job of the non-centric cusps.

stem: All of the following describe non-centric cusps EXCEPT:
choices: They maintain the vertical dimension of occlusion
They are relatively sharp, about 1/6 of the buccolingual width
They help keep the bolus on the occlusal table
They minimize cheek and tongue impingement
ex: Maintaining VDO is the job of the CENTRIC cusps. Non-centric (shearing or guiding) cusps are sharp, near-contact by design (functional outer aspect), shear food, minimize tissue impingement and hold the bolus on the table.
why: This is the false statement: maintaining the vertical dimension of occlusion is the job of the centric cusps.
Non-centric cusps are relatively sharp and about 1/6 of the buccolingual width, about half the size of centric cusps.
Non-centric cusps do help hold the bolus on the occlusal table.
Non-centric cusps do minimize cheek and tongue impingement.

stem: Non-centric cusps are sometimes called "shearing" cusps because:
choices: Their functional outer aspect is ideally a near-contact area that shears food
They make heavy contact in MIP and crush the bolus against the opposing central fossa
They guide the mandible into centric relation
They carry the occlusal load down the long axis
ex: The functional outer aspect of a non-centric cusp is ideally a near-contact area (no true contact) that shears food. The base of the cusp may get some grinding contact in full intercuspation, which is why they are also called "guiding" cusps.
why: Their functional outer aspect is ideally a near-contact area, with no true contact, which shears food.
Heavy MIP contact crushing food in the opposing central fossa describes centric (supporting) cusps.
Non-centric cusps do not guide the mandible into centric relation; CR is a joint position independent of the teeth.
Carrying the load down the long axis is the job of the centric (supporting) cusps.

stem: Maximum intercuspation (MIP, MICP, ICP) is defined as:
choices: The complete intercuspation of the opposing teeth independent of condylar position
The tooth contact that occurs when the condyles are fully seated in centric relation
The position of least EMG activity of the elevator muscles
The most retruded tooth contact the mandible can reach
ex: MIP is a tooth-to-tooth relationship, set by muscle engrams to give dental stability, regardless of where the condyles are. The contact of teeth with the condyles seated is centric occlusion (CO); least EMG activity is the clinical rest position.
why: MIP is complete intercuspation of the teeth, a tooth-to-tooth position set by muscle engrams, regardless of where the condyles are.
Tooth contact with the condyles seated in CR is centric occlusion (CO), not MIP.
Least EMG activity of the elevator muscles defines the clinical rest position.
MIP is set by maximum intercuspation of the teeth, not by the most retruded contact.

stem: Which statement about MIP matches Dr. Givan's lecture?
choices: It is neuromuscularly determined and changes whenever the teeth or restorations change
It is fixed once growth is complete, so it is always a safe and stable place to restore teeth
It is the same as centric occlusion in about 90% of people
It is set by the seated condyle, so it never shifts
ex: "MIP is a constantly updated position... not going to be the same this year as it was last year." Every restoration, tooth movement or loss changes it. That is why "I'll just keep restoring to MIP" can get you into trouble. CO is the structurally determined one; MIP and CO DIFFER in about 90% of people.
cue: MIP Moves; CO (condyle) stays.
why: MIP is neuromuscularly determined and constantly updated, so it changes with every restoration, tooth movement or loss.
MIP keeps changing after growth, which is why always restoring to MIP can get you into trouble.
MIP and CO differ in about 90% of people; they coincide in only about 10%.
The seated condyle sets centric occlusion. MIP is set by the teeth and muscles and shifts over time.

stem: Centric occlusion (CO), as Dr. Givan uses it on exams, means:
choices: The tooth contact when the mandible is in centric relation
The complete intercuspation of the teeth regardless of jaw position
The most stable tooth contact the patient can find
The denture tooth contact at the patient's vertical dimension of rest
ex: "If I use the term centric occlusion, this is what I mean": the contact of the teeth with the joints seated (CR). It is NOT a synonym for MIP, even though many people misuse it that way. "Centric" means the joint is centered; it has nothing to do with the teeth.
cue: "Centric" = the joint is centered. Hear "centric," think "joint."
why: Dr. Givan uses centric occlusion to mean the tooth contact with the mandible in centric relation (joints seated).
Complete intercuspation regardless of jaw position is MIP, which is often misused as a synonym for CO.
The most stable contact the patient can find is MIP; CO is defined by the seated joint.
CO is not tied to dentures or vertical dimension of rest; it is the tooth contact in centric relation.

stem: Dr. Givan's bottom line: MIP is neuromuscularly determined, while centric occlusion is:
choices: Structurally determined (by the seated joint)
Also neuromuscularly determined
Determined by the anterior guidance
Determined by the vertical dimension of rest
ex: "MIP is neuromuscularly determined. Centric occlusion is structurally determined. They're not the same." CO stays the same as long as the joint has no pathology; MIP adapts every time the occlusion changes.
why: Centric occlusion is structurally determined by the seated joint and stays the same if the joint has no pathology.
MIP is the neuromuscularly determined one; CO is set by joint structure.
Anterior guidance affects excursive movements, not where the teeth meet with the condyles seated.
Vertical dimension of rest is a muscle rest measure and does not define centric occlusion.

stem: About what share of people have a slide between the CO contact and MIP, and how large is it on average?
choices: About 90%; 1.25 ± 1 mm
About 10%; 1.25 ± 1 mm
About 50%; 3-5 mm
About 90%; 2-6 mm
ex: About 90% have a CO-MIP slide averaging 1.25 ± 1 mm. Only about 10% have CO and MIP coincident; most fully rehabilitated patients are built into that 10% on purpose. 2-6 mm is the freeway space; 3-5 mm is normal vertical overlap.
why: About 90% of people have a CO-to-MIP slide, averaging 1.25 ± 1 mm.
The slide size is right, but about 90% have one; only about 10% have CO and MIP coincident.
About half and 3-5 mm are both wrong; 3-5 mm is the normal vertical overlap of the incisors.
About 90% is right, but 2-6 mm is the freeway space; the slide averages 1.25 ± 1 mm.

stem: Which CO-to-MIP slide tends to be more problematic?
choices: A slide that deviates to the left or right
A straight anterior slide of about 1 mm
No slide at all (CO coincident with MIP)
A slide that occurs only in the supine position
ex: Handout: "A slide that deviates to the left or right tends to be more problematic." A small straight slide is common (90% of people). CO coincident with MIP is the goal of a rehabilitation, not a problem.
why: The handout says a slide that deviates to the left or right tends to be more problematic.
A small straight anterior slide is common, found in about 90% of people.
CO coincident with MIP is the goal of a full rehabilitation, not a problem.
The slide is between the CO contact and MIP; a supine-only slide is not the problematic type in the handout.

stem: A patient has wear facets, a fractured cusp and a mobile premolar. Dr. Givan links findings like these to:
choices: Closing into unstable centric occlusion contacts
Excess freeway space, letting the teeth close too hard
A cusp-fossa occlusal scheme
Canine guidance
ex: "CO is often unstable, and if closure without neuromuscular protection, then responsible for wear, fractures, mobility, etc." Our muscles seat the joints (especially in sleep), the teeth meet in CO, and in 90% of people that contact is unstable.
why: Closing without neuromuscular protection into unstable CO contacts is linked to wear, fractures and mobility.
Freeway space is the gap at rest between VDR and VDO; it does not cause the teeth to close too hard.
Cusp-fossa is the idealized contact scheme, not a cause of wear, fractures and mobility.
Canine guidance protects posterior teeth by discluding them in excursions; it does not cause this damage.

stem: Centric relation is the maxillomandibular relationship in which the condyles articulate with the:
choices: Thinnest avascular part of the discs, anterior-superior against the eminences
Thickest posterior band of their discs, in the rearmost, uppermost, midmost position
Retrodiscal tissues, in the most posterior position of the fossae
Articular eminences directly, with the discs displaced anteriorly
ex: CR: condyles against the thinnest avascular portion of the discs, the complex in the ANTERIOR-SUPERIOR position against the articular eminences. Independent of tooth contact, clinically discernable by directing the mandible superiorly and anteriorly, and restricted to pure rotation about the transverse horizontal axis. "Rearmost, uppermost, midmost" (RUM) is the old, incorrect gnathology idea.
cue: CR = Condyle Ready: up and forward, on the thin middle of the disc.
why: In CR the condyles sit against the thinnest avascular part of the discs, in the anterior-superior position against the eminences.
Rearmost, uppermost, midmost (RUM) is the old, incorrect gnathology idea; the thick posterior band is not where the condyle sits.
The condyle sitting on retrodiscal tissue in the back of the fossa is a displaced position, not CR.
An anteriorly displaced disc with the condyle on bone is joint pathology, not centric relation.

stem: All of the following are true of centric relation EXCEPT:
choices: It is determined by the tooth contacts in MIP
It is independent of tooth contact
It is clinically discernable when the mandible is directed superiorly and anteriorly
It is restricted to pure rotation about the transverse horizontal axis
ex: CR is a joint position, independent of the teeth. MIP is the tooth-determined position. Dr. Givan's short version: "it's where the condyle is seated in the joint. That's it." It is reproducible, which is why reorganized dentistry starts there.
why: This is the false statement: CR is a joint position independent of the teeth. MIP is the tooth-determined position.
True: centric relation is independent of tooth contact.
True: CR is clinically discernable when the mandible is directed superiorly and anteriorly.
True: CR is restricted to pure rotation about the transverse horizontal axis.

stem: How long are the teeth actually in contact in a typical day?
choices: About 17-18 minutes
About 2 hours
About 30 seconds
About 6 hours, mostly at night
ex: Teeth are apart most of our life: maxillary-mandibular contact is about 18 minutes a day (Lec3-2: 17.5 minutes, about 1,800 chewing strokes and 500 swallowing contacts). The rest of the time the muscles seat the condyles. Clenchers are the pathologic exception.
why: The teeth touch only about 17-18 minutes a day, from chewing strokes and swallowing contacts.
2 hours is far too long; the teeth are apart most of the day and touch for about 18 minutes.
30 seconds is far too short; chewing and swallowing add up to about 17-18 minutes a day.
6 hours would describe a heavy clencher; normally the teeth touch only about 18 minutes a day.

stem: About what share of the population falls into Angle Class II?
choices: About 25%
About 70%
About 5%
About 50%
ex: From lecture and the slides: Class I about 70%, Class II about 25% ("very common"), Class III about 5% ("much rarer").
why: Class II is very common, about 25% of the population.
About 70% is the share for Class I.
About 5% is the share for Class III, which is much rarer.
Half is too high; Class I is about 70%, Class II about 25% and Class III about 5%.

stem: Class II (distoclusion) is the dental relationship in which:
choices: The mandibular first molar is distal to the maxillary first molar
The mandibular first molar is mesial to the maxillary first molar
The molars interdigitate normally but there is crowding elsewhere
One side is distal and the other side mesial
ex: Class II: the mandibular arch is posterior to the maxillary arch in one or both lateral segments; the mandibular first molar is distal to the maxillary first molar. Mesial = Class III; normal molars + crowding = Class I malocclusion; one side each way = the retired Class IV.
why: In Class II the mandibular arch is posterior: the mandibular first molar is distal to the maxillary first molar.
A mandibular first molar mesial to the maxillary first molar is Class III (mesioclusion).
Normal molar interdigitation with crowding elsewhere is a Class I malocclusion.
One side distal and the other mesial is the retired Angle Class IV.

stem: Which feature usually comes with Angle Class III (mesioclusion)?
choices: Mandibular incisors in anterior crossbite
Retruded maxillary central incisors with flared laterals
A narrow maxillary arch with protruding incisors
A deep vertical overlap of the incisors
ex: Class III: the mandibular arch is anterior, the mandibular first molar mesial to the maxillary first molar, and the mandibular incisors are usually in anterior crossbite (or edge to edge). The other choices are Class II division 2, division 1 and deep bite.
why: In Class III the mandible is anterior, so the mandibular incisors are usually in anterior crossbite or edge to edge.
Retruded centrals with flared laterals describe Class II division 2.
A narrow maxillary arch with protruding incisors describes Class II division 1.
A deep vertical overlap goes with Class II division 2, not Class III.

stem: Class II division 1 is characterized by:
choices: A narrow maxillary arch and protruding maxillary incisors
Retruded maxillary centrals, labially malposed laterals and excessive vertical overlap
Mandibular incisors in anterior crossbite
Distal occlusion on one side and mesial on the other
ex: Division 1: bilateral distal retrusion with a narrow maxillary arch and protruding (flared) maxillary incisors, often a smaller arch. Division 2: normal or square arch, retruded centrals, labially malposed laterals, deep vertical overlap; teeth "huddled very closely together."
why: Division 1 has a narrow maxillary arch with protruding (flared) maxillary incisors.
Retruded centrals, labially malposed laterals and deep overlap describe Class II division 2.
Mandibular incisors in anterior crossbite go with Class III.
Distal on one side and mesial on the other is the retired Class IV.

stem: Dr. Givan called which relationship "a very difficult one sometimes for us to restore," especially if vertical dimension must change?
choices: Class II division 2
Class II division 1
Class III edge-to-edge
Class I with cusp-marginal ridge contacts
ex: In Class II division 2 the arch sizes are almost the same and the teeth are tightly huddled with a deep overlap: "a very tight occlusion to work with. If I have to change vertical dimension, this becomes a very challenging one."
why: Class II division 2 has nearly equal arch sizes with tightly huddled teeth and deep overlap, hard to restore if VDO must change.
Division 1 has a narrow maxillary arch with flared incisors, not the tight, deep-bite occlusion he called hard to restore.
Class III edge to edge was not the relationship he singled out as very difficult to restore.
A Class I with cusp-marginal ridge contacts is the common adult arrangement, not a hard case to restore.

stem: The old Angle Class IV described:
choices: Distal occlusion on one side and mesial occlusion on the other
Bilateral mesial occlusion with an anterior open bite
A Class I molar relationship with severe crowding
A Class II molar relationship with an anterior crossbite
ex: Class IV (no longer used): distal occlusion in one lateral half of the arch and mesial in the other. Today each side is simply classified on its own.
why: The retired Class IV was distal occlusion in one lateral half and mesial in the other; today each side is classified on its own.
Bilateral mesial occlusion is Class III; an open bite is a separate finding, not Class IV.
Class I molars with severe crowding is a Class I malocclusion.
A Class II molar relationship is Class II whatever the anterior teeth do; Class IV meant different classes on each side.

stem: "Class I malocclusion" means:
choices: Normal molar interdigitation, but crowding or rotation of teeth elsewhere
The mandibular first molar is slightly distal to the maxillary first molar
An end-to-end molar relationship
Normal molars with an anterior crossbite from a large mandible
ex: Class I malocclusion: normal anteroposterior jaw relationship (correct molar interdigitation) but crowding and rotations elsewhere, a dental dysplasia or arch length deficiency. Dr. Givan jokes that orthodontists call it a malocclusion because then there is something to fix.
why: Class I malocclusion has normal molar interdigitation, with crowding, rotations or arch length problems elsewhere.
A mandibular first molar distal to the maxillary first molar is a Class II molar relationship.
An end-to-end molar relationship is not normal Class I interdigitation.
An anterior crossbite from a large mandible points to a Class III relationship.

stem: An exam question about which cusp contacts where does not mention an Angle class or a contact scheme. What should you assume?
choices: Class I with idealized cusp-fossa contacts
Class II with cusp-marginal ridge contacts
Class I with cusp-marginal ridge contacts
Whatever class the canines show in the picture, with cusp-tip to cusp-tip contacts
ex: Help sheet and lecture: "If it's not mentioned in a test question, it should be a Class I." And unless "cusp-marginal ridge" is specified (or drawn), assume idealized cusp-fossa. Read carefully first in case the class is implied indirectly.
cue: No class named? Class I, cusp-fossa.
why: If a question doesn't say otherwise, assume Class I with idealized cusp-fossa contacts.
Class II must be stated or implied; the default is Class I.
Cusp-marginal ridge is used only when the question specifies or draws it; the default is cusp-fossa.
The default is Class I cusp-fossa; cusp-tip to cusp-tip is not a default contact scheme.

stem: In the cusp-marginal ridge arrangement, the mandibular second premolar buccal cusp and the mandibular molar mesiobuccal cusps contact:
choices: The opposing occlusal embrasures (marginal ridges), a one-to-two tooth relationship
The opposing central fossae, a tooth-to-tooth relationship found in most natural dentitions
The opposing buccal grooves, a cusp-to-cusp relationship
The opposing cusp tips, a tripodized relationship
ex: Cusp-marginal ridge: these cusps land in the opposing embrasures in MIP: a one-to-two tooth relationship. Most adults have it, and it was waxed with Payne's technique. Dr. Givan often chooses it on purpose because multiple contacts help prevent supereruption.
why: In cusp-marginal ridge, these cusps land in the opposing embrasures (marginal ridges), a one-to-two tooth relationship.
Centric cusps in the opposing central fossae, tooth to tooth, is the cusp-fossa arrangement, which is rare naturally.
Buccal grooves receive cusp tips in the classic molar relationship; this is not how cusp-marginal ridge is defined.
Tripodized contacts belong to the idealized cusp-fossa scheme, not cusp-marginal ridge.

stem: Which is true of the cusp-fossa arrangement?
choices: It is a tooth-to-tooth relationship considered ideal but rarely found in natural teeth
Most adults have it, and it is the scheme Payne waxed
It requires the curve of Spee to be flat
It is a one-to-two tooth relationship with the centric cusps contacting marginal ridges
ex: Cusp-fossa: centric cusps sit in opposing fossae, tooth to tooth. Considered "ideal" but rarely found naturally; follows ideal Spee and Wilson curves; tripodized contacts; waxed with P.K. Thomas's technique. The majority of adults have cusp-marginal ridge instead.
why: Cusp-fossa is a tooth-to-tooth relationship considered ideal, but it is rarely found in natural teeth.
Most adults have cusp-marginal ridge, and that is the scheme waxed with Payne's technique; cusp-fossa used P.K. Thomas's.
Cusp-fossa follows ideal curves of Spee and Wilson; it does not need a flat curve of Spee.
One-to-two tooth contacts on marginal ridges describe the cusp-marginal ridge arrangement.

stem: What vertical overlap (overbite) does Dr. Givan describe as the most accepted ideal, and why do orthodontists accept less?
choices: About 3 mm (3-5 mm normal); orthodontists accept about 1 mm for brackets
About 1 mm; orthodontists accept 3-5 mm because it is more stable after treatment
About 6 mm; orthodontics accepts 3 mm to reduce wear
About 2-6 mm, the same range as freeway space
ex: Vertical overlap 3-5 mm is normal, 3 mm the most accepted. Orthodontics often accepts 1 mm to make room for the lower anterior brackets. The proper terms are vertical overlap (lay: overbite) and horizontal overlap (lay: overjet).
why: About 3 mm is the most accepted ideal (3-5 mm normal); orthodontists often accept about 1 mm to make room for lower brackets.
This reverses the numbers: 3 mm is the ideal, and orthodontics accepts about 1 mm for bracket room.
6 mm is above the 3-5 mm normal range, and orthodontists accept less overlap, not 3 mm, for brackets.
2-6 mm is the freeway space, a different measurement from vertical overlap.

stem: The proper term for "overjet" is:
choices: Horizontal overlap
Vertical overlap
Anterior guidance
Incisal guidance
ex: Horizontal overlap = overjet; vertical overlap = overbite. Together they set the anterior guidance. Dr. Givan: overjet "makes no real sense at all," but you need to know both words. ("Underbite" isn't a recognized term.)
why: Overjet is the lay term for horizontal overlap.
Vertical overlap is the proper term for overbite, not overjet.
Anterior guidance is set by vertical and horizontal overlap together; it is not another name for overjet.
Incisal guidance is the guiding influence of the incisors in movement, not the overjet measurement itself.

stem: The proper name for an anterior open bite is:
choices: Anterior open occlusal relationship
Anterior reverse articulation (crossbite)
Class II division 1
Negative vertical overlap
ex: Anterior open occlusal relationship: the lack of anterior tooth contact in any occluding position of the posterior teeth. "A bite is a verb, like I bite an apple." With no anterior contact, the functional contacts fall on posterior teeth.
why: The proper term is anterior open occlusal relationship: no anterior contact in any posterior occluding position.
Reverse articulation (crossbite) means the cusps are flipped, not that the anterior teeth fail to meet.
Class II division 1 is a molar and incisor relationship with flared maxillary incisors, not an open bite.
Negative vertical overlap is not the term Dr. Givan uses; the proper name is anterior open occlusal relationship.

stem: What is the primary determinant of anterior guidance?
choices: The lingual (palatal) morphology of the maxillary anterior teeth
The steepness of the articular eminence
The height of the posterior cusps
The curve of Spee
ex: Anterior guidance: the guiding inclines of the anterior teeth, "particularly the shape of the lingual morphology or the palatal morphology of the maxillary incisor." The eminence is the condylar (posterior) guidance.
why: Anterior guidance comes mainly from the lingual (palatal) morphology of the maxillary anterior teeth.
The steepness of the articular eminence is the condylar (posterior) guidance.
Posterior cusp height must fit within the guidance; it does not determine anterior guidance.
The curve of Spee affects how posterior teeth clear, not what sets anterior guidance.

stem: The temporomandibular joint is described as a:
choices: Diarthrodial, bilateral ginglymus (ginglymoarthrodial) joint
Synarthrodial joint with a fibrous union
Ball-and-socket joint like the hip
Purely hinging joint like the elbow
ex: The TMJ both hinges (ginglymus) and slides (arthrodial): a ginglymoarthrodial joint, bilateral because one bone, the mandible, articulates at two joints. Dr. Givan thinks it is the most complicated joint in the body.
why: The TMJ both hinges and slides, so it is a diarthrodial, bilateral ginglymoarthrodial joint.
The TMJ is a freely movable synovial joint, not a synarthrodial joint with a fibrous union.
The TMJ is not a ball-and-socket joint; it hinges and also translates along the eminence.
A pure hinge leaves out the gliding (arthrodial) movement the TMJ also makes.

stem: An eccentric mandibular movement is:
choices: Any movement away from the intercuspal position
Any movement that keeps the condyles seated in CR
Only the lateral (working) movements
Only movements that keep posterior teeth in contact
ex: Eccentric = any movement away from the intercuspal (or seated) position: protrusive, retrusive, laterotrusive (working) and mediotrusive (non-working).
why: Eccentric means any movement away from the intercuspal position: protrusive, retrusive, working or non-working.
Movements that keep the condyles seated are hinge movements about CR, not the definition of eccentric.
Lateral (working) movements are only one kind of eccentric movement; protrusion and retrusion count too.
Eccentric movements are defined by moving away from intercuspation, whether or not posterior teeth stay in contact.

stem: In a protrusive movement, posterior teeth that fail to disclude contact on which inclines?
choices: Distal inclines of the maxillary teeth and mesial inclines of the mandibular teeth
Mesial inclines of the maxillary teeth and distal inclines of the mandibular teeth
Buccal inclines of the maxillary teeth and lingual inclines of the mandibular teeth
Lingual inclines of both arches
ex: As the mandible slides forward, the mandibular teeth move mesially under the maxillary teeth, so the mesial inclines of mandibular cusps run into the distal inclines of maxillary cusps. Dr. Givan: look at which arch the question is about; the contacts are relative to the motion of the mandible.
cue: Protrusion pushes Mandibular Mesial into Maxillary distal: the lower teeth lead with their mesial faces.
why: In protrusion, mandibular teeth move mesially, so mandibular mesial inclines run into maxillary distal inclines.
This reverses the inclines. The mandible moves forward, so its mesial inclines meet the maxillary distal inclines.
Buccal and lingual inclines collide in lateral movements, not straight protrusion.
Protrusive contacts are on mesial and distal inclines, not the lingual inclines of both arches.

stem: Christensen's phenomenon is:
choices: The space between posterior teeth in protrusion as the condyle descends the eminence
The shift of the non-working condyle toward the midline during a lateral movement of the mandible
The slide from the CO contact forward into MIP
The opening of the bite when the patient sits upright
ex: As the condyle slides down the eminence in protrusion, the back of the mandible drops and the posterior teeth separate. Dr. Givan: Christensen is remembered because he proposed that a protrusive record between those teeth reveals the angle of the eminence. The medial shift in lateral movement is mandibular lateral translation (Balkwill, Bennett).
why: Christensen's phenomenon is the space that opens between posterior teeth in protrusion as the condyle descends the eminence.
The medial shift of the mandible in a lateral movement is mandibular lateral translation (Bennett movement).
The slide from CO into MIP is the CO-MIP slide, not Christensen's phenomenon.
Christensen's phenomenon is about protrusion, not a change with posture.

stem: During a right working (laterotrusive) movement, what are the condyles doing?
choices: The right condyle mostly rotates; the left condyle orbits forward and down the eminence
The right condyle translates forward and down; the left condyle rotates in place in the fossa
Both condyles rotate without translating
Both condyles translate equally forward
ex: The working-side condyle mostly rotates (with possible lateral translation); the non-working (balancing) condyle orbits: forward, down and medially along the eminence. That orbiting is where the old term came from.
why: The working (right) condyle mostly rotates; the non-working (left) condyle orbits forward, down and medially.
This reverses the sides. The non-working condyle is the one that translates down the eminence.
In a lateral movement the non-working condyle must translate, so both cannot just rotate.
Equal forward translation of both condyles is straight protrusion, not a lateral movement.

stem: Mediotrusion is another name for which side of a lateral movement?
choices: The non-working (balancing) side
The working side
The protrusive path
The retrusive path
ex: Mediotrusion = moving toward the midline = non-working = balancing (orbiting condyle). Laterotrusion = moving away from the midline = working. "Balancing" came from dentures, where contact on that side kept the denture from tipping.
why: Mediotrusion means moving toward the midline: the non-working, balancing side with the orbiting condyle.
The working side moves away from the midline, which is laterotrusion.
Protrusion is a straight forward movement, not one side of a lateral movement.
Retrusion is a backward movement, not one side of a lateral movement.

stem: Canine guidance is:
choices: Mutually protected articulation in which the canines disengage the posterior teeth in excursions
Simultaneous contact of several teeth on the working side to share load
Bilateral contact of all the teeth in every excursion, to keep a complete denture stable on its ridges
Guidance provided by the condyle descending the articular eminence
ex: Canine guidance (canine-protected articulation): the vertical and horizontal overlap of the canines disengages the posterior teeth in excursive movements. Canines have buttressing bone and proprioception to take that load. Sharing it across several teeth is group function; all-teeth contact is balanced (denture) occlusion.
why: In canine guidance, the canines' overlap disengages the posterior teeth in excursions, a mutually protected articulation.
Several working-side teeth sharing the load is group function.
Bilateral contact of all teeth in every excursion is balanced occlusion, used for complete dentures.
Guidance from the condyle on the eminence is condylar guidance, not canine guidance.

stem: When is group function sometimes desired instead of canine guidance?
choices: When the canine has compromised periodontal support and the load should be shared
When the patient has a deep vertical overlap
When the posterior teeth have tall cusps
When restoring complete dentures, where every tooth must contact in balanced occlusion
ex: Group function: several teeth (e.g., working contacts on #7-6-5) share the lateral load, desirable when the canine has compromised periodontal support, or when the canine is missing or is an implant (no proprioception). Today it means a few anterior teeth and maybe the first premolar, not every tooth.
why: Group function shares the lateral load when the canine has compromised periodontal support, or is missing or an implant.
A deep vertical overlap makes canine guidance easier to get, so it is not a reason to choose group function.
Tall posterior cusps need more disclusion, which canine guidance provides, not group function.
Every tooth contacting in excursions is balanced (denture) occlusion, not group function.

stem: Which has more influence on separating the posterior teeth: anterior guidance or condylar guidance?
choices: Anterior guidance, because the closer determinant has the greater impact
Condylar guidance, because the eminence is steeper than the incisors
They are always equal
Neither; cusp height alone determines disclusion
ex: "The closest determinant has the greatest impact. It's just geometry." Good anterior guidance does more for the posterior teeth than the condyles, which are far away. The catch: many patients have little overlap, leaving only condylar guidance.
why: The closer determinant has the greater impact, so anterior guidance does more to separate the posterior teeth.
Condylar guidance is farther from the posterior teeth than the anterior guidance, so its effect there is smaller.
They are not equal; the closer determinant, anterior guidance, has more effect on the posterior teeth.
Cusp height has to work within both guidances; it does not decide disclusion by itself.

stem: Mutually protected articulation means:
choices: Posteriors take the force in MIP; anteriors disengage the posteriors in every excursion
All teeth contact simultaneously in MIP and keep contacting in every excursion to share the load
Canines and premolars share all excursive contacts equally
The condyles protect the teeth by staying seated in all movements
ex: Front teeth protect the back teeth by discluding them in excursions; back teeth ("big old bulky teeth") protect the front teeth by taking the force in MIP. Anterior teeth handle off-axis loads better and see less force.
why: Posterior teeth take the force in MIP, and anterior teeth disclude the posteriors in every excursion.
Simultaneous contact of all teeth in every excursion is balanced occlusion, used for dentures.
Shared canine and premolar contacts in excursions describe group function.
Mutually protected refers to the teeth protecting each other, not the condyles staying seated.

stem: Select every item on Dr. Givan's list of goals for ideal (modern) occlusion.
choices: Equal, simultaneous, stable centric contacts
Occlusal forces directed down the long axes
Elimination of balancing (mediotrusive) contacts
Bilateral posterior contacts in all excursions
Posterior contacts in protrusion to share load
ex: The goals: stable simultaneous centric contacts, force along the long axis, no balancing contacts, canine disclusion or anterior group function, i.e. mutually protected occlusion. Bilateral excursive contact is denture (balanced) occlusion; posterior protrusive contacts are what we try to eliminate. "I'll probably only show it to you 20 million times before you graduate."
why: Equal, simultaneous, stable centric contacts are on the list of goals for ideal occlusion.
Directing occlusal forces down the long axes of the teeth is one of the goals.
Eliminating balancing (mediotrusive) contacts is one of the goals.
Bilateral posterior contacts in all excursions is balanced occlusion for dentures, not the modern goal for natural teeth.
Posterior contacts in protrusion are what the modern scheme tries to eliminate; anterior teeth should disclude them.

stem: In Thielmann's formula, balanced occlusion = (CG × AG) / (CH × CC × PO). What does CC stand for?
choices: Compensating curvature
Condylar curvature
Cusp contact
Centric contact
ex: CG condylar guidance, AG anterior guidance, CH cusp height, CC compensating curvature (in natural teeth, the analog is the curves of Spee and Wilson), PO plane of occlusion. The factors are interrelated: change one and the others must change to keep balance.
why: CC is compensating curvature; in natural teeth the curves of Spee and Wilson are its analog.
Condylar guidance is CG; there is no condylar curvature term in the formula.
Cusp contact is not a factor; the cusp factor is CH, cusp height.
Centric contact is not a factor in Thielmann's formula.

stem: Which is Thielmann's formula for balanced occlusion?
choices: (CG × AG) / (CH × CC × PO)
(CH × CC × PO) / (CG × AG)
(CG × CH) / (AG × CC × PO)
(CG × AG × PO) / (CH × CC)
ex: Balanced occlusion = (condylar guidance × anterior guidance) / (cusp height × compensating curvature × plane of occlusion). The two guidances go on top; the three things you shape on the teeth go below. Change one factor and the others must change to keep the balance.
cue: The two Guidances Go on top; Cusp height, Compensating curve and Plane of occlusion below.
why: Condylar guidance times anterior guidance goes on top; cusp height, compensating curvature and plane of occlusion go below.
This flips the formula; the two guidances belong in the numerator.
Cusp height belongs below with the factors you shape on the teeth, and anterior guidance belongs on top.
Plane of occlusion belongs in the denominator with cusp height and compensating curvature.

stem: If the condylar guidance (eminence) is steeper, the posterior cusps can be:
choices: Taller
Shorter
Unchanged
Flattened to zero
ex: Steeper condylar guidance drops the back of the mandible more in protrusion, so taller posterior cusps can still clear. Dr. Givan: you can't change a patient's condylar guidance without surgery, but it tells you how cuspy your crowns can be.
why: A steeper eminence drops the back of the mandible more in protrusion, so posterior cusps can be taller.
Shorter cusps go with a flatter condylar guidance, not a steeper one.
Condylar guidance does affect cusp height; steeper guidance allows taller cusps.
Flattened cusps are needed when there is little guidance, not when the eminence is steep.

stem: Increasing the vertical overlap of the anterior teeth allows the posterior cusps to be:
choices: Taller
Shorter
Unchanged
More rounded but the same height
ex: More vertical overlap = steeper anterior guidance = better disclusion, so posterior cusps can be taller. More HORIZONTAL overlap does the opposite (shorter cusps).
why: More vertical overlap makes the anterior guidance steeper, so posterior teeth separate more and cusps can be taller.
Shorter cusps go with more horizontal overlap, not more vertical overlap.
Vertical overlap does change how much the posterior teeth separate, so cusp height is affected.
Steeper anterior guidance allows taller cusps, not just a change in shape at the same height.

stem: Increasing the horizontal overlap (overjet) means the posterior cusps must be:
choices: Shorter
Taller
Unchanged
Steeper on their mesial inclines only
ex: More horizontal overlap flattens the anterior guidance, so less separation of posterior teeth, so shorter cusps to avoid interferences. Dr. Givan's example: orthodontically flaring the arch increases overjet, which affects how posterior teeth can be shaped.
why: More horizontal overlap flattens the anterior guidance, so posterior teeth separate less and cusps must be shorter.
Taller cusps go with more vertical overlap, not more horizontal overlap.
Horizontal overlap does change the anterior guidance, so cusp height is affected.
The effect is on overall cusp height, not only on mesial inclines.

stem: The more parallel the plane of occlusion is to the condylar guidance, the posterior cusps must be:
choices: Shorter
Taller
Unchanged
Shorter only in group function
ex: When the occlusal plane parallels the condylar path, the teeth slide along rather than separate, so cusps must be shorter. A flatter plane relative to the condylar path allows taller cusps.
why: When the occlusal plane parallels the condylar path, the teeth slide along rather than separate, so cusps must be shorter.
Taller cusps are allowed when the plane is flatter relative to the condylar path, not more parallel to it.
The plane of occlusion is one of the factors that changes cusp height; it is not neutral.
The effect applies to posterior cusps in general, not only in group function.

stem: A more acute (sharper) curve of Spee means the most posterior cusps must be:
choices: Shorter
Taller
Unchanged
Taller only on the non-working side
ex: A more acute curve brings the posterior teeth up toward the path of the condyle, so the last molars must have shorter cusps to clear in protrusion. Do not mix it up with condylar guidance, where steeper means taller: a more acute curve of Spee is on the shorter side of the table.
why: A more acute curve brings the last molars up toward the condylar path, so their cusps must be shorter.
Taller is the trap from condylar guidance; a more acute curve of Spee calls for shorter cusps.
The curve of Spee does affect posterior cusp height, so it is not unchanged.
The curve of Spee is about protrusive clearance of the last molars, not only the non-working side.

stem: A greater immediate side shift (Bennett movement) means the posterior cusps must be:
choices: Shorter
Taller
Unchanged
Shorter on the working side only
ex: More lateral translation, and a more superior movement of the rotating condyle, both call for shorter posterior cusps. On the vertical determinants table, Bennett movement in every row means "shorter."
why: More lateral translation (side shift) means posterior cusps must be shorter to avoid interferences.
Taller cusps would collide more during a larger side shift; Bennett movement always calls for shorter cusps.
Side shift does affect posterior cusp height, so it is not unchanged.
Bennett movement calls for shorter cusps generally, not only on the working side.

stem: On the horizontal determinants of ridge and groove direction, increasing the intercondylar distance does what to the angle between the laterotrusive and mediotrusive paths?
choices: Decreases it
Increases it
No effect
Increases it on the working side only
ex: Intercondylar distance is the odd one out: more distance DECREASES the angle. Increasing the distance from the rotating condyle, the distance from the midsagittal plane, or the Bennett movement all INCREASE it. Why it matters: a small articulator moves on different arcs than your patient.
cue: Wider condyles, narrower angle: intercondylar distance is the only "decrease."
why: Intercondylar distance is the odd one out: more distance decreases the angle between the paths.
Increasing intercondylar distance decreases the angle; the other horizontal determinants are the ones that increase it.
Intercondylar distance does change the arcs the cusps travel, so it is not without effect.
The effect is a decrease of the angle, not an increase limited to the working side.

stem: Each of the following increases the angle between a cusp's laterotrusive and mediotrusive paths EXCEPT a greater:
choices: Intercondylar distance
Distance from the rotating condyle
Distance from the midsagittal plane
Bennett movement
ex: Increased intercondylar distance decreases the angle; the other three increase it. These are the horizontal determinants of ridge and groove direction: the cusps of one tooth must "escape" the opposing tooth through ridges and grooves.
why: This is the exception: a greater intercondylar distance decreases the angle between the paths.
A greater distance from the rotating condyle does increase the angle.
A greater distance from the midsagittal plane does increase the angle.
More Bennett movement does increase the angle.

stem: The vertical dimension of occlusion (VDO) is:
choices: The distance between two points when the occluding members are in contact
The distance between two facial points with the mandible at physiologic rest
The space between the teeth at rest
The opening at which the condyles begin to translate
ex: VDO: measured between two points (external landmarks clinically) with the teeth (or rims) in contact; supports facial height. VDR is the same measure at physiologic rest. VDR minus VDO = freeway (interocclusal rest) space.
why: VDO is the distance between two points with the teeth or occlusion rims in contact.
The same measure with the mandible at physiologic rest is the vertical dimension of rest (VDR).
The space between the teeth at rest is the freeway (interocclusal rest) space, VDR minus VDO.
VDO is a facial height measure with the teeth together, not the opening where translation starts.

stem: Interocclusal rest (freeway) space is calculated as ___ and is usually ___.
choices: VDR minus VDO; 2-6 mm
VDO minus VDR; 2-6 mm
VDR minus VDO; 20-25 mm
VDO plus VDR; 1-2 mm
ex: Freeway space = VDR - VDO, usually 2-6 mm in a dentate patient. "Is two better than six? No. Is six better than two? No." The 20-25 mm figure is pure rotation; 1-2 mm is the closest speaking space.
why: Freeway space is VDR minus VDO, usually 2-6 mm in a dentate patient.
VDR is the larger measure, so freeway space is VDR minus VDO, not the reverse.
The calculation is right, but 20-25 mm is the opening from pure rotation, not freeway space.
The two are subtracted, not added, and 1-2 mm is the closest speaking space.

stem: Posterior overclosure (old term: posterior bite collapse) is:
choices: Loss of occluding vertical dimension from loss or drifting of posterior teeth
Excess vertical dimension from posterior crowns built too tall, which props the bite open
Collapse of the curve of Wilson in complete dentures
Closure past MIP during a clench
ex: Posterior overclosure: the loss of occluding vertical dimension as posterior teeth are lost or drift; supereruption and tipping follow, so interferences and unhealthy loading. Treating it usually starts with correcting the plane of occlusion (molar uprighting, crown and bridge).
why: Posterior overclosure is loss of occluding vertical dimension as posterior teeth are lost or drift.
Posterior crowns built too tall increase vertical dimension, the opposite of overclosure.
The curve of Wilson in dentures is a setup feature; overclosure is about losing posterior support.
Overclosure is not a clenching event; it is lost occluding vertical dimension from losing or drifting posterior teeth.

stem: With the condyles seated, about how far can the incisors open by pure rotation before translation must begin?
choices: 2-4 mm
5-6 mm
ex: Pure rotation in CR gives about 20-25 mm of incisal opening. After that the condyles must translate down and forward; rotation plus translation reaches 40-60 mm at maximum opening.
why: Pure rotation with the condyles seated gives about 20-25 mm of incisal opening before translation must begin.
2-4 mm is the postural position below MICP, not the limit of rotation.
40-60 mm is maximum opening with rotation plus translation.
5-6 mm is too small; pure rotation opens about 20-25 mm.

stem: Rotation combined with translation allows a maximum incisal opening of about:
ex: 40-60 mm at maximum opening ("great for that extra big sandwich"). 20-25 mm is pure rotation; 16-18 mm is a typical chewing stroke.
why: Rotation plus translation gives about 40-60 mm of maximum incisal opening.
20-25 mm is pure rotation alone, before the condyles translate.
16-18 mm is about a typical chewing stroke, not maximum opening.
80-100 mm is far beyond normal; maximum opening is about 40-60 mm.

stem: What limits the superior border of the envelope of motion, and what limits the anterior and posterior opening borders?
choices: Tooth contact limits the superior border; ligaments and joint anatomy limit the opening borders
Ligaments limit the superior border; tooth contact limits the opening borders
Muscles limit all borders equally
The articular disc limits the superior border, and the teeth limit the anterior and posterior borders
ex: The superior contact border is dictated by the teeth ("yay, we like them"). The anterior and posterior opening borders are dictated by ligaments and joint anatomy, which keep us away from damaging the osseous structures.
why: Tooth contact limits the superior border; ligaments and joint anatomy limit the anterior and posterior opening borders.
This reverses them: teeth set the superior border, ligaments set the opening borders.
Muscles move the mandible within the envelope, but the borders are set by teeth, ligaments and joint anatomy.
The superior border is set by the teeth, not the disc, and the opening borders by ligaments and joint anatomy.

stem: The envelope of motion that combines the border movements in the sagittal, horizontal and frontal planes is credited to:
choices: Posselt
Bennett
Christensen
Bonwill
ex: Ulf Posselt (ca. 1958): a 3-D envelope of every motion the mandible can make, usually shown in the sagittal plane. Bennett: lateral translation; Christensen: posterior separation in protrusion; Bonwill: the 4-inch triangle.
why: Posselt described the 3-D envelope combining border movements in all three planes, usually shown sagittally.
Bennett is linked to lateral translation (side shift) of the mandible.
Christensen is linked to the posterior teeth separating in protrusion.
Bonwill is linked to the 4-inch equilateral triangle from condyle to condyle to incisors.

stem: The postural position (PP) of the mandible is about ___ below MICP and is maintained by ___.
choices: 2-4 mm; a myotactic reflex
8 mm; least EMG activity
2-4 mm; complete muscle relaxation
20-25 mm; the TM ligament
ex: Postural position: about 2-4 mm below MICP, kept by a myotactic reflex against gravity, so the teeth can be brought into function immediately. It is NOT the clinical rest position (CRP), which is the least-EMG position about 8 mm inferior and 3 mm anterior.
cue: Posture is Poised (reflex at work, 2-4 mm); rest is Relaxed (least EMG, ~8 mm).
why: Postural position is about 2-4 mm below MICP, kept by a myotactic reflex against gravity.
8 mm and least EMG activity describe the clinical rest position, not postural position.
The distance is right, but postural position is kept by a myotactic reflex, not complete relaxation.
20-25 mm is the opening from pure rotation, and the TM ligament does not hold postural position.

stem: The clinical rest position (least EMG muscle activity) is located about:
choices: 8 mm inferior and 3 mm anterior
2-4 mm inferior to MICP
1.25 mm anterior to CO
At the end of pure rotation
ex: CRP is where gravity is in equilibrium with muscles and soft tissues, at the least EMG activity: about 8 mm inferior and 3 mm anterior. Postural position (2-4 mm) is often wrongly called the rest position.
why: The clinical rest position, at least EMG activity, is about 8 mm inferior and 3 mm anterior.
2-4 mm below MICP is the postural position, often wrongly called the rest position.
1.25 mm is the average CO-to-MIP slide, not the rest position.
The end of pure rotation is about 20-25 mm of opening, far beyond the rest position.

stem: You seat a crown with the patient supine and it feels fine; sitting upright, the patient says it hits hard. The likeliest explanation from lecture is:
choices: Head posture changed the path of closure, moving contacts anteriorly when upright
The cement layer expanded as it set
The patient's freeway space increased while upright
Upright posture seats the condyles more posteriorly than the reclined (supine) position does
ex: "REALLY IMPORTANT: The tooth contacts recorded when a patient is inclined in a supine position may significantly change (toward the anterior) when seated upright." Dr. Givan checks every restoration with the patient upright; about 20% feel a difference. Eating happens in the "alert feeding position," face down about 30°.
why: Head posture changes the path of closure; contacts recorded supine can move anteriorly when the patient sits upright.
Setting cement is not the explanation given; the change comes from posture shifting the contacts.
Freeway space is about the gap at rest, not why a crown hits hard when the teeth close upright.
Upright posture shifts contacts toward the anterior, not the condyles posteriorly.

stem: Where do functional movements like chewing and speech occur in the envelope of motion?
choices: Well inside it, in a small teardrop zone, rarely reaching a border except the superior one
Along the posterior opening border, with the condyles seated in centric relation throughout
Along the anterior opening border at maximum protrusion
At the clinical rest position, about 8 mm open
ex: We rarely function near a border, except the superior (tooth contact) border. Functional movement is a small teardrop shape below MICP, and most functional activities begin or end at MICP.
why: Chewing and speech happen well inside the envelope in a small teardrop zone, rarely at a border except tooth contact.
Function does not run along the posterior opening border; most of it begins or ends at MICP.
Maximum protrusion is a border position rarely reached in function.
The clinical rest position is a resting point, not where chewing and speech take place.

stem: "Mandibular lateral translation" (Bennett movement) refers to:
choices: The translatory mediolateral shift of the mandible toward the working side
The forward and downward rotation of the non-working condyle along the eminence
The vertical drop of the mandible in protrusion
The posterior slide from MIP into CO
ex: Mandibular lateral translation: in a working movement the mandible shifts sideways in the direction of the movement (many names: side shift, Bennett shift, immediate side shift...). It occurs with joint laxity and its clinical importance is "still somewhat controversial."
why: Bennett movement is the sideways (mediolateral) translation of the mandible toward the working side.
The non-working condyle moving forward and down the eminence is its orbiting path, not lateral translation.
The mandible dropping in protrusion relates to condylar guidance and Christensen's phenomenon.
The slide between MIP and CO is the CO-MIP slide, not Bennett movement.

stem: An immediate lateral translation is measured in millimeters. A progressive one is measured as:
choices: An angle (the Bennett angle)
A ratio of opening to protrusion
A percentage of the freeway space
A time in milliseconds
ex: Immediate side shift: a jump measured in mm. Progressive lateral translation along an irregular path is measured as an angle, still called the Bennett angle (the angle between the straight protrusive path and the non-working condyle's path in the horizontal plane).
why: Progressive lateral translation is measured as an angle, the Bennett angle.
A ratio of opening to protrusion is not how lateral translation is measured.
Freeway space is a vertical rest measurement unrelated to lateral translation.
Lateral translation is measured as a distance or an angle, not a time.

stem: On the articulator, Dr. Givan prefers the term "anterior guide pin" over "incisal pin" because:
choices: The canines are anterior teeth too, so the pin represents all anterior guidance
The pin touches the incisal edges directly
"Incisal pin" is the name used only on fully adjustable, programmable instruments
The pin is placed posterior to the incisors
ex: "Some people call it an incisal pin, but I think it's kind of rude to the canines because they're an anterior tooth, too." The pin rides on the anterior guide table; the centric latch holds the instrument on its hinge axis; the condylar elements represent the fossa and condyle.
