why: The canines are anterior teeth too, so the pin stands for all anterior guidance, not just the incisors.
The pin rides on the anterior guide table; it does not touch the incisal edges.
Incisal pin is a common name on many articulators, not a term reserved for fully adjustable ones.
The pin sits at the front of the articulator, anterior to the casts, not behind the incisors.

stem: On the semi-adjustable articulator, the centric latch:
choices: Locks the instrument on its transverse horizontal hinge axis
Sets the Bennett angle
Holds the anterior guide pin at a fixed opening
Records the protrusive path of the condyle
ex: The articulator is designed to keep you in the hinge-axis position; the centric latch locks it there (as if the casts were mounted in CR). Know the parts: upper and lower members, anterior guide pin and table, mounting plates, condylar elements (with an articulating fossa), centric latch.
why: The centric latch locks the articulator on its transverse horizontal hinge axis.
The Bennett angle is set on the condylar elements, not by the centric latch.
The anterior guide pin sets the vertical opening; the latch holds the hinge axis.
Protrusive paths are recorded with a protrusive record and set on the condylar guidance, not with the latch.

stem: Dr. Givan: "In occlusion, we're talking in the language of ___." Why?
choices: Microns; you can feel a hair (about 15-25 µm) between your teeth
Millimeters; restorations are adjusted with a perio probe
Degrees; cusp angles determine everything
Pounds; bite force decides the design
ex: A millimeter "is like the size of Mount Everest" in occlusion. A hair is about 15-25 µm and easy to feel; PDL receptors detect about 20 µm. "You have to be a micron dentist."
why: Occlusion is a matter of microns: a hair of about 15-25 µm is easy to feel, and the PDL senses about 20 µm.
A millimeter is huge in occlusion, like Mount Everest, and a perio probe is not an adjustment tool.
Cusp angles matter, but the point was that tiny micron-level differences can be felt.
Bite force was not the point; the lesson is how precise contacts must be, measured in microns.

stem: Class I, cusp-fossa. The mesiobuccal cusp of #31 contacts:
choices: The mesial fossa of #2
The distal fossa of #3
The central fossa of #3
The distal marginal ridge of #3
ex: The help sheet's own example. The fence post makes it look like a cusp-marginal ridge contact between #3 and #2, but exam questions are cusp-fossa. Anchor on the first molar: its posterior contact is the DB cusp of #30 on #3; moving back from there, the MB cusp of #31 must be in the mesial fossa of #2. Not the central fossa of #3: #3 takes its contacts from #30, so the next cusp back, on #31, has to reach the next maxillary molar, #2.
cue: Mandibular molar cusps go to the SAME-numbered maxillary molar (#30 on #3, #31 on #2): mesial cusp to mesial fossa.
why: Anchor on the first molar: #3 takes its contacts from #30, so the MB cusp of #31, one tooth back, reaches the mesial fossa of #2.
The distal area of #3 is where #30's DB cusp makes the posterior contact on #3, not #31.
#3's fossae take their contacts from #30; #31 is one tooth back and lands on #2.
A marginal ridge contact is the cusp-marginal ridge reading the fence post suggests; questions assume cusp-fossa.

stem: Class I, cusp-fossa. The buccal cusp of #29 (mandibular right second premolar) contacts:
choices: The mesial fossa of #4
The distal fossa of #5
The distal fossa of #4
The mesial fossa of #3
ex: In Class I, maxillary premolars receive contacts in their MESIAL fossae and mandibular premolars in their DISTAL fossae. #29 sits a half tooth ahead of #4, so its buccal cusp lands in the mesial fossa of #4. "Distal fossa of #5" is the tempting look-alike, the same embrasure read as cusp-marginal ridge.
cue: Class I (and III) premolars: Maxillary Mesial, mandibular Distal.
why: In Class I, maxillary premolars take contacts in their mesial fossae, and #29 sits a half tooth ahead of #4.
Distal fossa of #5 is the same embrasure read as cusp-marginal ridge; Class I uses the maxillary mesial fossae.
Distal fossa of #4 is where #29 lands in Class II, when the mandible steps back.
The mesial fossa of #3 is a molar, one tooth too far back for #29 in Class I.

stem: Class I, cusp-fossa. The lingual cusp of #5 (maxillary right first premolar) contacts:
choices: The distal fossa of #28
The mesial fossa of #29
The mesial fossa of #28
The distal fossa of #29
ex: Mandibular premolars receive their contacts in their distal fossae in Class I. #5 sits a half tooth behind #28, so its lingual cusp falls in the distal fossa of #28. Mesial fossa of #29 is the same embrasure read the wrong way.
why: In Class I, mandibular premolars take contacts in their distal fossae, and #5 sits a half tooth behind #28.
Mesial fossa of #29 is the same embrasure read the wrong way; Class I uses the mandibular distal fossae.
Mesial fossa of #28 is where #5's lingual cusp lands in Class II.
Distal fossa of #29 is where #5's lingual cusp lands in Class III, with the mandible a tooth forward.

stem: Class I. The mesiolingual cusp of #3 occludes in:
choices: The central fossa of #30
The mesial fossa of #30
The distal fossa of #29
The buccal groove of #30
ex: The maxillary first molar's mesiolingual (centric) cusp sits in the central fossa of the mandibular first molar in Class I. The buccal groove of #30 receives the MESIOBUCCAL cusp tip of #3 in the classic Class I molar relationship, but that is a non-centric cusp.
why: The large mesiolingual centric cusp of #3 seats in the central fossa of #30 in Class I.
The mesial fossa of #30 is too far mesial for the big ML cusp, which seats in the central fossa.
The distal fossa of #29 receives the lingual cusp of #4, not a molar cusp.
The buccal groove of #30 receives the mesiobuccal cusp tip of #3, a non-centric cusp.

stem: Class I, cusp-fossa. The maxillary first molar (#3) takes an anterior and a posterior contact from the lower teeth. Which cusp makes the posterior one?
choices: The distobuccal cusp of the mandibular first molar
The mesiobuccal cusp of the mandibular second molar
The distolingual cusp of the mandibular first molar
The buccal cusp of the mandibular second premolar
ex: Help sheet: "the first molar posterior contact in the fencepost (which is the DB cusp of #30)." Molars have an anterior and a posterior opposing contact; the posterior one on the maxillary first molar is variable, anywhere from the oblique ridge to the distal fossa. The MB cusp of #31 is the tempting one, because the fence post (which looks like cusp-marginal ridge) puts it in the embrasure behind #3. Read as cusp-fossa, as the question says, it is the next cusp back and lands in the mesial fossa of #2, not on #3.
why: The help sheet names the distobuccal cusp of #30 as the posterior contact on the maxillary first molar.
The MB cusp of #31 sits in the embrasure behind #3 only in a cusp-marginal ridge reading; in cusp-fossa it lands in the mesial fossa of #2.
Mandibular lingual cusps are non-centric in a normal relationship and do not make this contact.
The buccal cusp of #29 lands in the mesial fossa of #4, not on the first molar.

stem: On which tooth is the location of the posterior opposing contact most variable?
choices: The maxillary first molar (from the oblique ridge to the distal fossa)
The mandibular canine
The maxillary first premolar
The mandibular second premolar
ex: Help sheet: molars have an anterior and a posterior opposing contact, and "the location of the posterior contact is highly variable, especially in the maxillary first molar (ranges from oblique ridge to distal fossa)."
why: Molars have an anterior and a posterior contact, and the posterior one on the maxillary first molar ranges from oblique ridge to distal fossa.
The mandibular canine was not the tooth singled out for a variable contact location.
Premolars have a single opposing contact with a set location, such as the mesial fossa of a maxillary premolar in Class I.
Premolars have a single opposing contact; the variable posterior contact is on the maxillary first molar.

stem: Class II, cusp-fossa. The buccal cusp of #29 contacts:
choices: The distal fossa of #4
The mesial fossa of #4
The mesial fossa of #3
The distal fossa of #5
ex: Class II steps the mandible back one post, and the premolar rule flips: maxillary premolars receive contacts in their DISTAL fossae, mandibular premolars in their MESIAL fossae. #29 now sits between #4 and #3, so it lands in the distal fossa of #4. The mesial fossa of #3 is the other side of the same embrasure: the Class II rule (maxillary premolars take contacts in their DISTAL fossae) puts the contact on #4.
cue: Class II flips it: Maxillary Distal, mandibular Mesial.
why: Class II steps the mandible back and flips the rule to maxillary distal fossae, so #29 lands in the distal fossa of #4.
Mesial fossa of #4 is the Class I answer for #29.
Mesial fossa of #3 is the other side of the same embrasure; the Class II rule puts the contact on #4's distal fossa.
Distal fossa of #5 is where #28 lands in Class II, one tooth forward.

stem: Class II, cusp-fossa. The lingual cusp of #4 contacts:
choices: The mesial fossa of #29
The distal fossa of #29
The distal fossa of #28
The mesial fossa of #30
ex: In Class II, mandibular premolars receive their contacts in their mesial fossae. With the mandible stepped back, the lingual cusp of #4 falls in the mesial fossa of #29.
why: In Class II, mandibular premolars take contacts in their mesial fossae, so #4's lingual cusp falls in the mesial fossa of #29.
Distal fossa of #29 is the Class I answer for #4's lingual cusp.
Distal fossa of #28 is the other side of the same embrasure; Class II uses the mandibular mesial fossae.
The mesial fossa of #30 is a molar, too far back for #4 when the mandible steps back.

stem: Class III, cusp-fossa. The buccal cusp of #29 contacts:
choices: The mesial fossa of #5
The mesial fossa of #4
The distal fossa of #5
The distal fossa of #6
ex: Class III steps the mandible forward ("you come forward one tooth from a Class I"). The premolar rule is the same as Class I (maxillary mesial fossae), but one tooth forward: #29 lands in the mesial fossa of #5 instead of #4.
why: Class III keeps the Class I rule (maxillary mesial fossae) but one tooth forward, so #29 lands in the mesial fossa of #5.
Mesial fossa of #4 is the Class I answer; Class III moves it one tooth forward.
Distal fossa of #5 is the wrong half of #5; Class III uses the maxillary mesial fossae, as in Class I.
#6 is the maxillary canine, which has no distal fossa to receive a premolar cusp.

stem: According to the help sheet, in Class I and Class III, premolar occlusal contacts are found in:
choices: The mesial fossae of the maxillary premolars and the distal fossae of the mandibular premolars
The distal fossae of the maxillary premolars and the mesial fossae of the mandibular premolars
The central fossae of both arches
The marginal ridges of both arches
ex: Class I and III: maxillary mesial fossae, mandibular distal fossae. Class II is the opposite (maxillary distal, mandibular mesial).
why: In Class I and III, premolar contacts are in the maxillary mesial fossae and the mandibular distal fossae.
Maxillary distal and mandibular mesial fossae is the Class II rule.
Central fossae receive molar centric cusps; premolar contacts are in the mesial or distal fossae.
Marginal ridge contacts belong to the cusp-marginal ridge scheme, not the help sheet's cusp-fossa rule.

stem: In a Class I relationship, where does the mandibular canine sit relative to the maxillary canine?
choices: Slightly in front (mesial), so the maxillary canine fits between it and the first premolar
Directly under it, cusp tip to cusp tip
Slightly behind (distal to) it, between the maxillary canine and first premolar
A full tooth behind it
ex: "The canines sit where the mandibular canines [are] slightly in front of the maxillary." In Class II the mandibular canine is stepped back; in Class III it is one step forward. Canines or first molars can both be used to classify.
why: In Class I the mandibular canine sits slightly mesial, so the maxillary canine fits between it and the mandibular first premolar.
Cusp tip to cusp tip is an end-to-end relationship, not Class I.
A mandibular canine behind the maxillary canine is stepped back, as in Class II.
A full tooth behind is a distal (Class II) relationship, not Class I.

stem: What does the fence post method tell you?
choices: Which opposing cusp comes closest; you still need anatomy to name the fossa
The exact fossa or marginal ridge every cusp contacts
Whether the patient has cusp-fossa or cusp-marginal ridge contacts in maximum intercuspation
The working and non-working interferences in lateral movements
ex: Help sheet: "The fencepost is a guide to 'what cusp comes closest' to the anatomical location, but the fenceposts are NOT anatomical. You must REMEMBER your tooth anatomy." They look like cusp-marginal ridge, but the questions are usually cusp-fossa.
why: The fence post shows which opposing cusp comes closest; you still need tooth anatomy to name the fossa.
The fence posts are not anatomical, so they don't give the exact fossa or marginal ridge.
The fence post doesn't tell you the patient's contact scheme; questions assume cusp-fossa unless stated.
Working and non-working interferences come from movement analysis, not the fence post.

stem: In a "cusp pathway" picture, where is the MIP contact, and what should you identify first?
choices: At the base of the arrow; identify the movement first, then the cusp
At the arrowhead; identify the cusp first, then the movement
At the base of the arrow; identify the cusp first, then the movement
At the arrowhead; identify the Angle class first
ex: "Remember the MIP contact is at the BASE OF THE ARROW." Treat these as two questions: first identify the movement and cross off every choice with the wrong movement; then identify the opposing cusp. Starting with the cusp is the common slip: movement first, then cusp.
why: The MIP contact is at the base of the arrow; identify the movement first, then the cusp.
The arrowhead is where the cusp travels to, not the MIP contact, and the movement comes first.
The base of the arrow is right, but identifying the cusp first is the common slip; start with the movement.
The MIP contact is at the base, and the first step is the movement, not the Angle class.

stem: Class I, cusp-fossa. The buccal cusp of #28 (mandibular right first premolar) contacts:
choices: The mesial fossa of #5
The distal fossa of #5
The mesial fossa of #4
The distal fossa of #4
ex: In Class I the mandibular first premolar post sits a half step in front of the maxillary first premolar, between the maxillary canine and #5. stem: Class III, cusp-fossa. The lingual cusp of #5 contacts:

stem: A crown on #3 shows a shiny contact on the FACIAL incline of its palatal cusp (the inner slope of that cusp, which faces the cheek and runs down into the central groove) during an excursion. Which movement made it?
choices: A left lateral movement (the right side is non-working)
A right lateral movement (the right side is working)
Straight protrusion
Closing into MIP
ex: Every cusp has two inclines, named for the side they face. The palatal cusp of #3 sits toward the tongue, so its LINGUAL incline is the outer slope facing the palate and its FACIAL incline is the inner slope facing the cheek, down into the central groove (incline 1 in the diagram). Help sheet method: draw the right molars in MIP and move the mandibular tooth. The facial incline of the maxillary palatal cusp meets the lingual incline of the mandibular buccal cusp only when the right side is the NON-working side, that is, when the mandible moves LEFT. In a right working movement the palatal cusp contacts on its LINGUAL incline instead (against the buccal incline of the mandibular lingual cusp). Protrusion uses the distal inclines of the maxillary teeth.
why: Moving left makes the right side non-working: the right mandibular buccal cusp's lingual incline rides across the facial incline of the #3 palatal cusp.
In a right working movement the #3 palatal cusp contacts on its lingual incline, against the buccal incline of the mandibular lingual cusp, not its facial incline.
Straight protrusion makes contacts on the distal inclines of the maxillary teeth, not the facial incline of the palatal cusp.
Closing into MIP seats cusp tips in fossae; a facet on an incline marks a sliding excursion, here the non-working (left) movement.

stem: Watching a mandibular buccal cusp on #14 (maxillary left first molar), you see it travel straight toward the BUCCAL of #14. Which way did the mandible move?
choices: To the left (the left side is working)
To the right (the left side is non-working)
Straight forward (protrusive)
Straight back (retrusive)
ex: On a maxillary tooth you watch a mandibular cusp: working (laterotrusive) runs toward the buccal, non-working toward the mesiopalatal, protrusive toward the mesial, retrusive toward the distal. #14 is a LEFT tooth, so a working path on it means the left side is working: the mandible moved left. A move to the right would make the left side non-working and send the cusp mesiopalatally.
why: On a maxillary tooth the working path runs toward the buccal. #14 is a left tooth, so the left side was working: the mandible moved left.
A move to the right makes the left side non-working, and the mandibular cusp would travel mesiopalatally across #14, not buccally.
In protrusion the mandibular cusp travels mesially across a maxillary tooth, not toward its buccal.
In retrusion the mandibular cusp travels distally across a maxillary tooth, not toward its buccal.

stem: In the diagram of #3 (maxillary right first molar), which movement does arrow A show?
choices: Protrusive
Laterotrusive (working)
Mediotrusive (non-working)
Retrusive
ex: On a MAXILLARY tooth you are watching a mandibular buccal cusp. In protrusion the mandible moves forward, so the mandibular cusp travels MESIALLY across the maxillary tooth. Working = toward buccal; non-working = toward mesiopalatal; retrusion = distal.
why: The mandible moves forward, so the mandibular buccal cusp travels mesially across the maxillary molar: protrusive.
The working (laterotrusive) path on a maxillary tooth runs straight toward the buccal, not mesially.
The non-working (mediotrusive) path on a maxillary tooth runs mesiopalatally, toward the palate as well as forward.
Retrusion moves the mandible back, so the mandibular cusp travels distally across the maxillary tooth, the opposite of this arrow.

stem: In the diagram of #3, arrow B is the path of the mandibular buccal cusp in which movement?
choices: Laterotrusive (working)
Mediotrusive (non-working)
Protrusive
Retrusive
ex: When this side is the working side, the mandible moves laterally (toward this tooth's buccal), so the mandibular buccal cusp slides out toward the maxillary buccal; the help sheet's pathway pictures draw it leaning a little mesially, because the jaw swings around the working condyle. The non-working path heads the other way, toward the palate and mesially.
why: On the working side the mandible moves out toward this tooth's buccal, so the mandibular buccal cusp slides straight buccally.
The non-working path heads the other way, mesially and toward the palate.
Protrusion sends the mandibular cusp mesially across a maxillary tooth, not buccally.
Retrusion sends the mandibular cusp distally across a maxillary tooth, not buccally.

stem: In the diagram of #3, arrow C shows which movement?
choices: Mediotrusive (non-working)
Laterotrusive (working)
Protrusive
Retrusive
ex: On the non-working side the mandible moves toward the midline AND forward (the orbiting condyle comes down and forward), so the mandibular cusp travels mesially and toward the palate across the maxillary tooth.
cue: Non-working = the jaw swings in and forward: on the upper tooth, the path runs mesio-palatal.
why: On the non-working side the mandible moves toward the midline and forward, so the mandibular cusp crosses the maxillary tooth mesially and palatally.
The working (laterotrusive) path on a maxillary tooth runs straight toward the buccal, not mesiopalatally.
Protrusion runs straight mesially; this arrow also angles toward the palate, which marks the non-working movement.
Retrusion runs distally across a maxillary tooth, away from the mesial.

stem: In the diagram of #30 (mandibular right first molar), arrow A is the path of the maxillary lingual cusp in which movement?
choices: Protrusive
Retrusive
Laterotrusive (working)
Mediotrusive (non-working)

"If I'm looking at the mandibular arch and the mandible is sliding forward, the contacts are going toward the posterior." Retrusive is the opposite: the mandible moves back, so the maxillary cusp travels MESIALLY (arrow D).
why: When the mandible slides forward, the maxillary cusp travels distally across the mandibular tooth: protrusive.
Retrusion is the opposite: the mandible moves back, so the maxillary cusp travels mesially across the mandibular tooth (arrow D).
On the working side the maxillary lingual cusp travels straight lingually across the mandibular tooth (arrow B).
On the non-working side the maxillary cusp travels distobuccally across the mandibular tooth (arrow C).

stem: In the diagram of #30, arrow B shows which movement?
choices: Laterotrusive (working)
Mediotrusive (non-working)
Protrusive
Retrusive

why: On the working side the mandibular tooth moves out to the buccal, so relative to it the maxillary lingual cusp travels lingually.
The non-working path on a mandibular tooth runs distobuccally, because that tooth moves medially and forward.
Protrusion sends the maxillary cusp distally across a mandibular tooth, not lingually.
Retrusion sends the maxillary cusp mesially across a mandibular tooth, not lingually.

stem: In the diagram of #30, arrow C shows which movement?

The working path on a mandibular tooth runs straight toward the lingual, not distobuccally.

stem: The diagram shows the RIGHT molars. In a LEFT working movement, which pair of inclines could make a non-working (mediotrusive, balancing) contact?

2 and 6: lingual incline of the maxillary palatal cusp and buccal incline of the mandibular lingual cusp
4 and 5: facial incline of the mandibular buccal cusp and lingual incline of the maxillary buccal cusp
1 and 6: facial incline of the maxillary palatal cusp and buccal incline of the mandibular lingual cusp
ex: Moving left makes the right side the non-working side; the right mandibular molar moves toward the midline (lingually). Its buccal cusp's lingual (inner) incline rides into the maxillary palatal cusp's facial incline. Help sheet: draw it in MIP, then move the mandibular tooth in your mind's eye.
cue: Non-working contacts are on the INNER inclines of the two centric cusps.
why: Moving left makes the right side non-working: the right mandibular buccal cusp's lingual incline (3) rides into the maxillary palatal cusp's facial incline (1).
2 and 6 meet when the right side is WORKING (a right movement), not on the non-working side.
4 and 5 are the buccal-cusp pair that meet in a RIGHT working movement (group function or an interference).

stem: The diagram shows the RIGHT molars. In a RIGHT working movement, which contacts could occur?
choices: 2 with 6, and 4 with 5
1 with 3 only
2 with 6 only
1 with 3, and 4 with 5
ex: Right working: the right mandibular molar moves buccally. The buccal incline of its lingual cusp (6) meets the lingual incline of the maxillary palatal cusp (2), AND the facial incline of its buccal cusp (4) meets the lingual incline of the maxillary buccal cusp (5). The second pair is an interference if unwanted, or part of group function if wanted. 1 with 3 is the NON-working pair: on these right molars it can only happen when the mandible moves LEFT.
why: Right working moves the right mandibular molar buccally: 6 meets 2, and the buccal cusp's facial incline (4) meets the maxillary buccal cusp's lingual incline (5).
1 with 3 is the non-working pair; on these right molars it happens only when the mandible moves left.
2 with 6 is right, but the buccal pair 4 with 5 can also touch in right working (group function or an interference).
1 with 3 is the non-working pair and can't occur in a right working movement; only 4 with 5 is right here.

stem: To answer an interference question about a protrusive movement, the help sheet suggests you:
choices: Draw a sagittal view and move the mandibular tooth forward
Draw a frontal view and move the mandibular tooth lingually
Draw a horizontal view and rotate around the working condyle
Assume Class II, because protrusion only occurs there

why: The help sheet says to draw protrusive questions in a sagittal view: move the mandibular tooth forward, and its mesial inclines meet the maxillary distal inclines.
A frontal view is for lateral (working/non-working) questions; protrusion is a forward movement, best seen sagittally.
Rotating around the working condyle describes a lateral movement, not protrusion.
Protrusion happens in every occlusion class; the help sheet gives no such rule.

stem: In the sagittal envelope, what is point A?
choices: Centric relation (tooth contact here is centric occlusion)
Maximum intercuspation
Edge-to-edge contact
Postural position
ex: A is the top of the posterior opening border: the condyles seated (CR); if the teeth touch there it is CO. From A the jaw closes up and forward to MICP (B) when CO and MICP differ (90% of people).
why: A is the top of the posterior opening border, the condyles seated in centric relation; tooth contact there is centric occlusion.
Maximum intercuspation is B, reached by closing up and forward from A in the 90% whose CO and MICP differ.
Edge-to-edge contact is C, at the bottom of the anterior guidance.
The postural position sits inside the envelope below MICP, not on its border at A.

stem: In the sagittal envelope, point B (above and in front of A) is:
choices: Maximum intercuspation (MICP)
Centric relation
Maximum protrusion
The end of pure rotation
ex: To fit the teeth together from the CO contact, the incisor moves upward and forward to MICP while the condyles come down and forward. If CO = MICP (the other 10%), the superior border runs straight from CR into the anterior guidance.
why: From the CO contact the incisor moves up and forward to fit the teeth together: B is MICP.
Centric relation is A, the top of the posterior opening border.
Maximum protrusion is D, at the front of the superior border.
The end of pure rotation is E, about 20-25 mm down the posterior opening border.

stem: In the sagittal envelope, the incisor slides down from B along the lingual of the maxillary incisors to point C. What is C?
choices: Edge-to-edge contact of the incisors
Maximum protrusion
Centric occlusion
The clinical rest position
ex: From MICP the lower incisor follows the anterior guidance down to edge-to-edge (C). The border then flattens: the jaw must keep moving forward past the incisal edges before it can rise again toward maximum protrusion (D).
why: The lower incisor follows the anterior guidance down from MICP to the incisal edges: C is edge-to-edge.
Maximum protrusion is D, reached after the jaw keeps moving forward past edge-to-edge.
Centric occlusion is tooth contact at A, with the condyles seated in CR.
The clinical rest position is inside the envelope, about 8 mm below and 3 mm in front of MICP, not on the contact border.

stem: In the sagittal envelope, what happens between A and E?
choices: Pure rotation with the condyles seated, about 20-25 mm of opening
Rotation plus translation, with the condyles moving down to maximum opening
Closing with the mandible fully protruded
The functional chewing stroke
ex: A to E is pure hinge rotation in CR (20-25 mm). Past E the condyles must translate down the eminence: E to F is rotation plus translation to maximum opening (40-60 mm).
why: A to E is pure hinge rotation with the condyles seated in CR, about 20-25 mm of incisal opening.
Rotation plus translation is E to F, past the end of pure rotation, ending at maximum opening (40-60 mm).
Closing with the mandible fully protruded forms the anterior opening border, F to D.
The chewing stroke is the dashed teardrop-shaped functional area inside the envelope, not a border segment.

stem: In the sagittal envelope, how is the border from F up to D formed?
choices: By closing from maximum opening with the mandible held maximally protruded
By hinge closure with the condyles seated in centric relation the whole way
By tooth contact as the incisors slide forward
By the mandible's rest position under gravity
ex: F to D is the anterior opening border: open fully, then close while keeping the jaw as far forward as possible, ending at maximum protrusion (D). Ligaments and joint anatomy limit it.
why: F to D is the anterior opening border: open fully, then close with the jaw held as far forward as possible to maximum protrusion.
Hinge closure with the condyles seated is the posterior border (A to E), not F to D.
Tooth contact forms the superior border (A-B-C-D); F to D is set by ligaments and joint anatomy.
Rest position is a point inside the envelope under muscle tone, not a border movement.

stem: In the sagittal envelope, which part is dictated by the teeth rather than by ligaments and joint anatomy?
choices: The superior contact border, A-B-C-D
The posterior opening border, A-E-F
The anterior opening border, F-D
The pure rotation segment, A-E
ex: The superior contact border (CR/CO up to MICP, down the anterior guidance to edge-to-edge, forward to maximum protrusion) is where teeth touch. The opening borders are limited by ligaments and joint anatomy. The dashed teardrop is the functional (chewing) area.
why: The superior border (CR/CO up to MICP, down the anterior guidance to edge-to-edge, forward to maximum protrusion) is where teeth touch.
The posterior opening border is limited by ligaments and joint anatomy, not by the teeth.
The anterior opening border is limited by ligaments and joint anatomy, not by the teeth.
Pure rotation (A to E) is part of the posterior opening border, set by the TM ligament, not by the teeth.

stem: In the horizontal envelope, which border is B?
choices: Left lateral with protrusion
Left lateral
Right lateral with protrusion
Right lateral
ex: From CR (apex) the mandible goes laterally to the left (A); from the left lateral extreme, moving forward to maximum protrusion traces left lateral with protrusion (B). C and D mirror these on the right. Note the side labels: these questions test whether you track the patient's left and right.
why: From the left lateral extreme, moving forward to maximum protrusion traces B: left lateral with protrusion.
Left lateral is A, from CR straight out to the patient's left.
Right lateral with protrusion is C, the mirror of B on the patient's right.
Right lateral is D, from CR out to the patient's right.

stem: In the horizontal envelope, which border is D?
choices: Right lateral
Right lateral with protrusion
Left lateral
Left lateral with protrusion
ex: D runs from CR out to the patient's right: right lateral. C, from the right extreme forward to maximum protrusion, is right lateral with protrusion.
why: D runs from CR out to the patient's right: right lateral.
Right lateral with protrusion is C, from the right extreme forward to maximum protrusion.
Left lateral is A, from CR out to the patient's left.
Left lateral with protrusion is B, from the left extreme forward to maximum protrusion.

stem: In the frontal envelope (viewed from the front), which border is A?
choices: Left lateral superior
Right lateral superior
Left lateral opening
Right lateral opening
ex: From the front, the patient's left is on your right. A starts at the intercuspal position and runs to the patient's left along tooth contact: left lateral superior. B continues down as left lateral opening; C and D are the right-side borders.
cue: Facing the patient, their left is your right.
why: From the front the patient's left is on your right; A runs from the intercuspal position along tooth contact to the left: left lateral superior.
Right lateral superior is D, on the patient's right (your left), along tooth contact.
Left lateral opening is B, which continues down from the left lateral extreme.
Right lateral opening is C, on the patient's right running down to maximum opening.

stem: In the frontal envelope, which border is C?
choices: Right lateral opening
Right lateral superior
Left lateral opening
Left lateral superior
ex: C is on the patient's right (your left) and runs down from the right lateral extreme to maximum opening: right lateral opening. D above it is right lateral superior, back along tooth contact to the intercuspal position (the slide numbers them 3 and 4).
why: C is on the patient's right (your left), running down from the right lateral extreme to maximum opening: right lateral opening.
Right lateral superior is D, the tooth-contact border above C.
Left lateral opening is B, on the patient's left (your right).
Left lateral superior is A, along tooth contact on the patient's left.

stem: In the frontal envelope, the point marked PP just below the intercuspal position is:
choices: The postural position, about 2-4 mm below MICP
The clinical rest position, about 8 mm below MICP
Centric relation
The end of pure rotation
ex: PP = postural position, the usual resting posture of the mandible (2-4 mm below MICP), kept by a myotactic reflex so the teeth can be brought into function immediately.
why: PP is the postural position, about 2-4 mm below MICP, held by a myotactic reflex so the teeth can come into function at once.
The clinical rest position (least EMG activity) is lower, about 8 mm below and 3 mm in front; the postural position is often wrongly called by that name.
Centric relation is a condylar position at the top of the posterior border, not a resting point below MICP.
The end of pure rotation is 20-25 mm of opening, far below a point just under MICP.

stem: In the Class I fence post shown, the mandibular P2 cusp points at the post between which two maxillary teeth?
choices: Maxillary PM1 and PM2
Maxillary PM2 and M1 mesial
Maxillary canine and PM1
Maxillary M1 mesial and M1 distal

In cusp-fossa terms its buccal cusp goes to the mesial fossa of the maxillary PM2 (#29 on #4). "The only thing you really have to remember on fence posts is how to draw fence posts and what their canine relationships are."
why: In Class I each mandibular post sits a half step mesial to its maxillary partner, so mandibular PM2 falls between maxillary PM1 and PM2.
Between maxillary PM2 and M1 mesial is where the mandibular M1 mesial post falls in Class I.
Between the maxillary canine and PM1 is where mandibular PM1 falls in Class I.

stem: She asks for longer, whiter crowns on #8 and #9. Which classification fits?
choices: Class II division 2
Class II division 1

stem: True or false: Occlusion and articulation mean the same thing.
choices: True
False

Occlusion is static contact; articulation is static and dynamic contact during function.

stem: True or false: Restored or orthodontically moved teeth should be placed within the neutral zone.
choices: True
False
ex: True. The neutral zone is where the forces of the tongue and of the lips and cheeks balance. Put a tooth in the way of those muscles "and they'll just sort of knock it out of the way."
why: Teeth outside the zone get pushed by the tongue, lips and cheeks.
The neutral zone is exactly where restored and moved teeth belong; outside it the muscles displace them.

stem: True or false: The sphere of Monson has a radius of about 4 inches, centered near the glabella.
choices: True
False
ex: True. Monson's spherical theory: each cusp conforms to an imaginary sphere of about 4-inch radius centered near the glabella.
why: That is Monson's sphere as taught: about 4 inches, centered near the glabella.
The 4-inch radius and the glabella center are both right; the condyles are not the center.

stem: True or false: A posterior crossbite is a functional problem that should be corrected before posterior implant crowns are made.

False

Dr. Givan: no functional problem; it comes from arch size or eruption, and implant crowns are often made in crossbite.

stem: True or false: Because posterior contacts sit buccal to the central fossa line, the buccal embrasures are larger than the lingual ones.

False

stem: True or false: In centric relation the mandible is restricted to pure rotation about the transverse horizontal axis.

False

CR allows only rotation about the transverse horizontal axis; translation means the condyles have left it.

stem: True or false: Non-working contacts are considered interferences.

Non-working contacts are interferences; only dentures want balancing contacts.

stem: True or false: Pure rotation with the condyles seated opens the incisors about 40-60 mm.

False

2. More horizontal overlap of the anterior teeth
3. More vertical overlap of the anterior teeth
4. A more acute curve of Spee
5. A greater Bennett movement
choices: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 3 only
1, 3 and 5
3, 4 and 5
ex: From the determinants table: steeper condylar guidance and more vertical overlap allow taller posterior cusps. More horizontal overlap, a more acute curve of Spee, a plane of occlusion more parallel to the condylar guidance and a greater Bennett movement all call for shorter ones.
why: It includes 2, which is false: more horizontal overlap calls for shorter posterior cusps.

Statements 1 and 3 are true. Statement 2 is false: more horizontal overlap calls for shorter posterior cusps. Statement 4 is false: a more acute curve of Spee calls for shorter cusps, the most posterior ones above all. Statement 5 is false: a greater Bennett movement (or a greater immediate side shift) calls for shorter cusps.
It includes 5, which is false: a greater Bennett movement (or a greater immediate side shift) calls for shorter cusps.

It includes 4, which is false: a more acute curve of Spee calls for shorter cusps, the most posterior ones above all. It includes 5, which is false: a greater Bennett movement (or a greater immediate side shift) calls for shorter cusps. It leaves out 1, which is true: in the determinants table, steeper condylar guidance allows taller posterior cusps.

stem: A ginglymus joint:
choices: Moves in one plane like a hinge, e.g. the elbow, knee and finger joints
Glides freely between flat surfaces, e.g. the wrist, the ankle and the spine
Rotates around a single pivot, e.g. the atlantoaxial joint
Is a fibrous joint with no movement, e.g. a cranial suture
ex: Ginglymus: a synovial joint with uniaxial (hinge) movement in one plane: elbow, knee, interphalangeal. Arthrodial: freely moving gliding joint with flat surfaces, tight capsule: wrist, ankle, spine. The TMJ is both: ginglymoarthrodial.
why: Ginglymus is a synovial joint with uniaxial hinge movement in one plane: elbow, knee and finger joints.
Free gliding between flat surfaces (wrist, ankle, spine) describes an arthrodial joint.
Rotation around a single pivot describes a pivot (trochoid) joint like the atlantoaxial, not a ginglymus.
An immovable fibrous joint like a suture is a synarthrosis, not a ginglymus, which is a movable hinge.

stem: Which part of TMJ function is the arthrodial (gliding) component?
choices: Translation of the condyle and disc down the articular eminence
Rotation of the condyle about the transverse horizontal axis
Elevation of the mandible by the masseter
Opening by the digastric muscle
ex: Hinging (rotation) is the ginglymus part; sliding (translation) is the arthrodial part. Together: ginglymoarthrodial. "Not many joints have both functions."
why: Sliding of the condyle and disc down the eminence (translation) is the arthrodial, gliding part.
Rotation about the hinge axis is the ginglymus (hinge) part of the joint.
Elevation by the masseter is a muscle action, not one of the joint's two movement types.
Opening by the digastric is a muscle action; the gliding component is translation in the upper compartment.

stem: "One bone, two joints." What does Dr. Givan mean?
choices: The mandible links both TMJs, so neither can move independently of the other
Each TMJ has two compartments that move independently
The disc acts as a second bone in each joint
The temporal bone forms two separate joints with each condyle, above and below the disc
ex: The mandible articulates at both TMJs: "There's no function of the left side that is not impacted by the right side and vice versa." That (plus hinge + slide) is why it may be the most complex joint in the body.
why: The mandible articulates at both TMJs, so nothing the left side does is free of the right side, and vice versa.
The two compartments split rotation and translation, but the phrase refers to one mandible joining two joints.
The disc functions as a third bone, which makes the TMJ compound; that is a different idea from one bone, two joints.
Each side is one joint, divided by the disc into compartments; the two joints are the left and right TMJs.

stem: Where is the condyle normally seated on the articular disc?
choices: The thin, avascular intermediate zone
The thick posterior border
The anterior border, beside the lateral pterygoid attachment
The retrodiscal tissues
ex: The condyle sits in the thinnest, avascular intermediate zone (no nerves either). From the side the disc is biconcave: the anterior border is considerably thicker and the posterior border even thicker. Loading the posterior border or retrodiscal tissues is painful.
why: The condyle normally sits in the thin, avascular, aneural intermediate zone.
The posterior border is the thickest part of the disc; the condyle sits in front of it.
The anterior border is thick and lies ahead of the condyle in the closed position.
The retrodiscal tissues are vascular and innervated; loading them is painful, not normal.

stem: Viewed sagittally, which part of the articular disc is thickest?
choices: The posterior border
The anterior border
The intermediate zone
All parts are the same thickness
ex: Slides: the anterior border is considerably thicker than the intermediate zone, and the posterior border is even thicker. The thin intermediate zone is where the condyle normally sits.
why: Sagittally the posterior border is the thickest, even thicker than the anterior border.
The anterior border is considerably thicker than the intermediate zone, but thinner than the posterior border.
The intermediate zone is the thinnest part, where the condyle sits.
The disc is biconcave, with thin and thick parts, not uniform.

stem: Viewed from the front, the disc is thicker ___, which is why a displaced disc tends to move ___.
choices: Medially; medially (or forward)
Laterally; laterally
Medially; laterally
Laterally; posteriorly
ex: The disc is slightly thicker medially than laterally; because of that wedge shape, if it slips off it tends to go forward or medially. For dislocation, the medial and lateral discal ligaments must be stretched or torn.
why: The disc is slightly thicker medially, so a displaced disc tends to slip forward or medially.
The disc is thicker medially, not laterally, and displaced discs go forward or medially.
The thicker medial side is right, but displacement goes forward or medially, not laterally.
The disc is thicker medially, and displacement is forward or medial, not posterior.

stem: Why is it improper to call the TMJ disc a "meniscus"?
choices: A meniscus is crescent-shaped (convex and concave sides), as in the knee
A meniscus is bone, while the disc is cartilage
A meniscus has no blood supply, while the TMJ disc is fully vascular throughout
A meniscus is found only in hinge joints
ex: A meniscus is crescent-shaped with a convex and a concave side (knee). The TMJ disc is a biconcave disc of dense fibrous connective tissue that functions like a bone, making the TMJ a compound joint.
why: A meniscus is crescent-shaped with a convex and a concave side, as in the knee; the TMJ disc is biconcave.
A meniscus is fibrocartilage, not bone; the difference is its crescent shape.
The TMJ disc's intermediate zone is avascular, so it isn't fully vascular; the difference is shape.
Menisci occur in the knee, not only in hinge joints; the issue is shape, not joint type.

stem: The TMJ is called a compound joint because:
choices: The disc functions like a third bone between the condyle and the temporal bone
It has both a hinge and a gliding component, rotating below and translating above the disc
The mandible forms two joints
It contains both cartilage and bone surfaces
ex: The tempting choice is true of the TMJ but explains a different word: hinge + glide is why it is GINGLYMOARTHRODIAL, not why it is compound. A compound joint has at least three bones; the TMJ has only two, but the disc, though dense fibrous connective tissue, functions as the third. (One bone, two joints = bilateral.)
why: A compound joint needs at least three bones; the TMJ has two, but the disc functions as the third.
Hinge plus glide is true of the TMJ but explains ginglymoarthrodial, not compound.
One bone forming two joints makes the TMJs bilateral, not compound.
All synovial joints have bone covered by articular tissue; that doesn't define a compound joint.

stem: Where does rotation occur in the TMJ, and where does translation occur?
choices: Rotation in the lower compartment; translation in the upper compartment
Rotation in the upper (superior) compartment; translation in the lower compartment
Both occur in the upper compartment
Both occur in the lower compartment
ex: The disc divides the joint into an upper (disc-to-fossa) and lower (disc-to-condyle) compartment. Hinge rotation happens between condyle and disc (lower); sliding out of the fossa happens between disc and temporal bone (upper). So the disc stays over the condyle wherever it goes.
cue: "Rotation Lower, Translation Upper": the condyle spins under the disc; the disc-condyle unit slides under the fossa.
why: Hinge rotation is between condyle and disc (lower compartment); sliding is between disc and temporal bone (upper).
This is reversed: rotation is in the lower (disc-to-condyle) compartment, translation in the upper.
Only translation occurs in the upper compartment; rotation happens below the disc.
Only rotation occurs in the lower compartment; translation happens above the disc.

stem: The retrodiscal tissues behind the disc are:
choices: Highly vascular and innervated, so loading them causes substantial joint pain
Avascular and aneural, like the intermediate zone, so they can carry the condyle's load
The attachment of the superior lateral pterygoid
The site of rotation in the lower compartment
ex: Retrodiscal tissues are "loaded with blood supply... loaded with nerves." Functioning on them creates substantial pain. The intermediate zone is the avascular, aneural part; the superior lateral pterygoid attaches anteriorly.
why: Retrodiscal tissues are loaded with blood vessels and nerves, so functioning on them causes substantial pain.
The avascular, aneural part is the intermediate zone; the retrodiscal tissues are the opposite.
The superior lateral pterygoid attaches to the disc anteriorly, not behind it.
Rotation in the lower compartment is between condyle and disc, not in the retrodiscal tissues.

stem: Of the two retrodiscal laminae, which is elastic?
choices: The superior retrodiscal lamina
The inferior retrodiscal lamina
Both are purely collagenous
Neither; the capsular ligament provides the elasticity
ex: Superior retrodiscal lamina (SRL) = elastic, helps pull the disc back; inferior retrodiscal lamina (IRL) = collagenous. On closing, the superior lateral pterygoid balances that elastic pull so the disc returns smoothly.
why: The superior retrodiscal lamina is elastic and helps pull the disc back.
The inferior retrodiscal lamina is collagenous, not elastic.
Only the inferior lamina is purely collagenous; the superior one is elastic.
The superior retrodiscal lamina provides the elastic pull; the capsular ligament isn't the source.

stem: The articulating surfaces of the condyle and temporal bone are covered by:
choices: Resilient, collagenous, fluid-filled articular tissue, not bare bone
Enamel-like hydroxyapatite
The retrodiscal tissues
Synovial membrane only
ex: As in all joints, the surfaces are fluid-filled and lined with a resilient collagenous articular covering that can swell and shrink. They are not meant to touch each other; if the disc perforates and bone meets bone, the joint breaks down.
why: The surfaces are lined with a resilient, collagenous, fluid-filled articular covering that can swell and shrink.
Hydroxyapatite is the mineral of enamel and bone; joint surfaces are lined with soft collagenous tissue.
Retrodiscal tissues lie behind the disc and don't cover the articulating surfaces.
Synovial membrane lines the joint spaces, but the articulating surfaces have their own collagenous covering.

stem: Is the TMJ a load-bearing joint?
choices: Yes; to crush a bolus you pivot against the seated joint
No; the disc absorbs everything and prevents any load on the condyle
Only in patients with missing posterior teeth
Only during clenching at night
ex: "At one time in dentistry, we said we don't really have a lot of forces at our joints... we know today that's not correct." Biting requires something to pivot against: the seated joint. That is why the joint seats essentially every time the elevator muscles contract.
why: Biting needs something to pivot against: the seated joint. So the joint seats and is loaded whenever the elevators contract.
The old belief that the joint carries little force is outdated; the disc doesn't prevent loading the condyle.
The joint is loaded in everyone who bites and chews, not only in patients missing posterior teeth.
Every crushing bite loads the joint, not just night clenching.

stem: Which ligament encases the whole joint like a curtain and resists downward displacement?
choices: The capsular ligament
The sphenomandibular ligament
The lateral discal ligament
The stylomandibular ligament
ex: The capsular ligament attaches to the condylar neck and spreads like a wall to the articular eminence and fossa, wrapping the joint medially, laterally, anteriorly and posteriorly. When you bite something hard, it keeps the condyle from dropping far out of the fossa.
why: The capsular ligament wraps the whole joint like a wall and keeps the condyle from dropping far out of the fossa.
The sphenomandibular ligament runs from the sphenoid spine to the lingula and limits opening and forward motion.
The lateral discal ligament ties the disc to the lateral pole of the condyle; it doesn't encase the joint.
The stylomandibular ligament runs from the styloid to the ramus and limits forward motion; it doesn't encase the joint.

stem: The medial and lateral discal (collateral) ligaments:
choices: Attach the disc to the medial and lateral poles of the condyle, keeping it on the condyle
Limit opening and forward movement of the mandible, running from the skull base to the ramus
Limit posterior movement of the condyle
Attach the disc to the articular eminence
ex: The discal ligaments run from the disc down to the medial and lateral poles and keep the disc on top of the condyle while allowing some rotation. Stretched or torn, they allow clicking and popping; about 50% of the class would click on stethoscope. Ligaments don't heal.
why: The discal ligaments tie the disc to the condyle's medial and lateral poles, keeping it on the condyle while allowing rotation.
Limiting opening and forward motion is the job of the stylomandibular and sphenomandibular ligaments.
Limiting posterior movement is the job of the TM ligament's inner horizontal portion.
The discal ligaments attach the disc to the condyle, not to the eminence.

stem: Which ligaments limit opening and forward (protrusive) movement of the mandible?
choices: Stylomandibular and sphenomandibular
Temporomandibular (inner horizontal and outer oblique)
Medial and lateral discal
Capsular and collateral
ex: The stylomandibular (styloid process → angle and posterior border of the ramus) and sphenomandibular (spine of the sphenoid → lingula) ligaments limit opening and forward motion. The TM ligament limits posterior movement and rotational opening.
why: The stylomandibular and sphenomandibular ligaments limit opening and forward motion of the mandible.
The TM ligament limits rotational opening (outer oblique) and posterior movement (inner horizontal), not protrusion.
The discal ligaments keep the disc on the condyle; they don't limit protrusion.
The capsular ligament encases the joint, and the collateral (discal) ligaments hold the disc; neither is the protrusion limiter.

stem: The outer oblique portion of the temporomandibular ligament limits:
choices: Rotational opening
Posterior movement of the condyle and disc
Lateral displacement of the disc
Forward movement of the mandible
ex: Outer oblique portion: a sling around the posterior condylar neck to the articular eminence; it limits rotational opening (which is why pure rotation stops at 20-25 mm). Inner horizontal portion: limits posterior movement of the condyle and disc.
cue: Oblique = Opening; Horizontal = Hold back (no posterior shove).
why: The outer oblique portion limits rotational opening, which is why pure rotation stops at about 20-25 mm.
Limiting posterior movement of the condyle and disc is the inner horizontal portion's job.
Lateral disc displacement is resisted by the discal (collateral) ligaments.
Forward movement is limited by the stylomandibular and sphenomandibular ligaments.

stem: A toddler swings a book into your chin. Which ligament protects the structures behind the condyle?
choices: The TM ligament's inner horizontal portion
The stylomandibular ligament
The outer oblique portion of the temporomandibular ligament
The sphenomandibular ligament
ex: A blow to the chin drives the mandible backward; the inner horizontal portion of the TM ligament (articular eminence to the disc and condyle) limits that posterior movement, protecting the retrodiscal tissues and other sensitive structures.
why: A blow to the chin drives the mandible back; the inner horizontal TM ligament limits that and protects the retrodiscal tissues.
The stylomandibular ligament limits forward movement, not backward displacement.
The outer oblique portion limits rotational opening, not posterior displacement.
The sphenomandibular ligament limits opening and forward motion, not posterior displacement.

stem: After a long appointment, a patient cannot close; the condyle is stuck in front of the eminence. What does Dr. Givan recommend?
choices: Gentle downward force on the buccal shelf to distract the condyle so it pops back
Firm posterior force on the chin to push the condyle back over the eminence into the fossa
Have the patient clench hard against a cotton roll
Inject the lateral pterygoid with local anesthetic
ex: Open lock: the condyle has gone past the height of the eminence. "We apply a little downward force on the buccal shelf. Not a posterior force, because you don't want to push it back against it." Distracting it downward usually lets it pop right back.
why: Gentle downward pressure on the buccal shelf distracts the condyle so it can pop back behind the eminence.
Pushing posteriorly drives the condyle against the eminence; Dr. Givan says not to push it back.
The patient can't close, and clenching won't bring the condyle down past the eminence.
Dr. Givan's fix is distracting the condyle via the buccal shelf, not injecting a muscle.

stem: "Muscles only pull." What follows from this for jaw movement?
choices: Every motion needs an agonist and an antagonist working together, never one muscle alone
Opening must be passive, by gravity only
The masseter must both open and close the jaw
Ligaments must push the mandible back into position after each movement, like elastic springs
ex: Muscles only contract (like a rope, you can't push it). They never work alone: an agonist-antagonist pair gives smooth motion at the right speed and force, and the opposing muscle never fully turns off.
why: Muscles can only contract, so movement needs agonist and antagonist pairs working together; the opposing muscle never fully turns off.
Opening is active, driven by the inferior lateral pterygoid and the suprahyoids, not gravity alone.
The masseter closes; it can't push the jaw open, which is why openers are needed.
Ligaments limit movement; they don't act as springs pushing the mandible back.

stem: Differences in muscle design depend on all of these EXCEPT:
choices: The muscle's cranial nerve innervation
Surface on bone available for attachment
Speed of contraction
Range and force of contraction
ex: Handout: muscle design depends on (1) surface available for attachment, (2) speed of contraction, (3) range of movement, (4) force of contraction. Dr. Givan said he will not test innervation (you covered it in gross anatomy); know function and roughly where each muscle attaches.
why: Innervation is not a factor in muscle design on the handout, and Dr. Givan said he won't test innervation.
Surface available for attachment is one of the handout's four design factors.
Speed of contraction is one of the handout's four design factors.
Range and force of contraction are two of the handout's four design factors.

stem: The masseter originates from ___ and inserts on ___.
choices: The zygomatic arch and malar process; the angle of the ramus
The temporal fossa and fascia; the coronoid process
The lateral pterygoid plate; the medial surface of the ramus
The greater wing of the sphenoid; the condylar neck
ex: Masseter: flat, thick, quadrangular, the most superficial muscle of mastication. Origin zygomatic arch and malar process; insertion angle of the ramus (and coronoid process per the handout). Temporal fossa to coronoid = temporalis; lateral pterygoid plate to medial ramus = medial pterygoid.
why: The masseter runs from the zygomatic arch and malar process to the angle of the ramus.
Temporal fossa and fascia to the coronoid process is the temporalis.
Lateral pterygoid plate to the medial ramus is the medial pterygoid.
The greater wing of the sphenoid to the condylar region is the lateral pterygoid, not the masseter.

stem: The two bellies of the masseter diverge by about 50°. What do they do?
choices: Superficial: elevation with some protrusion; deep: elevation with retrusion
Superficial: retrusion only; deep: protrusion only, with neither belly elevating
Both only elevate
Superficial: depression; deep: elevation
ex: Superficial (bigger, power) belly: elevation plus some protrusion. Deep belly: elevation plus retrusion. When the jaw is wide open the superficial belly lacks mechanical advantage, so the deep belly starts the closure and swings the superficial belly into position to apply power.
why: The superficial (power) belly elevates with some protrusion; the deep belly elevates with retrusion.
Both bellies elevate; the superficial adds protrusion and the deep adds retrusion, not the reverse.
Both elevate, but they also differ: superficial adds protrusion, deep adds retrusion.
Neither belly depresses the mandible; the masseter is a closing muscle.

stem: Why does contracting the masseter seat the condyles?
choices: Its fibers run up and forward, pushing the condyles superiorly and anteriorly
It pulls the condyle posteriorly and up into the retrodiscal tissues behind the disc
It lifts the disc off the condyle
It only works when the teeth are already in MIP
ex: The masseter is directed superiorly and anteriorly, the same direction as CR (anterior-superior against the eminence). "When this works, it's going to seat." To be anywhere else, other muscles must deliberately position the jaw.
why: The masseter's fibers run up and forward, the same direction as CR, so contracting it seats the condyles against the eminence.
Seating is anterior-superior against the eminence; pulling the condyle back into the retrodiscal tissues is the opposite.
The masseter doesn't act on the disc; it lifts the mandible up and forward.
The masseter seats the joints whenever it contracts, whether or not the teeth are in MIP.

stem: The temporalis (temporal fossa and fascia → coronoid process) is best described as:
choices: A fan-shaped positioner that elevates and retracts the mandible
The main power closer of the mandible
The primary depressor of the mandible
A muscle that stabilizes the disc during closure
ex: Temporalis: flat, fan-shaped, bipennate; inserts on the small coronoid process, "not a power position." It is the jaw's major, fast positioner (aligning teeth to crush food, shaping the oral cavity in speech). The masseter and medial pterygoid are the power closers.
why: The fan-shaped temporalis inserts on the small coronoid, not a power position: it is the jaw's fast positioner, elevating and retracting.
The power closers are the masseter and medial pterygoid; the temporalis is mainly a positioner.
The temporalis elevates; depression is done by the inferior lateral pterygoid and the suprahyoids.
Stabilizing the disc during closure is the superior lateral pterygoid's job.

stem: Which portion of the temporalis mainly retrudes the mandible?
choices: Posterior
Anterior
Middle
None; the temporalis cannot retrude
ex: Anterior fibers: elevation. Middle: elevation with some retrusion. Posterior: retrusion with some elevation ("you can feel it right there... those are the fibers you use to pull your mandible back").
why: The posterior, more horizontal fibers retrude the mandible, with some elevation.
The anterior fibers mainly elevate the mandible.
The middle fibers elevate with only some retrusion; the posterior fibers are the main retruders.
The temporalis does retrude, through its posterior fibers; it is on the exam slide for retrusion.

stem: According to Dr. Givan, what is the zygomatic arch protecting?
choices: The temporalis insertion on the coronoid process
The parotid duct
The articular disc
The masseteric nerve
ex: The temporalis is "so important that we are designed to build a tunnel around it." The zygomatic arch holds the area out so the coronoid process can move as the temporalis contracts.
why: Dr. Givan says the temporalis is so important that we build a tunnel around it: the arch lets the coronoid move as it contracts.
The parotid duct runs over the masseter, not through the arch; the arch tunnels the temporalis.
The disc sits inside the joint capsule; the zygomatic arch tunnels the temporalis insertion.
The masseteric nerve isn't what the arch is said to protect; it tunnels the temporalis and coronoid.

stem: The superior head of the lateral pterygoid inserts on the ___ and is active during ___.
choices: Articular capsule and disc; closure (mandibular elevation)
Pterygoid fovea of the condylar neck; opening and protrusion
Coronoid process; retrusion
Medial surface of the ramus; elevation only
ex: Superior head: from the infralateral greater wing of the sphenoid and infratemporal crest to the capsule and disc; active in CLOSURE, stabilizing the disc against the elastic pull of the retrodiscal lamina. Inferior head: from the lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate to the pterygoid fovea of the condylar neck; active in opening and protrusion.
cue: Superior = Stabilizer (closing). Inferior = In front (protrudes, opens).
why: The superior head inserts on the capsule and disc and works during closure, stabilizing the disc against the retrodiscal lamina's elastic pull.
The pterygoid fovea, active in opening and protrusion, describes the inferior head.
The coronoid process is the temporalis insertion, and retrusion is posterior temporalis and deep masseter.
The medial ramus is the medial pterygoid's insertion; the superior lateral pterygoid goes to the disc.

stem: Which muscle (or part) is active in opening and protrusion?
choices: Inferior head of the lateral pterygoid
Superior head of the lateral pterygoid
Medial pterygoid
Posterior temporalis
ex: The inferior belly pulls the condyle forward, down and medially: both sides together = protrusion and opening; one side alone = movement to the opposite side. The superior belly is inactive while opening. Dr. Givan: "I expect you to know which belly is doing what."
why: The inferior head pulls the condyle forward, down and medially: both sides together give opening and protrusion.
The superior head is inactive while opening; it works during closure.
The medial pterygoid elevates the mandible; it doesn't open it.
The posterior temporalis retrudes the mandible, the opposite of protrusion.

stem: Only the RIGHT inferior lateral pterygoid contracts. Which way does the mandible move?
choices: To the left (contralateral excursion)
To the right (ipsilateral excursion)
Straight forward
Straight back
ex: One inferior lateral pterygoid pulls its condyle forward, down and toward the midline, swinging the chin to the OPPOSITE side. "If I contract on the right side, I will move my jaw to the left." Both together = straight protrusion.
why: One inferior lateral pterygoid pulls its condyle forward and medially, swinging the chin to the opposite side: right contracts, jaw goes left.
Contracting the right one moves the jaw to the left, not the right.
Straight forward needs both inferior lateral pterygoids contracting together.
The lateral pterygoid pulls forward; retrusion comes from the posterior temporalis and deep masseter.

stem: The medial pterygoid:
choices: Arises from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and elevates the mandible
Arises from the lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate and protrudes the mandible
Inserts on the disc and stabilizes it during closure
Inserts on the coronoid process and retrudes the mandible
ex: Medial pterygoid: rhomboidal; origin medial aspect of the lateral pterygoid plate (plus palatine process and maxillary tuberosity); insertion inferoposterior medial surface of the ramus; action elevation. The "unsung hero," hard to palpate.
why: The medial pterygoid arises from the medial surface of the lateral pterygoid plate, inserts on the medial ramus and elevates.
The lateral surface of the lateral pterygoid plate is the origin of the inferior lateral pterygoid, which protrudes.
Inserting on the disc and stabilizing it in closure describes the superior lateral pterygoid.
The coronoid insertion and retrusion describe the temporalis.

stem: The pterygomasseteric sling is formed by:
choices: The masseter and the medial pterygoid
The masseter and the temporalis
The two heads of the lateral pterygoid
The digastric and mylohyoid
ex: The masseter on the lateral side and the medial pterygoid on the medial side of the ramus grab the mandible together: an extremely powerful sling for crushing food.
why: The masseter outside and the medial pterygoid inside the ramus grab the mandible together: the pterygomasseteric sling.
The temporalis inserts on the coronoid; the sling pairs the masseter with the medial pterygoid.
The two lateral pterygoid heads go to the disc and condyle, not around the ramus.
The digastric and mylohyoid are suprahyoid openers, not part of the sling.

stem: On Dr. Givan's exam slide, which muscles elevate the mandible?
choices: Temporalis, medial pterygoid and masseter
Inferior lateral pterygoid and suprahyoids
Superficial masseter and inferior lateral pterygoid
Posterior temporalis and deep masseter
ex: Exam slide (A, Elevation): temporalis, medial pterygoid, masseter. "If I ask a question regarding what muscle is involved in what motion, it will come from this slide," even though other sources list more contributors.
cue: "TMM lifts": Temporalis, Masseter, Medial pterygoid.
why: Exam slide, elevation: temporalis, medial pterygoid and masseter.
The inferior lateral pterygoid and suprahyoids open (depress) the mandible.
Superficial masseter plus inferior lateral pterygoid is the protrusion pair on the slide.
Posterior temporalis plus deep masseter is the retrusion pair on the slide.

stem: On the exam slide, which muscles depress (open) the mandible?
choices: Inferior lateral pterygoid with the suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles
Temporalis and masseter
Superficial masseter and medial pterygoid
Superior lateral pterygoid alone
ex: Exam slide (B, Depression): the lateral pterygoid (its inferior belly) plus the suprahyoid and infrahyoid groups. The infrahyoids fix the floating hyoid so the suprahyoids can pull the mandible down.
why: Exam slide, depression: the lateral pterygoid (inferior belly) with the suprahyoid and infrahyoid groups.
The temporalis and masseter are elevators that close the jaw.
The superficial masseter and medial pterygoid are elevators, not openers.
The superior lateral pterygoid is inactive during opening; it works in closure.

stem: On the exam slide, which muscles protrude the mandible?
choices: Inferior lateral pterygoid and superficial masseter
Posterior temporalis and deep masseter
Medial pterygoid and temporalis
Digastric and mylohyoid
ex: Exam slide (C, Protrusion): lateral pterygoid (inferior belly) and the SUPERFICIAL masseter. Know the belly: the deep masseter retrudes, not protrudes.

stem: On the exam slide, which muscles retrude the mandible?
choices: Temporalis (posterior, horizontal fibers) and deep masseter
Inferior lateral pterygoid and superficial masseter
Medial pterygoid and superior lateral pterygoid
Suprahyoid and infrahyoid muscles

cue: Deep goes back: deep masseter + back (posterior) temporalis retrude.
why: Exam slide, retrusion: the temporalis (posterior, horizontal fibers) and the deep masseter.

The medial pterygoid elevates, and the superior lateral pterygoid stabilizes the disc in closure.

stem: On the exam slide, moving the mandible to the RIGHT uses:
choices: Right temporalis and right masseter, with left lateral and left medial pterygoids
Left temporalis and left masseter, with right lateral and right medial pterygoids
Both lateral pterygoids equally
Right lateral pterygoid and right medial pterygoid only

cue: Pterygoids Push from the other side; T and M work on the side you move toward.
why: To the right: right temporalis and right masseter on the working side, with the LEFT lateral and LEFT medial pterygoids pulling from the opposite side.
This set moves the mandible to the LEFT, the mirror image.
Both lateral pterygoids contracting equally give straight protrusion, not a move to one side.

stem: All of the following help move the mandible to the LEFT EXCEPT the:
choices: Left lateral pterygoid
Right lateral pterygoid
Left temporalis
Right medial pterygoid
ex: To the left (exam slide F): left temporalis and left masseter, with the RIGHT lateral and RIGHT medial pterygoids. The left lateral pterygoid would swing the chin to the right.
why: The left lateral pterygoid pulls the left condyle forward and medially, swinging the chin to the RIGHT, so it doesn't help move left.
The right lateral pterygoid swings the chin to the left, so it is on the slide for a left movement.

The right medial pterygoid pulls from the opposite side to swing the chin left.

stem: Which muscles are the suprahyoid (inframandibular) group?
choices: Digastric, geniohyoid, mylohyoid, stylohyoid
Sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid
Masseter, temporalis, medial and lateral pterygoid
Sternocleidomastoid and trapezius
ex: Suprahyoid (inframandibular): digastric, geniohyoid, mylohyoid, stylohyoid; they help open the mandible. Infrahyoid: sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid, thyrohyoid; they stabilize the hyoid. Supramandibular = the four muscles of mastication.
why: Digastric, geniohyoid, mylohyoid and stylohyoid form the suprahyoid (inframandibular) group that helps open the jaw.
Sternohyoid, omohyoid, sternothyroid and thyrohyoid are the infrahyoids, which stabilize the hyoid.
These four are the muscles of mastication (supramandibular group).
The sternocleidomastoid and trapezius are neck muscles that maintain head position.

stem: What is the main job of the infrahyoid muscles in jaw opening?
choices: Stabilize the floating hyoid bone so the suprahyoids can pull against it
Pull the mandible down directly
Elevate the mandible during swallowing so that the teeth meet firmly in MIP
Protrude the tongue
ex: The hyoid "articulates with nothing"; it floats. To open, the infrahyoids first contract rigidly below it "and now it sits there like a rock," so the suprahyoids can depress the mandible. When swallowing they relax to let the hyoid move forward.
why: The hyoid floats, so the infrahyoids contract rigidly below it to make it a fixed base the suprahyoids can pull against.
The infrahyoids don't attach to the mandible; the suprahyoids pull it down once the hyoid is fixed.
The elevators bring the teeth into MIP; in swallowing the infrahyoids relax so the hyoid can move forward.
Protruding the tongue isn't their job; they stabilize the hyoid.

stem: The digastric acts through its intermediate tendon on the hyoid bone to:
choices: Depress (open) the mandible
Elevate the mandible
Retrude the mandible
Stabilize the disc
ex: The digastric has anterior and posterior bellies joined by an intermediate tendon on the hyoid; "a super important opening muscle." With the hyoid fixed, the anterior belly starts the opening and the posterior belly continues it.
why: With the hyoid fixed, the anterior belly starts opening and the posterior belly continues it: a key opening muscle.
The digastric is an opener; elevation is done by the masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid.
Retrusion is done by the posterior temporalis and deep masseter.
Disc stabilization is the superior lateral pterygoid's job.

stem: Besides helping open the mandible, the mylohyoid:
choices: Forms the floor of the mouth
Stabilizes the articular disc
Retrudes the mandible
Elevates the hyoid during speech only
ex: The mylohyoid forms the muscular floor of the mouth (a wall) and, by shortening, helps depress the mandible. The geniohyoid is important for tongue function.
why: The mylohyoid forms the muscular floor of the mouth and, by shortening, helps depress the mandible.
Disc stabilization belongs to the superior lateral pterygoid.
Retrusion belongs to the posterior temporalis and deep masseter.
Its extra role is forming the floor of the mouth, not a speech-only role.

stem: The sternocleidomastoid and trapezius matter to mandibular function because they:
choices: Act as a sling that maintains head position
Elevate the mandible during clenching
Pull the hyoid forward in swallowing
Limit opening like ligaments
ex: These superficial neck muscles stabilize the head (a sling for head position). Head posture in turn changes the path of closure and the tooth contacts, which is why chairside contacts change when the patient sits up.
why: These neck muscles act as a sling that keeps head position, and head posture changes the path of closure and the contacts.
They don't attach to the mandible; elevation is by the masseter, temporalis and medial pterygoid.
Moving the hyoid in swallowing is done by the suprahyoids, not these neck muscles.
They are muscles that stabilize the head; limiting opening is the job of ligaments.

stem: Dr. Givan compared jaws: dogs and alligators vs cows and camels. Where do humans fit?
choices: In between: we both hinge and slide, giving complex motion
Like dogs: a pure hinge, relying on powerful neck muscles to tear
Like cows: mostly lateral grinding
Like neither: humans have no translation
ex: Carnivores like dogs (and alligators) are locked into hinging and tear with powerful neck muscles; grazers like cows and camels have enormous lateral movement to grind plants. Humans are in between, which makes our motion complex and harder to predict.
why: Humans are in between: we both hinge and slide, so our motion is complex and harder to predict.
Dogs and alligators are locked into hinging; humans also translate.
Cows and camels grind with large lateral movement; humans have less, plus a hinge.

stem: What is happening, and what should you do?
choices: Open lock (condyle in front of the eminence): press down on the buccal shelf
The disc is displaced posteriorly; push the chin firmly back
The patient is locked in centric relation; have them bite firmly on a cotton roll
The masseter is in spasm; inject local anesthetic into it
ex: Long wide-open appointment + can't close + the condyle sitting in front of the articular eminence (empty glenoid fossa on the view) = open lock. Distract the condyle downward via the buccal shelf, "not a posterior force": pushing the chin back drives the condyle into the eminence it has to get under. CR is the seated position, the opposite of this.
pbox: 3-hour appointment with a rubber dam, mouth wide open
Cannot bring her teeth together; mild pain
See the lateral TMJ view, taken while she tries to close
why: Long wide opening, can't close, condyles felt in front of the eminences: open lock. Press down on the buccal shelf to distract the condyle.
