CR is the seated position in the fossa; here the condyle is out in front of the eminence, and biting can't fix that.
The palpation finding points to the condyle position, not a muscle spasm; the fix is distraction, not injection.

stem: Why press down on the buccal shelf instead of pushing her chin back?
choices: Downward force distracts the condyle so it can come back over the eminence
A backward push works too, but it is slower and tires the masseter
Downward pressure stretches the superior head of the lateral pterygoid
The TM ligament attaches at the buccal shelf, so pressing there pulls the disc back
ex: In an open lock the condyle is stuck in front of the eminence. Gentle downward pressure on the buccal shelf distracts it so it can clear the eminence and return. Dr. Givan: "Not a posterior force, because you don't want to push it back against it." A backward push is the mistake, not a slower option. The superior head of the lateral pterygoid isn't what you are working on (it is active in closing), and the TM ligament runs from the eminence to the condylar neck, not the buccal shelf.
pbox: 3-hour appointment with a rubber dam, mouth wide open
Cannot bring her teeth together; mild pain
See the lateral TMJ view, taken while she tries to close
why: The condyle is stuck in front of the eminence; pressing down distracts it so it can slide back over.
A posterior force is the mistake: it pushes the condyle against the eminence ("not a posterior force").
The maneuver repositions the condyle; it isn't about stretching the superior head, which is active in closing.
The TM ligament runs from the eminence to the condylar neck; the buccal shelf is just a firm place to press.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Translation happens in the upper (superior) compartment of the TMJ.
2. Rotation happens in the lower (inferior) compartment.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Both are true. The disc divides the joint: the upper compartment (disc to temporal bone) translates, the lower compartment (disc to condyle) rotates, so the disc stays over the condyle wherever it goes.
why: Statement 1 is true: translation is between the disc and the temporal bone. Statement 2 is true: rotation is between the disc and the condyle.
Statement 1 is true, not false: translation is between the disc and the temporal bone. Statement 2 is true, not false: rotation is between the disc and the condyle.
Statement 2 is true, not false: rotation is between the disc and the condyle.
Statement 1 is true, not false: translation is between the disc and the temporal bone.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The intermediate zone is the thickest part of the disc.
2. The disc is slightly thicker medially than laterally.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true

why: Statement 1 is false, not true: the intermediate zone is the thinnest part; the posterior border is the thickest.
Statement 2 is true, not false: the thicker medial side is why a slipped disc tends to go forward or medially.

Statement 1 is false, not true: the intermediate zone is the thinnest part; the posterior border is the thickest. Statement 2 is true, not false: the thicker medial side is why a slipped disc tends to go forward or medially.

stem:

choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true

Statement 1 is false: the superior lamina is elastic; the inferior lamina is the collagenous one. Statement 2 is false: they are loaded with vessels and nerves; the disc's intermediate zone is the avascular part.
Statement 1 is false, not true: the superior lamina is elastic; the inferior lamina is the collagenous one.

stem:

Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false

Statement 1 is true, not false: it pulls the condyle forward, down and toward the midline.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. The temporalis is the jaw's power closer.

choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true

Statement 2 is true: its fibers run up and forward, pushing the mandible superiorly and anteriorly, which is the seated (CR) position.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: the temporalis is a positioner on the thin coronoid process; the masseter is the power closer.
Statement 2 is true, not false: its fibers run up and forward, which seats the condyles.

stem: True or false: The TMJ disc is properly called a meniscus.
choices: True
False
ex: False. It is improper to call the disc a meniscus, which is crescent-shaped (one convex and one concave side), as in the knee. The TMJ disc is biconcave dense fibrous connective tissue.
why: A meniscus is crescent-shaped, as in the knee; the TMJ disc is biconcave.
Dr. Givan: calling it a meniscus is improper; it is a biconcave disc.

stem: True or false: Neither TMJ can move independently of the other.
choices: True
False
ex: True. One bone, two joints: no movement of one side happens without the other.
why: The mandible is one bone with two joints, so the joints always move together.
Both condyles belong to one mandible, so one can't move without the other.

stem: True or false: The TMJ is a ginglymoarthrodial joint: it both hinges and glides.
choices: True
False
ex: True. A ginglymus joint hinges in one plane (elbow, knee); an arthrodial joint glides (wrist, ankle). The TMJ does both.
why: It hinges (ginglymus) and glides (arthrodial).
Hinging and gliding together is exactly what ginglymoarthrodial means.

stem: True or false: The outer oblique portion of the TM ligament limits rotational opening.
choices: True
False
ex: True. The outer oblique portion slings around the posterior condylar neck to the eminence and limits rotational opening; the inner horizontal portion limits posterior movement of the condyle and disc.
why: That is the outer oblique portion's job.
The outer oblique portion does limit rotational opening; posterior movement is the inner horizontal portion.

stem: True or false: The stylomandibular ligament limits posterior movement of the condyle.
choices: True
False
ex: False. The stylomandibular (and sphenomandibular) ligaments limit opening and forward motion. Posterior movement of the condyle and disc is limited by the inner horizontal portion of the TM ligament.
why: It limits opening and forward motion; the inner horizontal TM ligament limits posterior movement.
Posterior movement is the inner horizontal TM ligament's job; the stylomandibular limits opening and forward motion.

stem: True or false: To reduce an open lock, push the mandible straight back.
choices: True
False
ex: False. Apply gentle downward pressure on the buccal shelf to distract the condyle from in front of the eminence, "not a posterior force."
why: Dr. Givan: gentle downward pressure on the buccal shelf, not a posterior force.
The condyle is stuck in front of the eminence, so you distract it downward on the buccal shelf.

stem: True or false: The medial pterygoid and the masseter form the pterygomasseteric sling.
choices: True
False
ex: True. The medial pterygoid, "the unsung hero," is a meaty elevator on the inside of the ramus; with the masseter outside it forms the powerful pterygomasseteric sling.
why: Inside and outside the ramus, they make the sling together.
That is the sling: medial pterygoid inside the ramus, masseter outside.

stem: True or false: To open, the suprahyoid muscles fix the hyoid first, then the infrahyoids pull the mandible down.
choices: True
False
ex: False, it is reversed. The infrahyoids first fix the hyoid "like a rock," then the suprahyoids (digastric, geniohyoid, mylohyoid, stylohyoid) pull the mandible down.
why: The roles are swapped: infrahyoids stabilize, suprahyoids open.
Infrahyoids fix the hyoid first; then the suprahyoids pull the mandible down.

stem:
Which statements about the TMJ and its disc are true?
1. Rotation happens in the lower compartment, between the disc and the condyle.
2. The intermediate zone is the thickest part of the disc.

choices: 1 and 3 only
1, 3 and 4
2 and 3 only
3 and 4 only

The disc is biconcave: a thick anterior border, a thinner avascular intermediate zone where the condyle sits, and an even thicker posterior border; it is slightly thicker medially. The retrodiscal tissues are loaded with vessels and nerves, so functioning on them hurts.
why: Statements 1 and 3 are true. Statement 2 is false: the intermediate zone is the thin part where the condyle sits; the posterior border is the thickest. Statement 4 is false: the retrodiscal tissues are loaded with vessels and nerves, and functioning on them causes substantial pain.

It includes 2, which is false: the intermediate zone is the thin part where the condyle sits; the posterior border is the thickest. It leaves out 1, which is true: the lower compartment (disc to condyle) is where rotation happens; translation is in the upper.

It includes 4, which is false: the retrodiscal tissues are loaded with vessels and nerves, and functioning on them causes substantial pain. It leaves out 1, which is true: the lower compartment (disc to condyle) is where rotation happens; translation is in the upper.

stem:
Which muscles move the mandible to the right, according to the exam slide?

2. Right lateral pterygoid

4. Right masseter
5. Left lateral pterygoid

It includes 2, which is false: the right lateral pterygoid swings the chin to the left; it's the left one that moves the jaw to the right. It leaves out 3, which is true: the left medial pterygoid works with the left lateral pterygoid to move the jaw to the right.

stem: Which are the three PRIMARY functions of the masticatory system?
choices: Mastication, swallowing and speech
Mastication, respiration and speech
Swallowing, respiration and expression of emotion
Mastication, swallowing and respiration
ex: Primary: mastication, deglutition (swallowing) and speech. Secondary: respiration and expression of emotions.
why: The three primary functions are mastication, deglutition (swallowing) and speech.
Respiration is a secondary function, so it replaces swallowing in error.
Respiration and expression of emotion are the secondary functions.
Respiration is secondary; speech is the third primary function.

stem: When the teeth are NOT in contact, what determines mandibular position?
choices: Muscles and ligaments
Anterior guidance
Condylar guidance
The teeth's cusp inclines
ex: "When the teeth are not in contact, mandibular position is determined by the muscles and ligaments (not AG or CG)!" Teeth only influence mandibular motion when they touch; most function happens with the teeth apart.

Anterior guidance only acts while the anterior teeth touch.
Condylar guidance shapes movement with the teeth in contact; apart, muscles and ligaments decide position.
Cusp inclines influence motion only when the teeth touch.

stem: Precise timing between antagonistic muscles during chewing comes from:
choices: A central pattern generator that runs learned patterns (engrams)
Conscious control of each muscle by the motor cortex
The myotactic reflex alone
The TM ligament limiting movement
ex: The central pattern generator (brainstem) times agonist and antagonist activity and creates learned patterns, "engrams." It is generally subconscious but can be brought under conscious control, like breathing and walking, and it keeps adjusting the stroke from sensory input (e.g., particle size).
why: The brainstem's central pattern generator times agonists and antagonists and runs learned patterns called engrams.
Chewing is generally subconscious, though it can be brought under conscious control, like breathing.
The myotactic reflex maintains posture and vertical dimension; it doesn't time the whole chewing cycle.
The TM ligament limits movement; it doesn't time muscle activity.

stem: Which sensory sources feed the CNS during chewing?
choices: PDL, tongue, TMJs, periosteum, muscle spindles and mucosa
Only the PDL
Only the muscle spindles of the masseter
Only the taste buds
ex: Receptors in the PDL, tongue, TMJs, periosteum, soft tissues, muscle spindles and mucosa report position, force and the bolus. Much of the processing is fast, at the brainstem and up to the thalamus; efferents activate some groups and inhibit others.
why: Receptors in the PDL, tongue, TMJs, periosteum, muscle spindles and mucosa all report position, force and the bolus.
The PDL is one source among many; the tongue, joints, spindles and mucosa feed in too.
Muscle spindles are one source; the PDL, tongue, TMJs, periosteum and mucosa also report.
Taste is only part of the input; position and force come from the PDL, TMJs, spindles and more.

stem: You bite unexpectedly on a cherry pit. Which reflex stops the closure and opens the jaw?
choices: A polysynaptic (nociceptive) reflex: elevators stop, openers fire
The myotactic reflex
The central pattern generator running its normal chewing engram unchanged
The gag reflex
ex: Noxious stimuli trigger a polysynaptic reflex: many closing muscles stop at once and many opening muscles activate, so you don't break a tooth. The simpler myotactic reflex maintains posture and vertical dimension.
why: A noxious bite triggers a polysynaptic reflex: many closers stop and many openers fire, so you don't break a tooth.
The myotactic reflex is simpler; it maintains posture and vertical dimension, not a protective opening.
The pattern generator adjusts from input; an unexpected pit triggers a protective reflex that stops the stroke.
The gag reflex protects the airway at the back of the mouth; it isn't what stops a biting closure.

stem: The chewing stroke is divided into an opening phase and a closing component. What are the two parts of the closing component, in order?
choices: Crushing phase, then grinding phase
Grinding phase, then crushing phase
Gliding phase, then single-contact phase
Incising phase, then crushing phase
ex: Opening phase: mostly vertical with a lateral slide at the end. Closing: the crushing phase (gradual vertical and horizontal motion trapping the bolus), then the grinding phase (a small lateral slide at the very end, back into ICP).
why: The closing component starts with the crushing phase, then ends with the grinding phase back into ICP.
The order is reversed: crushing comes first, and grinding is the small lateral slide at the very end.
Gliding and single are the two kinds of tooth contact, not the phases of the stroke.
Incising happens at the start of chewing a bite; the closing phases are crushing then grinding.

stem: A typical chewing stroke opens about ___ and moves about ___ laterally.
ex: Chewing opens only about 16-18 mm and moves about 5-6 mm laterally: "not a lot of lateral motion, but it's enough." 40-60 mm is maximum opening; 20-25 mm is pure rotation.
why: A chewing stroke opens about 16-18 mm and moves about 5-6 mm laterally.
40-60 mm is maximum opening, far more than a chewing stroke uses.
20-25 mm is the limit of pure rotation, and chewing moves 5-6 mm laterally, not 1-2.
2-4 mm is the postural position below MICP, too little opening for a chewing stroke.

stem: Put one chewing cycle in order, starting with the teeth together.
steps: Lateral shift at the end of opening
Crushing: closing at an angle to trap the bolus
Grinding: small lateral slide at the end
ex: Open mostly vertically, swing to the chewing side at the end of opening, close at an angle (the posterior teeth are inclined) to trap and crush the bolus, finish with a small grinding slide, and come back to ICP, "like coming back to home plate."

stem: When the teeth come together during chewing, which position do they return to?
choices: The intercuspal position (MIP), "home plate"
Centric occlusion, with the condyles seated
The edge-to-edge position
The clinical rest position
ex: "No matter how you run around the bases, you always come back to home plate." Chewing contacts return to MIP, the neuromuscularly found position of best stability, not to CO.
why: Chewing contacts return to MIP, the neuromuscularly found position of best stability: home plate.
CO (condyles seated) is not where chewing ends; the teeth return to MIP.
Edge-to-edge is the end of the anterior guidance, not the chewing endpoint.
The clinical rest position has the teeth apart, about 8 mm below MICP, so it is not a contact position.

stem: How does tooth contact change as a bolus is chewed?
choices: It increases; before the swallow, teeth contact on nearly every stroke
Contact frequency decreases as the food gets softer and the bolus is lubricated
There is never tooth contact during chewing
Contact occurs only on the first stroke
ex: Early studies predicted no contact during chewing, but some does occur, and it increases as the food breaks down, to nearly every stroke before swallowing. Average contact lasts about 194 ms (under two-tenths of a second).
why: Contact increases as the food breaks down, to nearly every stroke right before the swallow.
This is reversed: contact becomes more frequent as the food breaks down.
Early studies predicted no contact, but some does happen, and it increases.
Contact grows through the cycle; it isn't limited to the first stroke.

stem: The average duration of a tooth contact during chewing is about:
choices: 194 ms
2 seconds
683 ms
20 ms
ex: About 194 ms. 683 ms is the length of the swallowing contact; 20 µm (not ms) is what the PDL can detect.
why: An average chewing contact lasts about 194 ms, under two-tenths of a second.
Two seconds is far too long; even swallowing contact is only about 683 ms.
683 ms is the duration of the swallowing contact, not a chewing contact.
The 20 is the PDL's detection threshold, in micrometers, not a contact time.

stem: "Gliding" tooth contacts during chewing occur:
choices: In the opening and grinding phases, as cusp inclines pass each other
Only at MICP, as a single vertical tap at the very end of the closing phase
Only during swallowing
Only on the non-working side
ex: Two kinds of contact: gliding (cusp inclines glide across each other in the opening phase, 56%, and grinding phase, 60%) and single (a vertical tap close to MICP).
why: Gliding contacts happen as cusp inclines pass each other in the opening (56%) and grinding (60%) phases.
A vertical tap near MICP is the other kind, the single contact.
Gliding contacts are part of the chewing stroke, not only swallowing.
Gliding contacts happen across the chewing stroke, not only on the non-working side.

stem: Seen from the side on the working (food) side, the mandible opens ___ and then moves ___ in early closure.
choices: Anteriorly; posteriorly
Posteriorly; anteriorly
Straight down; straight up
Laterally; medially
ex: Working side, sagittal: the mandible opens anteriorly, then moves posteriorly during early closure, aligning the teeth with the masseter's maximum force vector. On the non-working side movement is mostly vertical and the condyle stays anteriorly positioned during closure.
why: On the working side the mandible opens anteriorly, then moves posteriorly in early closure to line up with the masseter's force vector.
The order is reversed: it opens anteriorly and moves back in early closure.
Straight down and up describes the non-working side better, where movement is mostly vertical.
Lateral and medial is the frontal view; the question asks about the side (sagittal) view.

stem: How does mandibular movement change from early to late in chewing a bite of food?
choices: Anterior (incising) and lateral movement are both greater early and decrease later
Lateral movement increases as the food is broken down and the bolus becomes smaller
Movement becomes larger as the bolus is lubricated
There is no change; every stroke is identical
ex: Early: substantial anterior movement for incising and more lateral movement. As the food breaks down, lateral movement decreases. Harder food also means more lateral movement.
why: Early on there is more anterior (incising) and lateral movement, and both decrease as the food breaks down.
Lateral movement decreases, not increases, as the bolus gets smaller.
Movement gets smaller, not larger, as the food is broken down and lubricated.
The stroke changes over a bite: larger early, smaller as the food breaks down.

stem: Compared with cheese, chewing a carrot typically involves:
choices: More lateral movement and more muscle power
Less lateral movement and less force
No tooth contact at all
A purely vertical chewing stroke
ex: "In general, harder the food, the more lateral movement. More muscle power needed." Some patients don't change their number of strokes with food texture.
why: Harder food generally means more lateral movement and more muscle power.
This is reversed: a carrot needs more lateral movement and force than cheese.
Tooth contact still happens with hard food and increases as it breaks down.
Harder food adds lateral movement; the stroke isn't purely vertical.

stem: About what share of patients chew mostly on one side, and which side?
choices: About 78%, usually the side with the most contacts in lateral glide
About 25%, usually the side with fewer teeth and the least tooth wear
About 50%, always the dominant-hand side
Nearly 100%, always the left
ex: 78% tend to chew on one side, usually the side with the most stable contacts in lateral glide. That loads the TMJs unequally, but Okeson says it normally isn't a problem because the superior lateral pterygoids stabilize the discs.
why: About 78% chew mostly on one side, usually the side with the most stable contacts in lateral glide.
The share is about 78%, and the preferred side is the one with the most contacts, not fewer teeth.
About 78%, not half, and the preferred side follows the contacts, not handedness.
Most chew on one side, but not nearly all, and not always the left.

stem: How does cusp form affect the chewing stroke?
choices: Tall cusps give a vertical stroke; flat cusps give a broader stroke
Tall cusps promote a broad, horizontal stroke; flat cusps a purely vertical one
Cusp height has no effect on the stroke
Flat cusps force a purely vertical stroke
ex: Tall cusps = mostly vertical strokes (so they don't hit each other); flattened cusps (natural or worn) = broader, more horizontal strokes. Matters when rehabilitating: a flat-cusped bruxer gets flatter crowns to fit the envelope of function.
why: Tall cusps give mostly vertical strokes so they don't collide; flattened cusps allow broader, more horizontal strokes.
This is reversed: tall cusps keep the stroke vertical, flat cusps let it broaden.
Cusp form matters; it's why a flat-cusped bruxer gets flatter crowns to fit their envelope of function.
Flat cusps allow a broader, more horizontal stroke, not a purely vertical one.

stem: In a heavily worn bruxer, where is MIP?
choices: It becomes a zone: the patient can close almost anywhere
It is the same as centric occlusion, because the joints seat
It cannot be reached at all
It is always 1.25 mm anterior to CR
ex: "I would say it becomes a range. It becomes a zone." With flattened teeth there is no single true MIP, and that is a warning about restoring such patients "in MIP."
why: With flattened teeth there is no single MIP; it becomes a range, a zone, which is a warning about restoring them in MIP.
Worn teeth don't make CO and MIP the same; MIP becomes a zone instead of a point.
The patient can still close into contact; MIP just spreads into a zone.
About 1.25 mm is the average CO-to-MIP difference in general, not a fixed rule for bruxers.

stem: Patients with TMJ pain tend to chew with:
choices: Slower, shorter, more irregular and less repeatable strokes
Faster, larger strokes to finish quickly
Strokes identical to pain-free patients
Exclusively vertical strokes on the painful side
ex: Guarded motion: less repeatable patterns, slower and shorter strokes, more irregular paths related to the painful condyle, and fewer strokes.
why: Guarded motion: slower, shorter, more irregular and less repeatable strokes, with fewer strokes.
Pain makes strokes slower and shorter, not faster and larger.
Patients with TMJ pain chew differently: guarded, slower and less repeatable.
Their strokes are irregular and related to the painful condyle, not purely vertical.

stem: Bite force at the first molar is about ___ that at the central incisor, which is one reason anterior teeth tolerate off-axis loading.
choices: Three to five times
The same as
Half of
Ten to twenty times
ex: Force falls off the farther you are from the condyles. "Our molars may be anywhere from three to five times the amount of force at the first molar than we have at the central incisor." (Slides: first molar 91-198 lb vs incisor 29-51 lb.)
why: Force at the first molar is about three to five times that at the central incisor, since force falls off away from the condyles.
Force isn't the same; it falls off the farther a tooth is from the condyles.
This is backwards: the molar has much more force than the incisor, not half.
Ten to twenty times overstates it; the lecture said three to five times.

stem: Which bite-force figures match the lecture slides?
choices: Male maximum 118-142 lb; female 79-99 lb; greatest ever measured 975 lb
Male maximum 975 lb; female 500 lb
Incisor 91-198 lb; first molar 29-51 lb; dentures about the same as natural teeth
Carrots need 16 lb and meat 30 lb
ex: Male max 118-142 lb, female 79-99 lb, greatest measured 975 lb (Gibbs). First molar 91-198 vs incisor 29-51. Carrots about 30 lb, meat about 16 lb (the swapped pair is the trap). Biting force increases with age to maturity and with practice (tough diets).
why: These match the slides: male maximum 118-142 lb, female 79-99 lb, and 975 lb the greatest ever measured.
975 lb is the record ever measured, not a typical male maximum; females are 79-99 lb.
The tooth values are swapped (first molar 91-198 lb, incisor 29-51 lb), and dentures give far less force.
The food values are swapped: carrots need about 30 lb and meat about 16 lb.

stem: About how much bite force does a complete denture wearer have compared with the natural dentition?
choices: A small fraction: 25% on the slide, closer to 15% per Dr. Givan
About the same
About 75%
More, because acrylic teeth do not flex and there is no PDL to cushion the bite
ex: The slide says dentures give 25% of maximum force; Dr. Givan added that most dentists would say closer to 15%. Either way, it is far less than natural teeth.
why: Dentures give a small fraction: 25% of maximum force on the slide, closer to 15% per Dr. Givan.
Denture wearers have far less bite force than natural teeth.
75% is far too high; the slide says 25%, and Dr. Givan says closer to 15%.
Denture bite force is much lower, not higher, than the natural dentition.

stem: Which patient is likely to have the HIGHEST bite force?
choices: A short, square face with a low Frankfort-mandibular plane angle (FMA)
A long face with a high FMA (divergent jaws)
A patient who chews only on bread
A complete denture wearer
ex: Markedly divergent jaws (large FMA, long face) = lower bite forces; roughly parallel jaws (low FMA, square face) = high forces. Dr. Givan can sometimes predict whether provisionals will survive from the facial profile alone.
why: Roughly parallel jaws (low FMA, short square face) give the highest bite forces.
Divergent jaws (high FMA, long face) give lower bite forces.
A soft diet like bread means less practice; tough diets raise bite force.
Denture wearers have only a small fraction of natural bite force.

stem: A restoration left 0.5 mm high in occlusion:
choices: Can produce about twice the normal force on that tooth
Is too small for the patient to notice
Reduces force on the tooth
Only matters on anterior teeth
ex: High occlusion of 0.5 mm resulted in twice the values of normal occlusion, and it becomes painful. Remember the PDL detects about 20 µm, so 500 µm is enormous.
why: A restoration 0.5 mm high produced about twice the normal force and becomes painful.
The PDL detects about 20 µm, so 500 µm high is enormous and easily felt.
A high restoration increases force on that tooth, roughly doubling it.
A high restoration matters on any tooth, not only anteriors.

stem: With tougher foods, most chewing happens in the area of the:
choices: Second premolar and first molar
Incisors
Second and third molars
Canines
ex: Serious chewing happens mostly at the second premolar and first molar, where the tongue can work. That supports the shortened dental arch concept: second and third molars add less function than you might think.
why: Serious chewing happens mostly at the second premolar and first molar, where the tongue can work.
Incisors cut food; heavy chewing of tough food happens further back.
Second and third molars add less function than you might think, which supports the shortened dental arch.
Canines guide and tear; the main chewing area is the second premolar and first molar.

stem: Dr. Givan described the tongue as the mouth's "knife, fork and spoon." Which muscle does he say it could not work without?
choices: The buccinator
The masseter
The digastric
The temporalis
ex: The tongue divides the food, moves it onto the chewing surfaces, gathers and sweeps the bolus back, and pushes it to the oropharynx. The buccinator contracts to make a controlled wall and returns food from the vestibule; it is not just something we bite.
why: The buccinator makes a controlled cheek wall and returns food from the vestibule, so the tongue can work.
The masseter is a closing muscle; the tongue's partner is the buccinator.
The digastric helps open the jaw; it isn't the tongue's partner in handling food.
The temporalis positions the jaw; the tongue's partner is the buccinator.

stem: Match the term: gustation is the action of:
choices: Tasting
Swallowing
Smelling
Chewing
ex: Deglutition = swallowing; gustation = tasting; olfaction = smelling. Anosmic = complete loss of smell; hyposmic = reduced sense of smell.
why: Gustation is tasting.
Swallowing is deglutition, not gustation.
Smelling is olfaction, not gustation.
Chewing is mastication, not gustation.

stem: A patient with a complete loss of the sense of smell is:
choices: Anosmic
Hyposmic
Agnostic
Dysgeusic
ex: Anosmic: complete loss of smell. Hyposmic: reduced sense of smell. (Ageusia and dysgeusia are taste terms.)
why: Anosmic means a complete loss of the sense of smell.
Hyposmic means a reduced, not lost, sense of smell.
Agnostic is not a smell term at all.
Dysgeusia is a taste term, a distorted sense of taste.

stem: The (not necessarily conscious) decision to swallow depends on all of these EXCEPT:
choices: The number of chewing strokes completed
Degree of fineness of the food
Intensity of taste extracted
Degree of lubrication of the bolus
ex: Three factors: fineness of the food, intensity of taste extracted, and lubrication of the bolus. There is no fixed stroke count; some people chew the same number of strokes regardless of texture.
why: There is no fixed stroke count; some people chew the same number of strokes whatever the food.
Fineness of the food is one of the three factors in the decision to swallow.
Intensity of taste extracted is one of the three factors in the decision to swallow.
Lubrication of the bolus is one of the three factors in the decision to swallow.

stem: She asks whether the stretched ligaments in her jaw joint will tighten back up. What is true?
choices: They won't: ligaments don't heal, so the joint has to adapt in other ways
They will: ligaments remodel to their old length within a few weeks of rest
They will: the disc reattaches once the swelling in the joint goes down
They won't, but only because she is over 40; younger ligaments heal
ex: Ligaments don't heal, so stretched discal ligaments require other adaptations (L2). They don't remodel back to length with rest, the disc doesn't simply reattach, and the notes give no age at which ligaments start healing.
pbox: 3-hour appointment with a rubber dam, mouth wide open
Cannot bring her teeth together; mild pain
See the lateral TMJ view, taken while she tries to close
why: Ligaments don't heal, so stretched discal ligaments require other adaptations (L2).
Ligaments don't remodel back to length with rest; they don't heal.
Nothing in the joint simply reattaches as swelling settles; stretched ligaments stay stretched.
Ligaments don't heal at any age; the notes give no age cutoff.

stem: How does a typical adult stabilize the mandible to swallow?
choices: Somatic swallow: the teeth are brought together in MIP
Visceral swallow: the tongue is thrust between the arches
By retruding the mandible into CR
By opening slightly so the tongue can move
ex: Adults use a somatic swallow: the elevators bring the teeth into MIP and hold the mandible there, so the suprahyoids can move the hyoid and open the esophageal path. Retrusion during swallowing "may not occur as once thought": ICP predominates.
why: Adults use a somatic swallow: the elevators hold the teeth in MIP so the suprahyoids can move the hyoid.
Tongue thrusting between the arches is the infantile (visceral) swallow.
Retrusion during swallowing may not happen as once thought; ICP predominates.
The mandible is braced with the teeth together, not held slightly open.

stem: Over-retention of the infantile (visceral) swallow can lead to:
choices: Anterior displacement of teeth, including anterior open bite
Posterior crossbite only
A deep vertical overlap
Increased bite force
ex: Visceral swallow: the mandible is braced by putting the tongue forward between the arches; normal until the posterior teeth erupt (and still used for liquids). Kept too long, the tongue pressure displaces teeth anteriorly, e.g. anterior open bite.
why: Kept too long, the tongue thrust between the arches pushes teeth forward, for example an anterior open bite.
Tongue pressure acts on the anterior teeth, producing open bite rather than a posterior crossbite.
Anterior tongue pressure opens the bite; it doesn't deepen the vertical overlap.
The visceral swallow affects tooth position, not bite force.

stem: Compared with chewing contacts, tooth contact during swallowing is:
choices: Heavier (about 66.5 lb) and longer (about 683 ms)
Lighter and shorter
The same force but shorter
Absent in adults
ex: Swallowing contact averages about 66.5 lb for about 683 ms, 7.8 lb more than average for mastication. "We find that we put a lot more force than we ever use in mastication."
why: Swallowing contact averages about 66.5 lb for about 683 ms, heavier and longer than a chewing contact.
Swallowing contact is heavier and longer than chewing contact, not lighter and shorter.
It is both heavier and longer: about 683 ms versus about 194 ms in chewing.
Adults swallow with the teeth together in MIP (somatic swallow).

stem: About how many times a day do we swallow?
choices: About 590 (146 at meals, 394 between meals awake, 50 asleep)
About 50, all during meals
About 1,800, mostly at night
About 5,000
ex: About 590 times: 146 during meals, 394 between meals while awake (mostly saliva) and 50 during sleep (less saliva). Lec3-2's 500 swallowing contacts and 1,800 chewing strokes describe daily tooth contact in MIP.
why: About 590 a day: 146 at meals, 394 between meals while awake (mostly saliva) and 50 asleep, when less saliva is made.
Far too few: meals account for only about 146 of the roughly 590 daily swallows; most happen between meals.
1,800 is the daily number of chewing strokes in MIP, and swallowing actually drops at night (about 50) because less saliva is made.
Much too high; the lecture's figure is about 590 swallows a day.

stem: Which event belongs to stage 1 of swallowing?
choices: The tongue presses the bolus on the palate with the lips sealed and teeth together
The pharyngeal constrictors carry the bolus into the esophagus with a peristaltic wave
The epiglottis closes over the trachea
Peristalsis carries the bolus to the cardiac sphincter
ex: Stage 1 (voluntary): the tongue separates the food and presses the bolus on the dorsum lightly against the palate, tongue tip behind the incisors; lips sealed, teeth closed; a reflex wave pushes the bolus to the back of the tongue and into the pharynx.
why: Stage 1 is the voluntary stage: lips sealed, teeth together, the tongue presses the bolus against the palate and pushes it back toward the pharynx.
Pharyngeal constrictor peristalsis carries the bolus through the pharynx in stage 2, not stage 1.
The epiglottis protects the trachea during stage 2, the pharyngeal stage.
Esophageal peristalsis to the cardiac sphincter is stage 3.

stem: All of the following happen in stage 2 of swallowing EXCEPT:
choices: The lips seal and the tongue tip presses on the palate behind the incisors
The pharyngeal constrictors produce a peristaltic wave
The soft palate rises and seals the nasal passage against the posterior pharyngeal wall
The pharyngeal openings of the Eustachian tubes open
ex: Lip seal and tongue-tip-on-palate are stage 1. Stage 2: pharyngeal constrictor peristalsis, soft palate seals the nasopharynx, epiglottis protects the trachea, Eustachian tubes open (normally closed). Stages 1 and 2 together take about 1 second.
why: This is the false one: lip seal and the tongue tip pressing the palate behind the incisors happen in stage 1, the voluntary oral stage.
Pharyngeal constrictor peristalsis is part of stage 2, so this does happen.
The soft palate rising to seal the nasopharynx is part of stage 2, so this does happen.
The Eustachian tube openings, normally closed, do open during stage 2.

stem: Stage 3 of swallowing (esophagus to stomach) takes about:
choices: 6-7 seconds
1 second
194 ms
30 seconds
ex: Stage 3: peristaltic waves carry the bolus to the cardiac sphincter, which relaxes to let it into the stomach: about 6-7 seconds. The upper esophagus has some voluntary control to return food for more chewing; the lower part is involuntary. Stages 1 + 2 take about 1 second.
why: Stage 3, esophageal peristalsis down to the cardiac sphincter, takes about 6-7 seconds.
About 1 second is how long stages 1 and 2 take together.
194 ms is far too short for the bolus to travel the esophagus; that figure is not the stage 3 time.
Too long; the bolus reaches the stomach in about 6-7 seconds.

stem: Do the teeth normally contact during speech?
choices: No; speech is too rapid, so the body keeps enough separation
Yes, on nearly every syllable
Only on "s" sounds
Only on fricatives like "f" and "v"
ex: "Tooth contacts typically do not occur in speech. It's too rapid... If the teeth hit, there will be damage." Malocclusion can still affect speech, through tooth and tongue positions, not contacts.
why: Speech is too rapid for tooth contact; the body keeps the teeth apart, and contact during speech would damage them.
Teeth do not touch on syllables; speech keeps them apart, even on the closest sounds.
Even on "s" the incisal edges come within about 1-2 mm but do not touch.
On "f" and "v" the maxillary incisal edge meets the lower lip, not the opposing teeth.

stem: In speech, what produces pitch, and what produces resonance and articulation?
choices: Pitch from the vocal cords; resonance and articulation from the oral structures
Pitch from the shape of the tongue; resonance and articulation from the vocal cords
Pitch from the lips; articulation from the diaphragm
Both come entirely from the teeth
ex: The diaphragm forces air from the lungs; contraction and relaxation of the laryngeal vocal cords sets pitch (B vs P differ only by this voicing). The tongue, lips, cheeks and mandible shape the cavity for resonance and articulation. After learning, speech is a subconscious "learned reflex."
why: The vocal cords set pitch (voicing is what separates B from P), while the tongue, lips, cheeks and mandible shape resonance and articulation.
Reversed: the vocal cords make pitch, and the tongue helps shape resonance and articulation.
The lips do not set pitch, and the diaphragm only drives air from the lungs; it does not articulate.
The teeth help shape some sounds, but pitch comes from the vocal cords and resonance from the whole oral cavity.

stem: When a patient says "f" or "v," where should the maxillary incisal edge be?
choices: Lightly touching the wet-dry line of the lower lip
Touching the mandibular incisal edges
1-2 mm above the lower lip
Against the lingual cingulum of the mandibular incisors
ex: Fricatives (f, v): the maxillary incisal edge should hit right at the wet-dry line of the lower lip. If the patient struggles to make the sound, the incisors may be too short; if they depress the lip, too long. Phonetics guides where to put incisors you are replacing.
cue: "F" for "Find the wet-dry line."
why: On "f" and "v" the maxillary incisal edge should lightly touch the wet-dry line of the lower lip.
Teeth do not contact during speech; on fricatives the upper incisors meet the lower lip, not the lower teeth.
Hovering above the lip suggests incisors too short; the edge should actually reach the wet-dry line.
The mandibular cingulum is not involved; fricatives are made between the upper incisal edge and the lower lip.

stem: When a patient with new maxillary anterior crowns says "f," the incisal edges press into and depress the lower lip. The crowns are probably:
choices: Too long
Too short
Too far lingual
Correct; some lip pressure is normal
ex: The incisal edge should just touch the wet-dry line. Depressing the lip = too long; failing to reach it (trouble making the sound) = too short.
why: Depressing the lower lip on "f" means the incisal edges reach too far, so the crowns are too long.
Too-short incisors fail to reach the wet-dry line and the patient struggles to make the sound; they don't press into the lip.
Lingual position isn't what this test shows; the lip-depression sign is about incisal length.
The edge should only lightly touch the wet-dry line; pressing into the lip is not normal.

stem: Which sound is most used to judge a functional vertical dimension (closest speaking space)?
choices: "Ah"
ex: "Let S be your guide." During "s" (counting 60-70) the incisal edges should come within about 1-2 mm. Fricatives (f, v) are used to place the incisal edge against the lip, not to judge the vertical.
why: "Let S be your guide": on "s" (counting 60-70) the incisal edges come within about 1-2 mm, giving the closest speaking space.
"F" is used to place the incisal edge against the lower lip, not to judge the vertical dimension.
"M" is a nasal sound with the teeth apart and is not used for the closest speaking space.
"Ah" opens the mouth widely, so it tells you nothing about the closest speaking space.

stem: What is happening during an "m" sound?
choices: The nasopharynx is open, the teeth are apart and the lips are together
The tongue presses the soft palate and the nasal passage is sealed
The incisal edge contacts the lower lip
The teeth touch lightly
ex: "M": nasal passages open, tongue in a neutral position, teeth separated, lips together and vibrating. "P" and "B" are plosives (lips together, soft palate sealed). Nasal sounds (m, n, ng) leave the nasal passage open.
why: On "m" the nasal passage is open, the tongue is neutral, the teeth are apart and the lips are together and vibrating.
A sealed nasal passage describes plosives like "p" and "b"; "m" is nasal, so the passage stays open.
The incisal edge meets the lower lip on fricatives ("f," "v"), not on "m."
Teeth don't touch during speech; on "m" they are separated.

stem: During sibilant sounds such as "s," the typical incisal separation is about:
choices: 2-4 mm
8 mm
ex: From the speech table (Table 11-3): sibilants (s, sh, ch, z) have a minimal separation of about 1-1.5 mm, which is why "s" is used for closest speaking space. Nasal consonants about 2-4 mm; diphthongs ("eight," "nine") about 5-10 mm.
why: Sibilants (s, sh, ch, z) have the smallest separation, about 1-1.5 mm, which is why "s" is used for closest speaking space.
5-10 mm is the separation for diphthongs such as "eight" and "nine."
2-4 mm is the separation for nasal consonants.
8 mm is far too wide for a sibilant; that range belongs to open sounds like diphthongs.

stem: What best explains this patient's anterior open bite?
choices: An over-retained visceral (infantile) swallow with a forward tongue
Over-erupted posterior teeth that prop the anterior teeth apart in MIP
A somatic swallow in MIP
A steep articular eminence
ex: The photo, taken mid-swallow, shows the back teeth together and the tongue pushed forward between the incisors. A visceral swallow braces the mandible with the tongue instead of the teeth; normal until the posterior teeth erupt, but retained it keeps pressing the anterior teeth apart (anterior open bite), a neutral zone imbalance that orthodontics alone may not fix. An adult somatic swallow closes the teeth in MIP with the tongue behind them.
pbox: "My front teeth don't touch, and I can't bite through a sandwich"
Class I; posterior teeth meet in MIP
No anterior contact in any closing position; see the photo, taken while swallowing
why: A retained visceral (infantile) swallow pushes the tongue forward between the arches, and that constant pressure can open the anterior bite.
Nothing in the case points to posterior over-eruption; the tongue pushing between the incisors on every swallow is the key finding.
A somatic (adult) swallow is done with the teeth together in MIP and the tongue behind the incisors, the opposite of this case.
A steep eminence affects posterior disclusion and cusp height; it doesn't explain a forward tongue thrust or an open bite.

stem: What should her swallow look like as an adult?
choices: Teeth together in MIP, with the elevators holding the mandible still
Tongue pushed forward between the arches to brace the mandible
Teeth apart, with the lips sealed and the jaw hanging at rest
Mandible pulled back into a retruded position before the swallow starts
ex: Adults use a somatic swallow: the teeth come together in MIP and the elevators hold the mandible there, so the hyoid can move. Bracing with the tongue forward between the arches is the visceral (infantile) swallow, normal only until the posterior teeth erupt (and with liquids); over-retained, it displaces teeth anteriorly, as in her open bite. Swallowing contacts happen in ICP, not a retruded position as once thought, and the mandible must be stabilized, not hanging at rest.
pbox: "My front teeth don't touch, and I can't bite through a sandwich"
Class I; posterior teeth meet in MIP
No anterior contact in any closing position; see the photo, taken while swallowing
why: The adult somatic swallow: teeth in MIP, elevators stabilizing the mandible so the hyoid can move.
Bracing with the tongue between the arches is the visceral (infantile) swallow; retained, it opens the anterior bite.
The mandible has to be stabilized to swallow, so the teeth come together; it isn't left hanging at rest.
Swallowing contacts happen in ICP, not a retruded position as was once thought.

stem: What does this tell you about the provisionals?
choices: They are too long: on "f" the edges should only lightly touch the wet-dry line of the lower lip
They are too short: she can't reach the lower lip, so the "f" sound is lost
The closest speaking space is too small, so she will whistle on "s"
Nothing: on "f" and "v" the incisal edges should press firmly into the lower lip
ex: Fricatives (f, v): the maxillary incisal edge should lightly touch the wet-dry line of the lower lip. Here the edge presses into the lip, so the crowns are too long (L3: "depressing the lip: too long"); too short shows as being unable to make the sound at all. The closest speaking space is checked with "s" (teeth about 1-1.5 mm apart), not with "f".
pbox: Try-in of provisional crowns on #8 and #9
"My lip feels pushed out when I talk"
See the drawing of her saying "fifty-five"
why: On "f" the incisal edge should lightly touch the wet-dry line; pressing into the lip means the crowns are too long.
Too short shows as being unable to make the "f" sound, not as the lip feeling pushed out.
The closest speaking space is checked with "s", not "f".
The edges should only lightly touch the lower lip; pressing into it is the sign of crowns that are too long.

stem: Next she counts from 60 to 70. On the "s" sounds, what should you see between her incisal edges?
choices: The closest speaking space, about 1-2 mm
Light contact of the upper and lower incisal edges
The freeway space, about 2-6 mm
The upper incisal edges resting on the wet-dry line
ex: Sibilants ("s") bring the teeth closest without touching: the closest speaking space, about 1-2 mm between the incisal edges while the patient unconsciously repeats "s" (counting 60 to 70). "Let S be your guide": it helps set a functional vertical dimension. Speech involves no tooth contact, the 2-6 mm freeway space is measured at rest, and the wet-dry line is the "f" and "v" check she just did.
pbox: Try-in of provisional crowns on #8 and #9

stem: True or false: A central pattern generator creates learned chewing patterns called engrams.

stem: True or false: About 78% of patients chew mostly on one side.

stem: True or false: A visceral (infantile) swallow is normal until the posterior teeth erupt.

False

stem: True or false: In an adult somatic swallow, the tongue pushes forward between the arches to brace the mandible.

stem: Who is called "the father of articulation," and what was his theory?
choices: W.G.A. Bonwill: the 4-inch equilateral triangle
George Monson: the 4-inch sphere centered near the glabella
Carl Christensen: posterior separation in protrusion
Norman Bennett: lateral translation of the mandible
ex: Bonwill (ca. 1858) measured thousands of skulls and found roughly a 4-inch (110 mm) equilateral triangle between the condyles and the mandibular symphysis. It led to the concept of the occlusal plane and the first scientifically based tooth arrangement: bilaterally balanced occlusion. Modern articulators commonly use 110 mm intercondylar widths.

why: W.G.A. Bonwill, the father of articulation, described a roughly 4-inch equilateral triangle between the condyles and the symphysis.
Monson's 4-inch sphere came later (ca. 1916) and built on Bonwill's triangle.
Christensen (1901) described posterior separation in protrusion, not the founding theory of articulation.
Bennett (1908) described the lateral translation of the mandible.

stem: Carl Christensen (1901) is best known for:

stem: Who first intentionally put curved condylar paths on an articulator (1902)?
choices: J.B. Parfitt
I.M. Bromill
George Monson
W.G.A. Bonwill
ex: Parfitt of England (1902) was first to place curved condylar paths on an articulator ("Parfitt Placed Paths"). Bromill (1897) diagrammed facial planes and used anatomic landmarks for tooth positions. Monson, the favorite wrong pick, came later (ca. 1916) with the 4-inch sphere: his curve is the occlusal plane, and his instrument had a central rotation center with no condyles at all, so it had no condylar paths to curve. Bonwill gave us the 4-inch triangle and bilateral balance.
why: J.B. Parfitt of England (1902) first put curved condylar paths on an articulator ("Parfitt Placed Paths").
Bromill (1897) diagrammed facial planes and used anatomic landmarks for tooth positions.

stem: George Monson's spherical theory (ca. 1916) combined all of these EXCEPT:

Bonwill's 4-inch triangle
Bilaterally balanced occlusion

ex: Monson combined the 4-inch triangle, bilateral balance, the curve of Spee and Balkwill/Christensen's condylar observations into a 4-inch sphere. His "mandibulo-maxillary instrument" did NOT reproduce the condyles: it used a central rotational center with set screws to vary the radius. Vestiges of the theory are still used today.
why: This is the one he did not include: Monson's instrument used a central rotational center with set screws and did not reproduce condylar motion.
Bonwill's 4-inch triangle was part of Monson's sphere, so it was included.

stem: How did Monson's articulator differ from a condylar articulator?
choices: It had a central rotational center for the sphere instead of reproducing the condyles
It was fully adjustable, programmed from pantograph tracings of each condyle's path
It had no anterior guide table

"Even though the geometric theory did not work... dentures built with this were generally very successful."
why: Monson's instrument had a central rotational center for the 4-inch sphere (set screws varied the radius) instead of reproducing the condyles.
Pantograph-programmed, fully adjustable articulators are gnathology, not Monson.

stem: The Pankey-Mann approach combined Monson's theory with Meyer's functionally generated path (FGP). How were the teeth restored?
choices: Lower posteriors to the 4-inch sphere; upper posteriors from an FGP
Upper posteriors to the 4-inch sphere; lower posteriors from a pantograph
All teeth on a fully adjustable articulator programmed from a pantograph
All teeth in cusp-fossa tripodization

They argued an instrument reproducing condylar motion was unnecessary because the FGP records it. A simple suspension articulator with a big base was used.
why: Pankey-Mann restored the lower posteriors to Monson's 4-inch sphere, then built the upper posteriors to a functionally generated path in wax.
Reversed: the lower teeth went to the sphere, and the uppers came from the FGP, not a pantograph.
They argued a fully adjustable instrument was unnecessary because the FGP records the motion; they used a simple articulator.
Cusp-fossa tripodization belongs to gnathology (P.K. Thomas), not Pankey-Mann.

stem: When Dr. Schuyler joined Pankey and Mann, the concept changed in all of these ways EXCEPT:

Eliminating mediotrusive (non-working) contacts
Elevating the importance of anterior guidance
Using contact areas rather than point contacts and simpler instruments

Bilateral balance was what they moved AWAY from.
why: This is the change that didn't happen: Schuyler moved the concept away from bilateral balance by eliminating balancing contacts.
Schuyler did eliminate mediotrusive (balancing) contacts, so this was a real change.
Schuyler elevated anterior guidance, so this was a real change.
Schuyler endorsed contact areas over point contacts and simpler devices like the Hanau H2, so this was a real change.

stem: Gnathology's early assumption was that:
choices: Recording the hinge axes and border movements lets a fully adjustable articulator reproduce the patient
Anterior guidance alone controls occlusion, so a simple hinge instrument and intraoral adjustment are all that is needed

It "could rarely be achieved," and failures were blamed on the instruments rather than the philosophy.

stem: Early gnathologists wanted MICP to coincide with centric relation defined as:

The anterior-superior position against the eminence
The position of least EMG activity

stem: Stallard and Stuart modified gnathology by proposing:

Restoring the lower teeth to a 4-inch sphere

stem: D'Amico's mutually protected occlusion was based on the idea that:

Canines must disclude everything because they have the longest roots of any tooth in the arch
All teeth should share excursive contacts to spread force

why: D'Amico held that anterior teeth handle off-axis force better, so they take excursive contacts while posteriors support MICP. Keyword: FORCE.
Root length isn't the rationale; D'Amico's idea was force management, and he gave excursions to the anterior teeth generally.

stem: How has digital dentistry affected gnathology?

stem: Which modern concept, while respecting CR, elevates anterior guidance as the major controlling factor?

Pankey/Dawson centers on anterior guidance rather than replicating condylar motion.
Conformative simply copies the existing occlusion.
Bioesthetics focuses on linking form, function and esthetics with a fixed interarch VDO.

stem: Bioesthetics is characterized by:
choices: Form, function and esthetics linked; VDO set from a fixed interarch measurement
Restoring at the point of least muscle activity, measured with a TENS unit (Myo-Monitor)
Copying the existing occlusion without change
Replicating condylar motion with a pantograph
ex: Bioesthetics: ideal anatomy, position and relationships are both functional and esthetic. It sets VDO from a fixed interarch measurement and promotes strong anterior vertical overlap, which allows more esthetic cusps on posterior teeth. It suits some patients (often steep guidance), not all.
why: Bioesthetics links ideal form, function and esthetics and sets VDO from a fixed interarch measurement.
Least muscle activity found with a TENS unit (Myo-Monitor) describes neuromuscular dentistry.
Copying the existing occlusion is the conformative approach.
Replicating condylar motion with a pantograph is gnathology.

stem: Neuromuscular dentistry (Jankelson, LVI) restores patients at:
choices: The myocentric point of least muscle activity, found with a TENS unit
Centric relation, found by bimanual manipulation with the teeth held apart
The existing MIP
The rearmost, uppermost, midmost position
ex: Neuromuscular dentistry uses the Myo-Monitor (a specialized TENS unit) to find the myocentric point of least muscle activity. Patients tested this way need an increased vertical, i.e. full-mouth rehabilitation regardless of condition, and a more forward jaw position without good joint stability. That is why it is not taught at UAB.
why: Neuromuscular dentistry restores at the myocentric point of least muscle activity, found with a TENS unit (Myo-Monitor).
CR by bimanual manipulation is how UAB records a seated joint position, not the neuromuscular method.
Keeping the existing MIP is the conformative approach.
RUM was the early gnathologists' definition of CR.

stem: Dr. Givan's concerns about neuromuscular dentistry include all of these EXCEPT:
choices: It restores patients in centric relation with the joints seated
It usually requires an increased vertical dimension and full-mouth rehabilitation
It places the jaw more forward, without good joint stability
It has no conservative option for patients who don't need restorations
ex: The neuromuscular myocentric point is NOT centric relation; it is a forward position of least EMG activity. The other three are his objections ("which should raise a red flag to you already").
why: This is the false one: the neuromuscular myocentric point is a forward position of least EMG activity, not centric relation with seated joints.
True concern: tested patients usually need an increased vertical dimension and full-mouth rehabilitation.
True concern: it puts the jaw more forward without good joint stability.
True concern: there is no conservative version, so it fails Speer's second test.

stem: Despite their differences, what do the modern occlusal concepts agree on?
choices: All teeth touch at once, and the back teeth should not interfere when the jaw moves
The same vertical dimension for every patient
Restoring every patient in centric relation at a slightly increased vertical dimension of occlusion
Using a fully adjustable articulator
ex: All have some success because patients adapt. Similarities: all teeth touch at once; back teeth don't interfere when the jaw moves. Differences: the maxillomandibular (condylar) relationship, VDO, and the envelope of function and anterior guidance.
why: Every modern concept agrees that all teeth should touch at once and the back teeth should not interfere when the jaw moves.
Vertical dimension is one of the main points they disagree on.
Centric relation and raised VDO are not shared by all; conformative and neuromuscular differ sharply here.
Instrument choice differs; Pankey/Dawson and others use simpler articulators than gnathology.

stem: "What a patient does to an occlusion may be more important than the occlusion itself." Frank Speer suggested testing any occlusal philosophy with which two questions?
choices: Can you apply it to all patients? Can you apply it without having to restore teeth?
Does it use CR? Does it use a face-bow?
Is it evidence-based? Is it profitable?
Does it give canine guidance in every case? Does it raise the vertical dimension of occlusion?
ex: Speer's two questions: can it be applied to all patients, and can it be applied without restoring teeth? Neuromuscular dentistry fails the second; there is no conservative version.
why: Speer asked whether a philosophy can be applied to all patients and whether it can be applied without restoring teeth.
CR and face-bow use are techniques, not Speer's two tests of an occlusal philosophy.
Evidence and profit are not Speer's questions; his tests were universality and whether it works without restoring teeth.
Canine guidance and a raised VDO are features of particular philosophies, not Speer's tests.

stem: Which four modern concepts guide how Dr. Givan approaches a rehabilitation?
choices: Posterior support, plane of occlusion, occlusal contacts, anterior guidance
Neutral zone, curve of Spee, curve of Wilson, sphere of Monson
Face-bow, articulator, CR record, MIP record
Canine guidance, group function, balance, long centric
ex: The outline: posterior support (first), plane of occlusion, occlusal contacts (point to surface), and anterior guidance. "Anterior guidance without these other elements is kind of pointless."
why: Dr. Givan's four: posterior support (first), plane of occlusion, occlusal contacts and anterior guidance.
These are curves and the neutral zone, not his four rehabilitation concepts.
These are instruments and records used to carry out treatment, not the guiding concepts.
These are occlusal schemes and contact ideas, not the four planning concepts.

stem: What is usually the FIRST consideration in a restorative treatment plan ("building the dance floor")?
choices: Developing posterior support
Restoring the anterior guidance
Treating the "social six" the patient asks about
Choosing the articulator
ex: "Support first, disclusion second." Posterior support establishes and holds the vertical dimension and takes force off the anterior teeth; anterior guidance follows closely as the second consideration.
cue: Build the dance floor (posterior support) before you choreograph the dance (anterior guidance).
why: "Support first, disclusion second": posterior support holds the vertical and keeps force off the anteriors.
Anterior guidance comes second, right after posterior support.
Treating the social six without support dooms the anterior work.
Choosing an articulator is a technique decision, not the first treatment-planning concept.

stem: A patient with no posterior occlusal contacts wants only the maxillary anterior six teeth made beautiful. What does Dr. Givan predict?
choices: The anterior work is doomed without posterior support to take the force
It will last if the porcelain is strong enough
Canine guidance will protect the new crowns
It is fine as long as the vertical overlap is 3 mm
ex: Without posterior support, the anterior teeth take all the force and chewing work they are not designed for and decline quickly ("while they may survive past your graduation..."). Give occlusal support first: implants, a partial, or teeth.
why: Without posterior support the anterior teeth take forces they weren't designed for, so the anterior work is doomed to decline.
Stronger porcelain won't fix the problem; the anteriors are still overloaded without posterior support.
Canine guidance can't help when there are no posterior teeth for it to protect or to hold the vertical.
Overlap doesn't matter if nothing in the back holds the vertical and takes chewing force.

stem: The shortened dental arch concept says that, for function, it is enough to restore back to the:
choices: Second premolar
First molar
Second molar
Third molar
ex: Shortened dental arch: restoring to the second premolar shows no difference in masticatory ability, TMD, tooth migration, periodontal support or comfort (the WHO considers at least 20 teeth functional and esthetic). Esthetics may suffer if maxillary first molars show in the smile.
why: Restoring to the second premolar shows no difference in chewing, TMD, migration, periodontal support or comfort.
Molars aren't required for function under the shortened dental arch concept; second premolars are enough.
Second molars are not needed; the concept stops at the second premolar.
Third molars are never the target; the concept stops at the second premolar.

stem: Why does losing posterior teeth make later restoration harder?
choices: Posterior overclosure: less restorative space and overloaded anteriors
The condyles move back into the rearmost, uppermost, midmost (RUM) position
The curve of Wilson flattens and the cusps wear
The freeway space shrinks to zero
ex: Without posterior teeth the patient can close down farther (posterior overclosure, the old "posterior bite collapse"), leaving less room for restorations, while the anterior teeth take forces they weren't built for.
why: Without posterior teeth the patient closes farther (posterior overclosure), leaving less restorative space and overloading the anteriors.
RUM is an old CR definition, not what happens when posterior teeth are lost.
The curve of Wilson is not the reason; the problem is the lost vertical support.
Freeway space is the gap at rest; the issue is lost vertical dimension of occlusion and restorative space.

stem: Dr. Givan's regretted case: crowns placed against an opposing molar extruded beyond the occlusal plane. What was the problem?
choices: The extruded tooth hits in every excursion, so the posteriors can't disclude
The crowns were made too short
The patient was restored in centric relation instead of in the existing MIP
The implants were placed in crossbite
ex: "No matter what I'm able to do when I go into a left or right working or a protrusive motion, I'm going to have an interference." Correct the plane first: enameloplasty for about 0.5 mm, a crown to shorten more, or extraction when the fix (intentional endo, crown lengthening into the furcation) is too much.
why: The extruded molar hits in every excursion, so the posteriors can't disclude no matter what the crowns do.
Crown length wasn't the issue; the opposing tooth broke the occlusal plane.
The problem was the extruded opposing tooth, not the choice between CR and MIP.
The case involved no implants in crossbite; the fault was an uncorrected plane of occlusion.

stem: A molar is extruded about half a millimeter beyond the occlusal plane. The simplest correction is:
choices: Enameloplasty (reshaping the enamel)
Extraction
Intentional root canal and crown lengthening
Orthodontic intrusion of the whole arch
ex: Mild extrusion (about 0.5 mm) can often be fixed with enameloplasty. More needs a crown to shorten the tooth; severe extrusion into a space may make extraction the most practical answer.
why: About 0.5 mm of extrusion can usually be corrected with enameloplasty.
Extraction is for severe extrusion when the fix would be too much, not for half a millimeter.
Intentional endo and crown lengthening are for severe extrusion, far more than 0.5 mm needs.
Intruding a whole arch is far beyond what a 0.5 mm single-tooth problem needs.

stem: Which of these does NOT prevent an ideal plane of occlusion?
choices: A shortened dental arch to the second premolar
Supraeruption
Tilting and rotation of teeth
Interferences and malocclusion
ex: Plane of occlusion problems: supra-eruption, tilting/rotation, interferences, malocclusion (the deck's "STIM"). A shortened dental arch is a legitimate treatment endpoint, not a plane violation.
why: A shortened dental arch to the second premolar is a legitimate treatment endpoint, not a problem with the plane of occlusion.
Supraeruption does break the plane of occlusion (the S of STIM).
Tilting and rotation do disturb the plane of occlusion (the T of STIM).
Interferences and malocclusion do disturb the plane of occlusion (the I and M of STIM).

stem: Tripodization (cusp tip contacting a fossa on three surfaces):
choices: Very stable, but hard to make (especially in porcelain) and needs immediate disclusion
Is the modern concept used for every restoration
Allows horizontal freedom so an immediate lateral translation can happen without an interference
Directs force down the long axis with a single flat contact
ex: Tripodization came out of gnathology: as many as 27 contacts across a quadrant, excellent stability, but difficult to achieve (extremely so in porcelain), no wiggle room, so immediate disclusion is required. Suggested only when the opposing surfaces are controlled or in full reconstruction.
why: Tripodization is very stable but hard to make, extremely so in porcelain, and it leaves no wiggle room, so it needs immediate disclusion.
Point to surface, not tripodization, is the modern contact concept used for any restoration.
Horizontal freedom for immediate lateral translation describes point-to-surface contact; tripodization has no freedom.
A cusp tip on a flat surface directing force down the long axis is point to surface, not tripodization.

stem: Why is "point to surface" the modern contact concept?
choices: A cusp tip meets a flat area: force down the long axis, plus horizontal freedom
The cusp tip contacts three inclines of the opposing fossa for maximum stability
It eliminates the need for anterior guidance
It recreates bilateral balance in natural teeth
ex: Point to surface: a cusp tip contacts a flat surface, so force goes down the long axis instead of pushing the tooth sideways, and there is "freedom" before any incline is hit. It suits immediate lateral translation, and can be used for anything from a Class I composite to a full-mouth reconstruction.
why: A cusp tip meeting a flat area sends force down the long axis and gives horizontal freedom before any incline is hit.
Contact on three inclines of a fossa is tripodization.
Contact type doesn't replace anterior guidance; the posteriors still need to disclude.
Bilateral balance is not used on natural teeth today and isn't the point of point-to-surface contact.

stem: Anteroposterior "freedom" in the functional area allows:
choices: A slide from the CR contact to MICP (a "long centric")
Immediate lateral translation without interference
Bilateral balanced contact in protrusion
A taller cusp height
ex: Freedom in the functional area: mediolateral freedom lets the immediate lateral translation (Bennett movement) happen without an interference; anteroposterior freedom allows the slide from the CR contact to MICP, a "long centric."
why: Anteroposterior freedom allows the slide from the CR contact into MICP, a "long centric."
Immediate lateral translation without interference comes from mediolateral freedom.
Freedom in the functional area isn't about balance; modern schemes avoid balancing contacts on natural teeth.
Freedom is about a flat area around the contact, not about the height of the cusp.

stem: Of the five determinants, which is the most important and the one you have the most control over?
choices: Anterior guidance
Condylar guidance
Plane of occlusion
Cusp height
ex: Anterior guidance is "by far the most important determinant" and the one you can control (through the lingual contours of the maxillary anterior teeth). Modern philosophy sides with Schuyler (anterior guidance) over the gnathologists' focus on posterior (condylar) guidance.
why: Anterior guidance is the most important determinant and the one you control, through the maxillary anterior lingual contours.
Condylar guidance is fixed anatomy you can't change, and it sits far back, so it controls less.
The plane of occlusion matters, but the lecture names anterior guidance as most important and most controllable.
Cusp height is set to fit the other determinants; it is not the controlling one.

stem: For anterior guidance to work, the lingual contours of the maxillary anterior teeth must accommodate:
choices: The envelope of function: the functional opening, closing and eccentric pathways
The full envelope of motion, including maximum opening
The patient's freeway space
The curve of Wilson
ex: Lingual contours must accommodate the functional opening, closing and eccentric pathways: the envelope of function. Ideally contact at the cingulum area, a somewhat flat zone, then steeper; this follows the chewing pattern.
why: The lingual contours must fit the envelope of function: the functional opening, closing and eccentric chewing pathways.
The envelope of motion is the border movements, including maximum opening, which teeth don't need to accommodate.
Freeway space is the gap at rest, not a pathway the lingual contours must follow.
The curve of Wilson is a posterior mediolateral curve, unrelated to anterior lingual contours.

stem: Where is the anterior guidance in a patient with an anterior open bite?
choices: On posterior teeth, or effectively none (condylar guidance only)
On the canines, as usual
On the labial surfaces of the mandibular incisors, which now lead in protrusion
In the TM ligament
ex: With no anterior contact, guidance falls on posterior teeth (or is lost), and you rely on condylar guidance, which is far less effective because it is so far back. The same is true with minimal overlap or edge-to-edge incisors.
why: With no anterior contact, guidance falls on posterior teeth or is lost, leaving only condylar guidance, which is far less effective.
Canines can't guide if the anterior teeth don't touch in an open bite.
The mandibular labial surfaces don't take over guidance; in an open bite there's no anterior contact at all.
The TM ligament limits posterior condylar movement; it does not provide anterior guidance.

stem: How do you carry a tested anterior guidance from provisionals into the final crowns on a conventional articulator?
choices: Record their pathways in a custom anterior guide table; build the finals to it
Copy the curve of Spee from the original wax-up
Use a fully adjustable articulator set from a pantograph
Adjust the final crowns intraorally until the patient stops noticing them at all
ex: Wax-up, provisionals tried in the mouth and adjusted, then the guide pin pathways are captured in a custom anterior guide table; the final crowns follow those pathways. Digitally: scan the provisional contours and mill the finals to match.
why: Capture the guide pin pathways on the tested provisionals in a custom anterior guide table, then build the finals to it.
The curve of Spee is a posterior curve and doesn't carry the anterior lingual contours forward.
A pantograph records condylar movement, not the tested anterior guidance on the provisionals.
Adjusting finals by trial and error throws away the guidance you already tested; the custom table copies it.

stem: In Dawson's 7-step smile design, what is step 1?
choices: Develop centric stops
Check the cingulum contour for "d" and "t"
Verify with "s" sounds
Evaluate lip support
ex: 1 centric stops, 2 lip support (emergence), 3 lip closure, 4 tooth-to-lip relations (f, v; smile line), 5 lingual contours (disclusion without violating the envelope of function), 6 cingulum contour (d, t), 7 verify with "s" (closest speaking space).
why: Step 1 of Dawson's smile design is developing centric stops.
Checking the cingulum for "d" and "t" is step 6.
Verifying with "s" is step 7, the last.
Evaluating lip support is step 2.

stem: Which smile design step determines the lingual contours that give disclusion without violating the envelope of function?
choices: Step 5
Step 1
Step 3
Step 7
ex: Step 5: determine lingual contours: verify CR holding contacts, check for a long centric, develop smooth protrusive function, and decide single vs group lateral guidance so the posteriors disclude (mutually protected). Step 7 verifies with "s."
why: Step 5 sets the lingual contours that give disclusion without violating the envelope of function.
Step 1 develops the centric stops.
Step 3 is lip closure.
Step 7 verifies the work with "s" sounds.

stem: Testing new anterior provisionals with "s" sounds: too much interdental space between the mandibular incisal edges and the maxillary cingula causes ___, too little causes ___.
choices: A lisp; the teeth to bump or whistle
A whistle; a lisp
Fricative errors; nasal speech
No change; a lisp
ex: "Let /s/ be your guide." Too much space = lisp; too little = teeth bump or whistle. If all steps are followed, the contours stay within the neutral zone.
why: Too much space on "s" lets air escape and causes a lisp; too little makes the teeth bump or whistle.
Reversed: too much space is the lisp, too little the bump or whistle.
"S" tests the sibilant space, not fricatives or nasal resonance.
Too much space does change speech; it causes a lisp.

stem: A rounded cingulum is preferred for normal "d" and "t" sounds. What risk comes with over-bulking it on a tongue-thrust patient?
choices: Labial movement of the tooth
Lingual tipping of the mandibular incisors
Loss of the incisal edge on "f"
A deeper curve of Spee
ex: Over-bulked cingulum + tongue thrust = labial tooth movement. You may still need some bulk for a proper holding contact ("vitally important"); explain that "d" and "t" take time to readjust. The tongue pushes on the extra bulk from behind, so it is THIS tooth that moves outward (labially); lingual tipping of the mandibular incisors is not the risk.
why: The tongue thrust pushes on the extra cingulum bulk from behind, so the tooth itself is pushed labially.
The added bulk is on the maxillary tooth and the thrust pushes it outward; lingual tipping of the lower incisors isn't the risk.
The incisal edge position on "f" isn't changed by cingulum bulk.
The curve of Spee is a posterior curve and isn't affected by cingulum contour.

stem: A bulge toward the gingival on anterior crowns is a common lab "mistake." What is it usually compensating for?
choices: The clinician under-preparing the tooth
Too much lip support
A short incisal edge
A deep vertical overlap
ex: Step 2 (lip support): a gingival bulge usually means the lab lacked room because the tooth was under-prepared. Measure the thickness of contoured temporaries to check preparation depth.
why: A gingival bulge usually means the lab had no room because the tooth was under-prepared.
The bulge creates excess lip support; it isn't compensating for too much.
Incisal edge length has nothing to do with a bulge near the gingiva.
Vertical overlap concerns the incisal third, not a cervical bulge.

stem: What should the treatment plan address first?
choices: Posterior support, e.g. implants or a partial in the posterior areas
Veneers on #6-11 first, to meet the patient's main goal and build trust
Equilibrating the anterior guidance
A fully adjustable articulator mounting
ex: The chart shows why: every posterior tooth in the upper arch is missing (lower too), and the six anteriors left carry the whole bite, so they are mobile (class 1-2), flaring and opening diastemas. With no posterior support the anteriors are being destroyed. Support first, disclusion second; and the shortened dental arch means support only to the second premolars may be enough, which fits a limited budget ("putting in two implants down in the lower is going to be life-changing"). Veneers on mobile, flaring teeth with no back support would fail.
pbox: "I want my front teeth to look nice"
Flared and worn; diastemas opening; see the chart
why: With no posterior support the anteriors are being destroyed, so support comes first; to the second premolars may be enough on a limited budget.
Veneers without posterior support would fail like the original teeth are failing; support first, disclusion second.
Adjusting anterior guidance can't help while the anteriors carry all the load without back teeth.
Instrument choice doesn't address the real problem, the lack of posterior support.
