stem: Why are her anterior teeth flaring and spreading apart?
choices: They carry all the force with no posterior support
An over-retained visceral swallow is pushing them forward
Her canine guidance is too steep for her chewing pattern
A posterior crossbite that forces the anterior teeth apart
ex: Without posterior teeth the anteriors take all the force and chewing work and decline fast, and the jaw overcloses (posterior overclosure, old term posterior bite collapse), leaving less room to restore. That is why posterior support comes first. A retained visceral swallow shows up early as an anterior open bite; nothing here points to too-steep guidance; and she has no posterior teeth to be in crossbite (a crossbite is "absolutely functionally no problem" anyway).
pbox: "I want my front teeth to look nice"
Flared and worn; diastemas opening; see the chart
why: Without posterior teeth the anteriors take all the force and decline fast, and the bite overcloses.
A retained visceral swallow shows up as an anterior open bite; her problem is missing posterior support.
Nothing in her findings points to the guidance; she has no back teeth supporting the bite.
She has no posterior teeth to be in crossbite, and a crossbite is functionally no problem anyway.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Bonwill's equilateral triangle runs about 4 inches from condyle to condyle to the mandibular symphysis.
2. Balkwill described the medial movement of the translating condyle about 40 years before Bennett.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Both are true. Bonwill (ca. 1858) measured the 4-inch (110 mm) triangle from thousands of skulls; articulators still use 110 mm intercondylar widths. Balkwill (1866) saw the translating condyle move medially in lateral movement, 40 years before Bennett (1908).
why: Statement 1 is true: Bonwill's triangle is about 4 inches (110 mm) on each side. Statement 2 is true: Balkwill (1866) came about 40 years before Bennett (1908).
Statement 1 is true, not false: Bonwill's triangle is about 4 inches (110 mm) on each side. Statement 2 is true, not false: Balkwill (1866) came about 40 years before Bennett (1908).
Statement 2 is true, not false: Balkwill (1866) came about 40 years before Bennett (1908).
Statement 1 is true, not false: Bonwill's triangle is about 4 inches (110 mm) on each side.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Pankey, Mann and Schuyler programmed a fully adjustable articulator from pantograph tracings.
2. Gnathology's early goal put MICP coincident with CR in the rearmost, uppermost, midmost position.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Statement 1 is false: that is gnathology. PMS argued an instrument reproducing condylar motion was unnecessary because Meyer's functionally generated path recorded it, and used a simple suspension articulator. Statement 2 is true (RUM, wrong by today's understanding).
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: PMS relied on the functionally generated path and a simple articulator; the pantograph and fully adjustable articulator are gnathology.
Statement 2 is true, not false: that was the RUM position: "you need a good glass of rum."

Statement 1 is false, not true: PMS relied on the functionally generated path and a simple articulator; the pantograph and fully adjustable articulator are gnathology. Statement 2 is true, not false: that was the RUM position: "you need a good glass of rum."

Statement 1 is false: PMS relied on the functionally generated path and a simple articulator; the pantograph and fully adjustable articulator are gnathology. Statement 2 is true: that was the RUM position: "you need a good glass of rum."

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Stallard and Stuart's keyword was force.
2. D'Amico's keyword was disclusion.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Both are false; the keywords are swapped. Stallard and Stuart: cuspid protection, keyword disclusion. D'Amico: mutually protected occlusion, keyword force (anterior teeth handle off-axis forces better).
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: Stallard and Stuart's keyword was disclusion (cuspid protection). Statement 2 is false, not true: D'Amico's keyword was force (anterior teeth handle off-axis forces better).
Statement 1 is false: Stallard and Stuart's keyword was disclusion (cuspid protection). Statement 2 is false: D'Amico's keyword was force (anterior teeth handle off-axis forces better).
Statement 1 is false, not true: Stallard and Stuart's keyword was disclusion (cuspid protection).
Statement 2 is false, not true: D'Amico's keyword was force (anterior teeth handle off-axis forces better).

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Posterior support is usually the first consideration in a restorative plan.
2. Restoring only to the second premolar (a shortened dental arch) worsens chewing ability and TMD.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Statement 1 is true: "support first, disclusion second." Statement 2 is false: restoring to the second premolar shows no difference in chewing ability, TMD, tooth migration, periodontal support or comfort.
why: Statement 2 is false, not true: the shortened dental arch shows no difference in chewing ability, TMD, migration, periodontal support or comfort.
Statement 1 is true, not false: "support first, disclusion second."
Statement 1 is true: "support first, disclusion second." Statement 2 is false: the shortened dental arch shows no difference in chewing ability, TMD, migration, periodontal support or comfort.

Statement 1 is true, not false: "support first, disclusion second." Statement 2 is false, not true: the shortened dental arch shows no difference in chewing ability, TMD, migration, periodontal support or comfort.

stem:
Read the two statements.
1. Tripodization gives horizontal freedom for an immediate lateral translation.
2. Point-to-surface contacts direct force down the long axis of the tooth.
choices: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; statement 2 is true
ex: Statement 1 is false: tripodization has no wiggle room and requires immediate disclusion. Point to surface is the contact that gives horizontal freedom. Statement 2 is true: a cusp tip on a flat surface sends force down the long axis.
why: Statement 1 is false, not true: tripodization leaves no wiggle room; point-to-surface contacts give the freedom.
Statement 2 is true, not false: a cusp tip on a flat surface sends force down the long axis.

Statement 1 is false, not true: tripodization leaves no wiggle room; point-to-surface contacts give the freedom. Statement 2 is true, not false: a cusp tip on a flat surface sends force down the long axis.
Statement 1 is false: tripodization leaves no wiggle room; point-to-surface contacts give the freedom. Statement 2 is true: a cusp tip on a flat surface sends force down the long axis.

stem: True or false: Conformative dentistry covers about 90-98% of general dentistry.
choices: True
False
ex: True. Match what is there and don't change the existing occlusion, when the patient is healthy and asymptomatic.
why: About 90-98% of general dentistry is conformative.
Most general dentistry (about 90-98%) is conformative.

stem: True or false: The neuromuscular concept is taught at UAB.
choices: True
False
ex: False. Neuromuscular dentistry (Jankelson, the LVI) restores at a TENS-found "myocentric point," which requires an increased vertical and a more forward position without joint stability. It is not taught at UAB.
why: It is described in lecture but not taught at UAB.
Dr. Givan described it as not taught at UAB.

stem: True or false: Neuromuscular dentistry restores at a "myocentric point" of least muscle activity found with a TENS unit.
choices: True
False
ex: True. The Myo-Monitor (a TENS unit) is used to find it; it requires an increased vertical dimension, i.e. full-mouth rehabilitation.
why: That is the neuromuscular idea (Jankelson, the LVI).
The myocentric point and the TENS unit are the core of that concept.

stem: True or false: Modern philosophy sides with the gnathologists that posterior guidance matters more than anterior guidance.
choices: True
False
ex: False. Gnathologists focused on posterior guidance; modern philosophy sides with Schuyler that anterior guidance matters more. It is the most important determinant and the one you control most.
why: Modern philosophy sides with Schuyler: anterior guidance matters more.
Anterior guidance is the most important determinant and the one you control most.

stem: True or false: Peter K. Thomas is known for cusp-fossa waxing.
choices: True
False
ex: True. P.K. Thomas, one of the gnathologists, gave us cusp-fossa waxing (your PKT instruments).
why: Cusp-fossa waxing is his contribution.
His name is on your PKT waxing instruments.

stem: True or false: The WHO considers at least 20 natural teeth functional and esthetic.
choices: True
False
ex: True. That supports the shortened dental arch concept: restoring to the second premolar can be enough, though esthetics may suffer where first molars show.
why: That is the WHO figure quoted in lecture.
At least 20 natural teeth is the WHO's functional and esthetic threshold.

stem: True or false: Over-bulking the cingulum on a tongue-thrust patient tends to move the tooth lingually.
choices: True
False
ex: False. An over-bulked cingulum on a tongue-thrust patient moves the tooth LABIALLY. The cingulum should be rounded for normal d and t sounds, but the holding contact is still vital.
why: The tongue pushes the bulky cingulum forward, so the tooth moves labially.
Tongue pressure on the extra bulk moves the tooth labially.

stem: True or false: Too much closest speaking space causes a whistle.
choices: True
False
ex: False. Too much space gives a lisp; too little and the teeth bump or whistle.
why: Too much space is a lisp; a whistle comes from too little.
A whistle (or bumping teeth) means too little space.

stem:
Which pairings of a name and an idea are correct?
1. Bennett: the occlusal curve in the sagittal plane
2. D'Amico: cusp-fossa waxing
3. Bonwill: the 4-inch triangle from condyle to condyle to the symphysis
4. Christensen: posterior separation in protrusion and the protrusive record
choices: 1, 3 and 4
2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4
3 and 4 only
ex: Bonwill described the 4-inch (110 mm) equilateral triangle, and Christensen the posterior separation in protrusion and the protrusive record. The sagittal occlusal curve is von Spee's; Bennett described lateral translation of the mandible. Cusp-fossa waxing is Peter K. Thomas's; D'Amico's idea was mutually protected occlusion.
why: It includes 1, which is false: the sagittal occlusal curve is von Spee's (1890); Bennett described lateral translation of the mandible (1908).

It includes 2, which is false: cusp-fossa waxing is Peter K. Thomas's; D'Amico gave us mutually protected occlusion (keyword force). It leaves out 4, which is true: Christensen (1901) described posterior separation in protrusion and the protrusive record.
It includes 2, which is false: cusp-fossa waxing is Peter K. Thomas's; D'Amico gave us mutually protected occlusion (keyword force).

Statements 3 and 4 are true. Statement 1 is false: the sagittal occlusal curve is von Spee's (1890); Bennett described lateral translation of the mandible (1908). Statement 2 is false: cusp-fossa waxing is Peter K. Thomas's; D'Amico gave us mutually protected occlusion (keyword force).

stem:
Which statements about the four modern concepts are true?
1. Tripodization suits every crown because it leaves horizontal freedom.
2. Posterior support is usually the first consideration in a restorative plan.
3. Restoring to the second premolar (the shortened dental arch) shows no difference in chewing ability or TMD.
4. Condylar guidance is the determinant the dentist controls most.
choices: 1, 2 and 3
2 and 3 only
2, 3 and 4
3 and 4 only
ex: Support first, disclusion second: posterior support usually comes first, and the shortened dental arch (to the second premolar) shows no difference in chewing, TMD or comfort. Point-to-surface contacts give horizontal freedom; tripodization leaves no wiggle room and is suggested only when the opposing surfaces are controlled. Anterior guidance is the determinant you control most.
why: It includes 1, which is false: tripodization leaves no wiggle room and is suggested only when the opposing surfaces are controlled; point to surface is what gives freedom.

Statements 2 and 3 are true. Statement 1 is false: tripodization leaves no wiggle room and is suggested only when the opposing surfaces are controlled; point to surface is what gives freedom. Statement 4 is false: anterior guidance, through the lingual contours of the maxillary anteriors, is the determinant you control most.
It includes 4, which is false: anterior guidance, through the lingual contours of the maxillary anteriors, is the determinant you control most.

It includes 4, which is false: anterior guidance, through the lingual contours of the maxillary anteriors, is the determinant you control most. It leaves out 2, which is true: support first, disclusion second: anterior guidance follows as the second consideration.

stem: Which are the three accepted occlusal schemes listed in Lec3-2?
choices: Balanced occlusion, mutually protected occlusion, group function
Canine guidance, cusp-fossa contact, cusp-marginal ridge contact, tripodization
Conformative, reorganized, neuromuscular
Tripodization, point to surface, long centric
ex: Accepted schemes: balanced (dentures), mutually protected, and group function. Conformative/reorganized are restorative approaches, not schemes.
why: The three accepted schemes are balanced occlusion (dentures), mutually protected occlusion and group function.
These mix one scheme (canine guidance) with contact types (cusp-fossa, cusp-marginal ridge, tripodization).
Conformative and reorganized are restorative approaches, and neuromuscular is a philosophy, not an occlusal scheme.
These are contact concepts and a CR-to-MICP slide, not occlusal schemes.

stem: A patient needing a crown on #6 has group function, with no signs or symptoms. What guidance should the new crown have?
choices: Copy the existing guidance (group function)
Convert to canine guidance
Convert to balanced occlusion
Remove all lateral contact from #6
ex: "In the absence of signs or symptoms, it is best to copy the existing guidance when restorations are required." That is good conformative dentistry; canine guidance is not automatically "better."
why: With no signs or symptoms, copy the existing guidance (group function) when restoring.
Canine guidance isn't automatically better; converting a healthy occlusion is not conformative dentistry.
Balanced occlusion is for dentures, not natural teeth.
Removing #6's lateral contact changes a healthy, functioning group function scheme.

stem: Which statement about MIP comes from Lec3-2?
choices: The end of the chewing cycle, where force peaks and swallowing is stabilized; not stable long term
It is the most stable long-term reference position, so every restoration should be built to it without question
It is the same as centric relation
It is used only for dentures
ex: MIP: the end of the chewing cycle, where teeth apply maximum force and the mandible is stabilized to swallow; "not stable over the long term" because it changes with every change in the occlusion.
why: MIP is the end of the chewing cycle, where force peaks and the mandible is stabilized to swallow; it changes as the occlusion changes.
MIP is not stable long term; it changes whenever the occlusion changes, so it is not unquestionable.
MIP is a tooth-determined position; CR is a joint-determined position, and the two often differ.
MIP is used every day in natural dentitions, not just for dentures.

stem: In a day, the teeth contact in MIP for about 17.5 minutes. That comprises roughly:
choices: 1,800 chewing strokes and 500 swallowing contacts
500 chewing strokes and 1,800 swallowing contacts
590 chewing strokes and 146 swallowing contacts
18,000 chewing strokes and 5,000 swallowing contacts
ex: 17.5 minutes = about 1,800 chewing strokes + 500 swallowing contacts (1,800 × 365 = 657,000 chewing strokes a year). The 590 swallows a day in Lec2-2 counts all swallows, not tooth contacts.
why: 17.5 minutes of daily MIP contact is about 1,800 chewing strokes plus 500 swallowing contacts.
Reversed: 1,800 are the chewing strokes and 500 the swallowing contacts.
590 is the total swallows per day and 146 the swallows at meals, not tooth contacts in MIP.
These numbers are about ten times too high for one day.

stem: When evaluating working side contacts (canine guidance or group function), what should you check?
choices: Mobility of the guiding teeth, and whether the glide is smooth or restricted
Only the shade of the guiding teeth
The vertical dimension at rest and the freeway space in that guiding position
The curve of Wilson
ex: Working side: check mobility of the guiding teeth (do they need splinting?) and whether the movement is smooth or restricted. Changing mobility is pathologic, not adaptation.
why: On the working side, check the guiding teeth's mobility (do they need splinting?) and whether the glide is smooth or restricted.
Shade has nothing to do with whether working-side contacts are healthy.
VDR and freeway space are measured at rest, not in a guiding excursion.
The curve of Wilson isn't what you check for working-side guidance.

stem: A non-working side contact tends to:
choices: Guide the mandible during lateral excursion
Protect the canine from overload
Improve chewing efficiency
Stabilize the disc
ex: Non-working contacts tend to guide the mandible during lateral excursion. Check the mobility of the teeth on the non-working side and the corresponding working side contacts. If a patient has adapted to one over years, leave it; don't introduce one in an afternoon.
why: Non-working side contacts tend to guide the mandible during lateral excursion.
A non-working contact doesn't protect the canine; it takes over guidance on the wrong side.
Non-working contacts are interferences and don't improve chewing.
Non-working contacts are not described as stabilizing the disc.

stem: The sensory elements of the periodontal ligament can detect material between the teeth down to about:
choices: 20 µm
200 µm
2 mm
0.2 µm
ex: About 20 µm. Shimstock is about 12 µm; a hair is about 15-25 µm. "We work in microns."
why: The PDL's sensory elements can detect about 20 µm between the teeth.
200 µm is ten times thicker than the PDL threshold.
2 mm is a hundred times larger than what the PDL can detect.
0.2 µm is far below the roughly 20 µm threshold.

stem: Before restoring the anterior teeth, what must be done about posterior protrusive interferences?
choices: Eliminate them first
Leave them; they protect the new anterior crowns
Add more of them for stability
Copy them into the new restorations
ex: Posterior protrusive interferences must be eliminated prior to restoring the anterior teeth. Sometimes better anterior contours give enough separation, but a badly tipped molar must be fixed first.
why: Posterior protrusive interferences must be eliminated before the anterior teeth are restored.
Posterior protrusive interferences don't protect the crowns; they take over guidance and must go first.
Adding posterior protrusive contacts creates more interferences.
Copying an interference into new restorations keeps the problem.

stem: In the conformative approach, the occlusion is modified only by localized adjustments. Which is NOT one of them?
choices: Moving the whole occlusion to centric relation
Shortening an opposing cusp
Eliminating non-working side interferences
Removing a deflective contact on the tooth to be restored
ex: Conformative = in harmony with existing jaw relationships, with only localized adjustments (shorten an opposing cusp, remove NW interferences, remove a deflective contact). Rebuilding the whole scheme in CR is the reorganized approach.
why: Not a localized adjustment: moving the whole occlusion to CR is the reorganized approach.
Shortening an opposing cusp is one of the localized conformative adjustments.
Eliminating non-working interferences is one of the localized conformative adjustments.
Removing a deflective contact on the tooth to be restored is one of the localized conformative adjustments.

stem: How far back does her posterior support need to go for her to function well?
choices: To the second premolars: a shortened dental arch
To the second molars, in every quadrant
To the first premolars, just behind the canines
Only the canines, since anterior guidance matters most
ex: The shortened dental arch: restoring to the second premolar shows no difference in chewing ability, TMD, tooth migration, periodontal support or comfort (the WHO considers at least 20 natural teeth functional and esthetic), and with tough foods most chewing happens at the second premolar and first molar. Molars aren't required; the first premolars are not enough; and anterior guidance comes second ("support first, disclusion second").
pbox: "I want my front teeth to look nice"
Flared and worn; diastemas opening; see the chart
why: Restoring to the second premolar shows no difference in chewing, TMD, migration, perio support or comfort.
Molars aren't required; a shortened dental arch to the second premolars functions well.
The first premolars alone fall short; the shortened dental arch goes to the second premolars.
Posterior support comes first ("support first, disclusion second"); canines alone aren't enough.

stem: The reorganized approach modifies the entire occlusal scheme. What are its goals?
choices: A reproducible start, an even stable occlusion, no iatrogenic deflective contacts
Copying the existing MIP contacts as closely as possible, with only local adjustments
Raising the vertical dimension in every case
Bilateral balance in all excursions
ex: Reorganized: provide a reproducible starting point (joints seated, CR, first and foremost), an even and stable occlusion, and avoid iatrogenic deflective contacts. "That'd be like trying to build a house... start on the second floor before you've done the foundation."
why: Reorganized goals: a reproducible starting point (joints seated in CR), an even stable occlusion, no iatrogenic deflective contacts.
Copying MIP with local adjustments is the conformative approach.
Reorganizing doesn't require raising the vertical in every case.
Bilateral balance is for dentures, not a goal for natural teeth.

stem: When should you use a centric relation record?
choices: Reorganizing, and mounting diagnostic casts for treatment planning
For a conformative single crown
For building restorations on working casts in MIP when the occlusion is healthy
Whenever the patient has canine guidance
ex: CR record: reorganized approach, diagnostic casts for treatment planning, obtained by bimanual manipulation. MIP record: conformative approach, restorations on working casts, used as minimally as required.
why: Use a CR record when reorganizing and when mounting diagnostic casts for treatment planning.
A conformative single crown uses an MIP record or hand articulation.
Working casts for a healthy occlusion are mounted in MIP, used as minimally as needed.
Canine guidance has nothing to do with choosing a CR record.

stem: What is the most reliable method to capture centric relation, according to Lec3-2?
choices: Bimanual manipulation
Having the patient retrude as far as possible
Recording the myocentric point with a TENS unit
A full-arch PVS bite in MIP
ex: Bimanual manipulation: an upward, anterior force at the back of the jaw seats the condyles while the teeth are held apart, and a record is captured there. (Lec1 also lists a leaf gauge or Lucia jig.)
why: Bimanual manipulation seats the condyles with an upward, anterior force while the teeth are held apart, then the record is taken.
Forcing the jaw back as far as it goes recreates the old RUM position, not today's anterior-superior CR.
The TENS myocentric point is neuromuscular and is not CR.
A full-arch bite in MIP records the tooth position, not CR, and full-arch records add mounting errors.

stem: Which is NOT one of the commonly used occlusal registration materials listed?
choices: Irreversible hydrocolloid (alginate)
Polyvinyl siloxane (Regisil)
Thermoplastic wax (Aluwax)
Zinc oxide eugenol plaster
ex: Listed: elastomeric PVS (Regisil), thermoplastic waxes (Aluwax), ZOE plaster, acrylics, plaster of Paris ("EZ TAP"). Alginate is an impression material, not a bite registration material.
why: Not a bite registration material: alginate (irreversible hydrocolloid) is an impression material.
PVS (Regisil) is one of the listed registration materials.
Aluwax is one of the listed registration materials.
ZOE plaster is one of the listed registration materials.

stem: Why does Dr. Givan like a warmed wax record cooled with an air-water syringe over PVS?
choices: It hardens in 1-2 seconds, while PVS takes 20-30 seconds during which the patient moves
It is more accurate than any impression material, including polyvinyl siloxane and polyether
It needs no trimming
It records the CR position automatically
ex: PVS is an excellent impression material but sets in 20-30 seconds: "your patients do a lot of stuff in 20 or 30 seconds." Wax chilled with the syringe hardens in 1-2 seconds.
why: Wax chilled with the syringe hardens in 1-2 seconds; PVS takes 20-30 seconds, and patients move during that time.
PVS is an excellent impression material; the advantage is wax's fast set, not superior accuracy.
Wax records still need trimming like any other record.
A material can't find CR by itself; CR comes from how you guide the jaw.

stem: Which are the two common occlusal registration errors named in lecture?
choices: A full-arch registration, and untrimmed excess
Using wax, and using a semi-adjustable articulator
Taking the record upright, and taking it supine
Using too little material, and trimming to the cusp tips
ex: Full-arch registration introduces mounting errors (material between teeth that should touch); untrimmed excess makes it impossible to verify the mounting (it rocks on soft tissue and fine anatomy).
why: The two errors: a full-arch registration (material where teeth should touch) and untrimmed excess (the record rocks and can't be verified).
Wax is one of Dr. Givan's preferred materials, and a semi-adjustable articulator isn't an error.
Patient posture is not one of the two errors named.
Trimming to the cusp tips is the right way to trim; it isn't an error.

stem: A correct MIP record for a posterior bridge should:
choices: Sit only where teeth don't touch, trimmed to the cusp tips and off soft tissue
Cover the whole arch so nothing can move
Be thick enough to separate all of the teeth slightly so nothing touches during setting
Include the palate for stability
ex: "The last thing you want to do is put something between teeth that normally should be in contact. MIP is teeth in contact." Put the record only in the prepared area, trim to the cusp tips, keep it off soft tissue, and confirm the patient's contacts (e.g. #26 touching #8) show on the mounting.
why: A correct MIP record sits only where teeth don't touch, trimmed to the cusp tips and kept off soft tissue.
Full-arch coverage is a named error: it puts material between teeth that should touch.
MIP means teeth in contact, so a record that separates them is no longer MIP.
Soft tissue and palate coverage make the record rock and add error.

stem: Using an elastomeric registration material (PVS or polyether), you should do all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: Release biting pressure as soon as the material is placed
Apply a constant occlusal pressure during setting
Trim excess with a scalpel blade before mounting
Hold pressure on the casts while mounting to avoid rebound
ex: Keep constant occlusal pressure while it sets, trim excess with a scalpel before mounting, and press the casts while mounting so the teeth don't rebound in the record.
why: This is the wrong step: keep a constant occlusal pressure while the material sets; releasing it early ruins the record.
Constant occlusal pressure during setting is correct technique.
Trimming excess with a scalpel before mounting is correct technique.
Holding pressure on the casts while mounting prevents rebound and is correct technique.

stem: For a posterior intracoronal restoration, which is a desirable occlusal outcome?
choices: Simultaneous contact of the restoration and the other teeth in MIP
A slight infraocclusion to protect the new restoration from heavy force
A light non-working contact to share load
The first contact in MIP being on the restoration
ex: Yes: a stable relationship with the opposing tooth and simultaneous contacts with the other teeth in MIP. No: deflective contacts, high spots, infraocclusion, non-working contacts, working interferences.
why: The restoration should contact at the same time as the other teeth in MIP.
Infraocclusion lets teeth supererupt into poor contacts; it is not protective.
Non-working contacts on a restoration are interferences to avoid.
A restoration hitting first is a high spot or deflective contact.

stem: Why is leaving a restoration out of occlusion (infraocclusion) a problem?
choices: The tooth or its opponent supererupts, and it never erupts into a good contact
It increases the bite force on the restoration and on the opposing tooth in MIP
It causes immediate pulpal pain
It moves the condyle out of CR
ex: "The tooth will... supererupt, and it never supererupts in a good contact." Interferences develop and the patient is unhappy.
why: Out of occlusion, the tooth or its opponent supererupts and never erupts into a good contact, so interferences develop.
Infraocclusion removes contact from the restoration; it doesn't increase bite force on it.
Leaving a tooth out of occlusion does not cause immediate pulpal pain.
Infraocclusion doesn't move the condyle; the problem is drifting and supereruption.

stem: Before a LARGE posterior intracoronal restoration, you should:
choices: Check the opposing cusp for over-eruption and NW contacts; adjust first
Take a CR record and reorganize the whole quadrant around the restoration
Raise the vertical dimension 1 mm
Mount casts on a fully adjustable articulator
ex: Small restoration: fit it to the existing jaw relationships. Large one: look before you cut. Check for an over-erupted opposing cusp, a plane violation or non-working contacts, and make localized adjustments before placing it.
why: Before a large restoration, look before you cut: check for an over-erupted opposing cusp, plane violations and NW contacts, and adjust first.
One large restoration calls for localized adjustment, not reorganizing the quadrant.
Raising the vertical isn't called for to place one restoration.
A fully adjustable articulator isn't needed for a single intracoronal restoration.

stem: A "plunger cusp" is:
choices: A cusp violating the plane of occlusion that plunges into the opposing tooth
A non-centric cusp that is ground flat
The mesiolingual cusp of a maxillary molar in Class I, which seats in the central fossa
A cusp that contacts only during swallowing
ex: A plunger cusp is an over-erupted cusp violating the plane of occlusion, plunging into a worn or scooped-out restoration or an embrasure. It is an indication for localized modification before restoring.
why: A plunger cusp is an over-erupted cusp that breaks the plane of occlusion and plunges into the opposing tooth or embrasure.
A ground-flat non-centric cusp is not a plunger cusp.
That describes a normal Class I centric holding cusp, not a plunger.
Swallowing contacts are not what defines a plunger cusp.

stem: Multiple LARGE posterior restorations in quadrants are an indication for:
choices: The reorganized approach, with high-strength materials
The conformative approach, with no occlusal adjustments at all
Leaving the teeth in infraocclusion
Bilateral balanced occlusion
ex: Multiple small restorations: conformative. Over-erupted cusp into a scooped-out restoration, non-working contacts, plunger cusps, deflective contacts: localized modification. Multiple large posterior restorations: reorganized.
why: Multiple large posterior restorations in quadrants call for the reorganized approach with high-strength materials.
Conformative suits multiple small restorations, not many large ones.
Infraocclusion is never the goal; it leads to supereruption.
Bilateral balance is for dentures.

stem: A single BOUNDED posterior crown is usually made with:
choices: Conformative; hand articulation; no face-bow; a hinge articulator
The reorganized approach with a CR record and an arbitrary face-bow
A fully adjustable articulator and a pantograph
A full-arch PVS record and a semi-adjustable articulator in every case
ex: Single bounded crown: conformative; registration by hand articulation (preferred: "any material... is going to increase error"), PVS or Aluwax; no face-bow; hinge-type articulator (semi-adjustable rarely). Check the opposing cusp and adjust before you start.
why: A single bounded crown is conformative: hand articulation (or PVS/Aluwax), no face-bow, a hinge articulator.
Reorganizing with CR and a face-bow is far more than a single bounded crown needs.
A fully adjustable articulator with a pantograph is not needed for one bounded crown.
Full-arch records are a named error, and a semi-adjustable is only rarely used here.

stem: At try-in of a crown, what do you verify BEFORE checking the occlusion?
choices: The proximal contacts and complete seating
The shade
The vertical dimension at rest
The patient's chewing side
ex: Seat it fully: check proximal contacts first ("if your proximal contacts are too tight, you're not seated down all the way") and any intaglio interference. Then occlusion: stable contact and simultaneous contact with adjacent teeth in MIP; no deflective contacts, high spots, infraocclusion or posterior working/non-working contacts.
why: Seat the crown fully first: check proximal contacts and complete seating, since tight contacts keep it from seating.
Shade is not what must be verified before occlusion; seating comes first.
VDR is a rest measurement, not part of crown try-in.
The patient's chewing side doesn't need to be checked before occlusion; seating does.

stem: How does a single crown at the END of the arch differ from a bounded one?
choices: Adjust any retruded deflective contact first, and mount with a registration
No registration is ever needed
It must always be reorganized
It should be left slightly out of occlusion, since it is the last tooth in the arch
ex: End of arch: adjust a retruded deflective contact before restoring, and you need an occlusal registration to mount the casts; with only hand articulation the cast easily drops posteriorly and the crown ends up out of proper contact.
why: At the end of the arch, adjust any retruded deflective contact first and mount with a registration, since hand-articulated casts drop back.
An end-of-arch crown does need a registration because the cast drops posteriorly without one.
A single end-of-arch crown is usually still conformative, not reorganized.
Infraocclusion lets teeth supererupt; the last tooth needs proper contact too.

stem: For a three-unit bounded posterior bridge, which is recommended?
choices: Conformative, a good opposing plane, and a semi-adjustable (arcon) articulator
Reorganized approach with a CR record and a fully adjustable articulator in every case
A hinge articulator in every case
No registration material
ex: Three-unit bounded FPD: usually conformative; check and adjust the opposing cusp; ensure the opposing arch has a desirable occlusal plane; PVS or Aluwax; semi-adjustable (arcon) articulator (hinge sometimes OK). Lecture: conformative generally works up to a three-unit posterior prosthesis.
why: A three-unit bounded bridge: conformative, a good opposing plane, and a semi-adjustable (arcon) articulator.
Reorganizing with a fully adjustable articulator is not needed for a three-unit bridge in every case.
A hinge articulator is only sometimes acceptable here; semi-adjustable is recommended.
A registration (PVS or Aluwax) is used to mount a three-unit bridge.

stem: Who benefits from a small hinge articulator, according to Dr. Givan?
choices: Only the laboratory
The dentist, because adjustments are fewer
The patient, because crowns fit better
Everyone equally
ex: "There's never an advantage to the dentist [of] a hinge articulator... The advantage is entirely to the laboratory." An articulator about the patient's size, even a semi-adjustable at average settings, moves on arcs closer to the patient, so less chairside adjustment.
why: Dr. Givan says the hinge articulator's advantage is entirely to the laboratory.
The dentist actually makes more adjustments, because a small hinge moves on arcs unlike the patient's.
Crowns from a small hinge fit the patient's movement worse, so the patient gains nothing.
The benefit isn't shared; it goes only to the lab.

stem: Quadrant restorations may first require all of these to give the opposing arch a desirable occlusal plane EXCEPT:
choices: Bilateral balanced contacts
Crown lengthening
Crowns on opposing teeth
Root canal therapy
ex: Quadrants: ensure the opposing plane, which may need crown lengthening, opposing crowns and RCT (the lecture lists root canal therapy, so it is not the exception); more indication for equilibration before restoring. Restoring opposing quadrants lets you restore a favorable plane and curve of Spee with optimum intercuspation.
why: Not needed: bilateral balanced contacts are a denture scheme, not a step to fix the opposing plane.
Crown lengthening may be needed to give the opposing arch a good occlusal plane.
Crowns on opposing teeth may be needed to correct the opposing plane.
Root canal therapy is on the lecture's list with crown lengthening and opposing crowns, so it may be needed first.

stem: Dr. Givan's warning about a four-unit posterior bridge was that:
choices: It replaces about half the occlusion, so copying MIP is questionable
It can always be made conformatively in MIP, exactly like a single bounded crown
It should be built in bilateral balance
It needs no occlusal record
ex: "If you do a four-unit bridge in the posterior, you just replaced 50% of a patient's occlusion... half of their MIP is gone." What you put back has to be decided, not just copied.
why: A four-unit posterior bridge replaces about half the occlusion, so what goes back must be decided, not just copied from MIP.
That's exactly his warning: it is not like a single bounded crown, since half the MIP is gone.
Bilateral balance is for dentures, not fixed bridges.
A bridge this size definitely needs an occlusal record.

stem: For a Class III composite, the occlusal goals are:
choices: Copy existing contacts; keep centric and protrusive contact off the composite
Put all the centric contacts on the composite so the tooth structure is protected
Give the composite the canine guidance
Leave the tooth out of occlusion
ex: Class III: copy the existing occlusal contacts and keep centric and protrusive contact off the restorative material as much as possible; contact on composite is a compromise and won't last like natural tooth.
why: For a Class III, copy the existing contacts and keep centric and protrusive contact off the composite where possible.
Putting all centric contact on the composite is the opposite of the goal; composite won't last like tooth.
Guidance on a Class III composite would load the weaker material.
Leaving the tooth out of occlusion lets it drift or supererupt.

stem: For a Class IV composite (especially in an edge-to-edge relationship), you should aim for:
choices: Shared centric and protrusive contact on tooth and restoration
All centric and protrusive contact on the composite, protecting the tooth
No contact on the natural tooth
Canine guidance on the restored incisor
ex: Class IV restorations replace the incisal edge, so contacts are hard to avoid. Share centric and protrusive contact between natural tooth and restoration to reduce fracture and differential wear. "I would not want all of my guidance to be on a Class IV restoration. That would be a recipe for disaster."
why: Share centric and protrusive contact between tooth and composite to reduce fracture and differential wear.
All contact on the composite is "a recipe for disaster."
Taking contact off the natural tooth puts it all on the composite.
Canine guidance belongs on canines, not on a restored incisor.

stem: Before a single anterior crown, which posterior problem should you correct?
choices: Deflective contacts that cause an anterior slide of the mandible into the incisors
A shortened dental arch
Group function on the working side, which must be converted to canine guidance first
A vertical overlap of 3 mm
ex: Single anterior crown: in the absence of symptoms, harmonize with the existing occlusion, but correct posterior deflective contacts that slide the mandible forward into the incisors, especially with a history of previous fracture.
why: Fix posterior deflective contacts that slide the mandible forward into the incisors, especially after a previous fracture.
A shortened dental arch is an acceptable endpoint, not a problem to fix before an anterior crown.
Healthy group function should be copied, not converted to canine guidance.
A 3 mm vertical overlap is not a posterior problem that must be corrected.

stem: A customized anterior guide table is needed when fixed restorations involve:
choices: Both maxillary central incisors, or one or both maxillary canines
A single maxillary lateral incisor or any single maxillary premolar crown
Any posterior crown
A Class III composite
ex: Multiple maxillary anterior crowns need a custom anterior guide table when restoring both centrals or one or both canines (laterals "get thrown in" since they do little). The incisal pin's pathways represent the full functional range of the anterior guidance.
why: A custom anterior guide table is needed when restoring both maxillary centrals or one or both canines.
A single lateral or a premolar crown doesn't need one; laterals do little of the guiding.
Posterior crowns don't set the anterior guidance.
A Class III composite doesn't change the guidance pathways.

stem: If new maxillary anterior crowns are to copy the existing guidance unchanged, when do you make the impression for the custom anterior guide table?
choices: Before the anterior teeth are prepared
After the teeth are prepared
After the final crowns are seated
It is not needed when copying
ex: To duplicate the patient's own guidance, capture it before you cut it away: make the impression for the custom guide before preparation.
why: To copy the guidance unchanged, make the custom guide impression before the anterior teeth are prepared.
After preparation the original guiding surfaces are gone.
After the finals are seated it is too late; the table guides how they are built.
Copying still needs the table; it is how the existing guidance is carried into the new crowns.

stem: Order the steps for restoring INADEQUATE anterior guidance (missing, malaligned or broken-down anteriors).
steps: Diagnostic wax-up at a tentative VDO
Provisionals made from the wax-up matrix
Observe the patient for several weeks
Custom anterior guide table from the accepted provisionals
Definitive lingual contours follow the guide
ex: Wax-up (at the tentative VDO), provisionals from its matrix (guidance and esthetics), observe for weeks (at least 3 weeks if mild and asymptomatic; months in a bruxer), capture the corrected provisionals in a custom guide table, then make the definitive lingual contours follow it.

stem: How long does Dr. Givan leave a mild, asymptomatic patient in new anterior provisionals before copying them?
choices: At least about three weeks (months for a bruxer)
One day
One year
No time; finals are made the same day
ex: "Typically, at a minimum, I would give three weeks if everything was very mild and asymptomatic. On a bruxing patient... sometimes go months."
why: At least about three weeks for a mild, asymptomatic patient, and months for a bruxer.
One day is too short to test new guidance.
A year is far longer than needed for a mild case.
Same-day finals skip the test period that proves the provisionals work.

stem: Closest speaking space, used to develop a tentative VDO, should be about:
choices: 1-2 mm between the incisal edges while the patient counts 60-70 ("s")
2-6 mm on "s," the same range as the freeway space at physiologic rest
5-10 mm on "ah"
0 mm: the teeth should touch on "s"
ex: Closest speaking space (vertical dimension of speech): no more or less than 1-2 mm of clearance between the incisal edges when the patient unconsciously repeats "s," e.g. counting from 60 to 70.
cue: "Sixty-six" sits 1-2 mm apart.
why: Closest speaking space is 1-2 mm between the incisal edges while the patient says "s" (counting 60-70).
2-6 mm is the freeway space at rest, not the closest speaking space on "s."
"Ah" opens the mouth wide; closest speaking space is measured on "s."
Teeth don't touch on "s"; there should be about 1-2 mm of space.

stem: Under about 10 lb of force, a natural tooth moves about ___ apically, while an implant moves about ___.
choices: 28 µm; 2-3 µm
2-3 µm; 28 µm
100 µm; 50 µm
28 µm; 28 µm
ex: Natural tooth: apical 28 µm (into the PDL), lateral 56-75 µm posterior and 90-108 µm anterior. Implant: apical 2-3 µm (bone microstrain only), lateral 10-50 µm. There is no ligament, so implant occlusion is built differently.
cue: Teeth have a cushion (PDL, 28); implants are locked in bone (2-3).
why: A natural tooth moves about 28 µm apically into its PDL; an implant moves only 2-3 µm through bone microstrain.
Reversed: the tooth moves 28 µm, the implant only 2-3 µm.
Both values are too high for apical movement under about 10 lb.
An implant has no PDL, so it moves far less than a natural tooth.

stem: How should a posterior implant crown contact in MIP?
choices: Very light on casual closure, equal to the natural teeth on a firm clench
Heavier than the natural teeth, so the implant protects them from overload
Completely out of contact to protect the implant
Only in lateral excursions
ex: Light in casual intercuspation, equal on a firm clench: the natural teeth drop into their PDL under load but the implant doesn't. With no contact at all, the opposing tooth can supererupt.
why: Very light on casual closure and equal on a firm clench, because the teeth sink into their PDL and the implant doesn't.
Heavier implant contact overloads the implant, which has no PDL cushion.
Leaving it with no contact lets the opposing tooth supererupt.
Posterior implants should avoid excursive contact, not have it only in excursions.

stem: Delivering an implant crown on #13, you test with shimstock (about 12 µm) on a light closure. What result do you want?
choices: Light closure: holds on #12 and #14, drags on #13. Clench: holds on all three
It holds firmly on #13 and pulls freely through #12 and #14, both on light closure and on a firm clench
It pulls freely through all three on a firm clench
It holds firmly on all three on a light closure
ex: Light closure: adjacent teeth hold, the implant holds "with some resistance," slightly out of occlusion. Clenching: the teeth drop in their sockets, the implant doesn't, and all hold equally. "So you're delivering occlusion differently."
why: Light closure: shimstock holds on #12 and #14 and drags on #13; on a clench all three hold.
On a clench the teeth sink into their PDL, so all three should hold; #12 and #14 shouldn't pull through.
On a firm clench the teeth should hold shimstock, not let it pull through.
On light closure the implant should be slightly lighter, dragging rather than holding firmly.

stem: When restoring an implant in the canine position, how should lateral excursions be handled?
choices: No immediate canine disclusion; share the load with the natural teeth
Give the implant full canine guidance, just like a natural canine would have
Remove all contacts from every anterior tooth
Use bilateral balanced occlusion
ex: An implant has no PDL proprioception, so don't give it immediate canine disclusion. Share guidance with natural teeth (a shared group function). Centric: very light in casual closure, equal to neighbors in MIP.
why: Skip immediate canine disclusion on an implant (no PDL proprioception); share the load with natural teeth.
An implant lacks a PDL, so it shouldn't carry full canine guidance alone.
Removing all anterior contact would lose the anterior guidance entirely.
Bilateral balance is for dentures.

stem: In lateral excursions and protrusion, a POSTERIOR implant crown should:
choices: Avoid contact if possible (mutually protected occlusion)
Carry the working contacts
Carry the non-working contacts to balance the arch
Contact first to protect the natural teeth
ex: Posterior implants: avoid excursive contact if possible; mutually protected occlusion. "We don't really want implants having lateral contacts in the posterior mouth."
why: Posterior implants should avoid excursive contact if possible, in a mutually protected occlusion.
Working contacts on a posterior implant are avoided.
Non-working contacts are interferences, and especially unwanted on implants.
An implant contacting first overloads it; it can't sense or cushion force.

stem: How do you decide whether the conformative approach is safe before restoring?
choices: Compare the CO and MIP contacts, and look for wear, fracture and mobility
Check that the patient has canine guidance on both sides and no group function
Measure freeway space
Assume it is safe if the patient has all 28 teeth
ex: At diagnosis, compare the CO contact with the MIP contact: a large or deviating discrepancy plus wear, fractures, mobility or tooth movement warns that copying MIP is not safe. If the occlusion is healthy and asymptomatic, conformative is the way to go.
why: Compare the CO and MIP contacts and look for wear, fracture and mobility; a big discrepancy with damage says conformative isn't safe.
Group function is a perfectly healthy scheme; canine guidance isn't the test for conformative safety.
Freeway space doesn't tell you whether copying MIP is safe.
Having all teeth doesn't rule out wear, fracture or mobility.

stem: What is the right approach for this crown?
choices: Conformative: fix #30's plunging cusp, then an MIP record and copied contacts
Reorganized: a CR record and a full-mouth rehabilitation at a new vertical dimension
Leave #3 in slight infraocclusion to protect the crown
Give #3 the working-side contacts in a right excursion
ex: On the bitewing the distobuccal cusp of #30 rises above the plane into a scooped-out amalgam on #3: a plunger cusp (a cusp violating the plane of occlusion). Asymptomatic, healthy, with canine guidance: copy what is there (conformative), but first make the localized change L5 allows, reshaping the opposing cusp. Then use an MIP record limited to the prepared area. Infraocclusion lets #30 supererupt further ("it never supererupts in a good contact"), and adding working contacts would change guidance that is healthy.
pbox: Canine guidance both sides; no mobility, no wear facets
why: Asymptomatic with healthy canine guidance: stay conformative, but first fix #30's over-erupted (plunger) cusp, then use an MIP record.
A healthy, asymptomatic patient needs no full-mouth reorganization.
Infraocclusion would let teeth supererupt, and #30 has already over-erupted.
Canine guidance already protects the posteriors; adding working contacts on #3 makes an interference.

stem: On the bitewing, a cusp of #30 rises above the plane of occlusion into the failing amalgam on #3. What is it called, and when do you deal with it?
choices: A plunger cusp; adjust it before you prepare #3
A non-working cusp; leave it, since he has adapted
A centric stop; build the new crown around it unchanged
A plunger cusp; leave it until the crown is cemented
ex: A cusp that violates the plane of occlusion is a plunger cusp, often over-erupted into a worn or scooped-out restoration. For a large restoration or a crown, check the opposing cusp for over-eruption and make the localized adjustment first; otherwise the new crown has to be built around a cusp that is out of the plane. It isn't a non-working contact, copying it unchanged keeps the problem, and adjusting after cementation is backwards.
pbox: Canine guidance both sides; no mobility, no wear facets
why: A cusp violating the plane of occlusion is a plunger cusp; check and adjust the opposing cusp first.
It isn't a non-working contact, and a cusp over-erupted into the restoration should be corrected first.
Copying it unchanged keeps the cusp out of the plane and builds the problem into the crown.
Right name, wrong time: adjust it before the prep, not after cementation.

stem: The patient likes her current guidance and wants it unchanged. When do you make the impression for the custom anterior guide table?
choices: Before preparing #6-11
After preparing #6-11
After cementing the final crowns
Never; copying guidance doesn't need one
ex: Both centrals and both canines are being restored, so L5 calls for a customized anterior guide table, and to copy the guidance unchanged you must capture it before the teeth are cut; once they are prepped, the guiding surfaces are gone. The guide pin's pathways then carry the full functional range of her guidance onto the new lingual contours.
pbox: Crowns #6-11 (failing, discolored PFMs; see the photo)
why: Restoring both centrals and both canines needs a custom guide, and copying requires capturing it before #6-11 are cut.
After preparation, the guidance she likes is gone.
After cementation is too late; the table guides how the crowns are built.
Copying still needs a custom anterior guide table, because both centrals and canines are being restored.

stem: Why does her plan need a custom anterior guide table at all?
choices: It restores both central incisors and both canines
Every anterior crown, even a single one, needs one
Because her PFMs are being replaced with all-ceramic crowns
Only because she wants a different color
ex: Multiple maxillary anterior crowns need a customized anterior guide table when they restore both central incisors or one or both canines, and #6-11 includes all four. A single anterior crown is made in harmony with the existing occlusion without one, and neither the crown material nor the shade decides it: the guide table records guidance, not color.
pbox: Crowns #6-11 (failing, discolored PFMs; see the photo)
why: A custom guide table is needed when restoring both centrals or one or both canines; #6-11 includes all four.
A single anterior crown is made in harmony with the existing occlusion, without a guide table.
The crown material doesn't decide it; which teeth are being restored does.
The guide table records guidance, not color.

stem: #3 has #2 and #4 on either side. How do you record and mount the casts for this crown?
choices: By hand articulation or a small PVS record; no face-bow, hinge articulator
Face-bow transfer and a CR record on a fully adjustable articulator
A full-arch PVS registration so the lab sees every tooth in contact
A protrusive record first, to set the condylar guidance on the articulator
ex: A single bounded crown is usually conformative: check and adjust the opposing cusp first, then register by hand articulation, PVS or Aluwax, with no face-bow, on a hinge-type articulator (a semi-adjustable one rarely). A CR record on a complex articulator belongs to reorganized work, a full-arch registration puts material between teeth that should touch, and a protrusive record isn't part of the bounded-crown recipe.
pbox: Canine guidance both sides; no mobility, no wear facets
why: Single bounded crown: hand articulation, PVS or Aluwax; no face-bow; a hinge-type articulator.
A CR record on a complex articulator belongs to reorganized work, not one bounded crown.
A full-arch registration puts material between teeth that should touch: a classic record error.
A protrusive record isn't part of the single bounded crown recipe.

stem: How should the occlusion on this restoration be finished?
choices: Share centric and protrusive contacts between composite and tooth
Put all protrusive contact on the composite
Leave #8 just out of contact in both protrusion and centric to protect it
Give #8 all the anterior guidance
ex: The incisors meet edge to edge, and the fracture line runs through the old composite at the mesioincisal corner of #8. For a Class IV: simultaneous centric and protrusive contact on the natural tooth AND the restoration, to reduce fracture and differential wear. All the guidance on the composite is "a recipe for disaster," and leaving #8 out of contact lets it supererupt into the same trouble.
pbox: Class IV composite on #8, mesioincisal corner, replacing one that broke
why: Edge to edge with a history of fracture: share centric and protrusive contacts between composite and natural tooth.
All protrusive contact on the composite is "a recipe for disaster," especially with prior fractures.
Leaving #8 out of contact lets it drift or supererupt and shifts load elsewhere.
All the anterior guidance on #8 would overload the restoration.

stem: If this had been a Class III composite on #8 (proximal, no incisal corner), how would its contacts differ?
choices: Keep centric and protrusive contact off the composite
Give the composite all of the protrusive contact
Share centric and protrusive contact, as for Class IV
Make the composite the only centric stop on #8
ex: Class III composite: copy the existing contacts and avoid centric and protrusive contact on the restorative material. Class IV is the one that shares: simultaneous centric and protrusive contact on the natural tooth AND the restoration, to reduce fracture and differential wear (especially edge to edge, as he bites). Putting all the protrusive contact, or the only centric stop, on composite is what both rules avoid.
pbox: Class IV composite on #8, mesioincisal corner, replacing one that broke
why: Class III composite: copy the existing contacts and avoid centric and protrusive contact on the material.
Loading the composite with all the protrusive contact is what both rules avoid.
Sharing is the Class IV rule; a Class III keeps contact off the composite.
The only centric stop on composite would put the load where the Class III rule keeps it off.

stem: Which approach fits her plan?
choices: Conformative: copy her guidance, since she has no signs or symptoms
Reorganized: seat the joints and record CR, since six crowns is a big case
Reorganized: open the VDO so that the new crowns can be longer
Neuromuscular: find her myocentric point with a TENS unit
ex: In the absence of signs or symptoms, copy the existing guidance when restorations are needed: that is conformative dentistry, and the guide-table impression made before preparation is how the lab copies it. The number of crowns alone doesn't make a case reorganized (that is for occlusions showing damage, like a big deviating slide with wear), nothing here calls for a new VDO, and the neuromuscular approach is not taught at UAB.
pbox: Crowns #6-11 (failing, discolored PFMs; see the photo)
why: No signs or symptoms: copy the existing guidance. That is conformative dentistry.
The number of crowns alone doesn't make a case reorganized; damage and an unstable occlusion do.
Nothing here calls for a new VDO; she wants the same bite.
The neuromuscular approach is not taught at UAB.

stem: She needs a crown on #8. Before you prepare it, what do you do?
choices: Correct the posterior deflective contact that drives the mandible forward into the incisors
Splint #8 and #9 together with the crowns, since the mobility means they need support
Refer for periodontal surgery on #8 and #9 before any restorative work
Make the new #8 crown thicker lingually so it can take the force
ex: The chart shows fremitus and class I mobility on #8 and #9 with healthy 1-3 mm probing depths and no bleeding; the radiograph shows widened, funnel-shaped PDL spaces and thickened lamina dura on the same two teeth. Those are signs of force, not periodontal disease, and the force is the slide from the first molar contact forward into the incisors. L5 (single anterior crown): in harmony with the existing occlusion, but "correct posterior deflective contacts that slide the mandible forward into the incisors, especially with a history of fracture." Replacing a fractured crown doesn't fix the force that broke it; splinting, surgery or a bulkier crown leave the cause in place.
pbox: "The edge of my front tooth broke again" (third time on #8)
First contact on #2 and #31; the jaw then slides forward about 1.5 mm and the lower incisors strike #8 and #9
See the perio chart and the radiograph
why: Fremitus and mobility with healthy probing point to force from the slide into the incisors; correct that deflective contact first.
Splinting supports the teeth but leaves the force that keeps breaking #8 in place.
Probing depths are 1-3 mm with no bleeding: this isn't periodontal disease, so surgery treats the wrong problem.
A bulkier crown still takes the same force from the slide and will fracture again.

stem: Once the deflective contact is corrected, how is the single #8 crown designed?
choices: In harmony with her existing occlusion
From a custom anterior guide table
With all the protrusive guidance on #8
Out of contact, so it can never break again
ex: A single anterior crown, without symptoms, is made in harmony with the existing occlusion, after correcting any posterior deflective contact that slides the mandible forward into the incisors (especially with a history of fracture). A custom anterior guide table is for restoring both central incisors or one or both canines, not one central. All the guidance on one crown overloads it, and a tooth left out of contact supererupts.
pbox: "The edge of my front tooth broke again" (third time on #8)
First contact on #2 and #31; the jaw then slides forward about 1.5 mm and the lower incisors strike #8 and #9
See the perio chart and the radiograph
why: A single anterior crown is made in harmony with the existing occlusion, once the deflective contact is fixed.
A custom guide table is for both centrals or one or both canines, not one central.
All the guidance on one crown overloads it.
A tooth left out of contact supererupts.

stem: What is causing it, and what do you do?
choices: A non-working contact on the new crown: remove it in the left excursion and keep its MIP contacts
A working interference on #3: add group function on the right so the load is shared
Nothing yet: non-working contacts are common, and patients adapt to them over a few weeks
A high MIP contact on #3: remake the crown from a full-arch MIP registration
ex: In a LEFT excursion the right side is the non-working (mediotrusive) side, and the red streak sits on the facial incline of #3's mesiolingual (palatal) cusp, where the help sheet says a right-side non-working contact lands (against the lingual incline of the mandibular buccal cusp). L5: a patient who has adapted to a non-working contact over years can keep it, but "patients don't tolerate one you introduce in an afternoon"; the new mobility is the warning. Adjust the crown so the left excursion is free and keep the blue MIP contacts. Group function is a working-side scheme, and the MIP contacts are not the problem.
pbox: "#3 aches when I chew on the LEFT side, and it feels a little loose"
#3 mobility class I (was 0); see the articulating paper
why: In a left excursion the right side is non-working; a newly added non-working contact on #3 must be removed while keeping its MIP contacts.
Group function is a working-side scheme; in a left excursion #3 is on the non-working side.
Patients can adapt to old non-working contacts, but not to one introduced in an afternoon; the new mobility is the warning.
The blue MIP contacts aren't the problem, and a full-arch registration is a record error, not a fix.

stem: In her left excursion, what is the right side called, and what does its condyle do?
choices: Non-working (mediotrusive): the condyle orbits forward, down and medially
Working (laterotrusive): the condyle mostly rotates in place
Non-working (laterotrusive): the condyle mostly rotates in place
Working (mediotrusive): its condyle orbits forward, down and medially along the eminence
ex: The working (laterotrusive) side is the side the mandible moves toward, and its condyle mostly rotates; in a left excursion that is the left side. The right side is the non-working (mediotrusive; "balancing" is a denture term) side, and its condyle orbits forward, down and medially along the eminence. That is why a mark on #3 in a left excursion is a non-working contact, an interference.
pbox: "#3 aches when I chew on the LEFT side, and it feels a little loose"
#3 mobility class I (was 0); see the articulating paper
why: In a left move the right side is non-working (mediotrusive); its condyle orbits forward, down and medially.
The working side is the side the jaw moves toward, here the left; the right side is non-working.
Laterotrusive is the working side's term, and the condyle that mostly rotates is the working one.
Mediotrusive and orbiting describe the non-working side, not the working side.

stem: He wants veneers on #7-#10. What has to happen before you prepare the incisors?
choices: Eliminate the protrusive contacts on the molars before restoring the anteriors
Nothing: give the veneers steeper guidance, which will lift the molars apart in protrusion
Keep them: back teeth that touch in protrusion are part of a balanced occlusion
Splint #14 and #15 to the premolars so the protrusive load spreads over more roots
ex: Red streaks on the distal inclines of the upper molars' lingual cusps are protrusive contacts (protrusion runs the mandibular mesial inclines into the maxillary distal inclines), here from the mesially tipped #18. L5: "posterior protrusive interferences must be eliminated before restoring the anterior teeth." Sometimes anterior contours give enough separation, but "you can't make guidance steep enough to clear a badly tipped molar," and veneers asked to do it will fail. Balanced occlusion is for dentures, and splinting treats mobility, not the interference.
pbox: #19 was extracted years ago and never replaced; #18 has tipped mesially into the space
He slides straight forward to edge to edge; see the red marks
why: Posterior protrusive interferences must be eliminated before restoring the anterior teeth.
Steeper guidance can't clear a badly tipped molar, and veneers asked to do it will fail.
Balanced occlusion is for dentures; in natural teeth, molar contacts in protrusion are interferences.
Splinting treats mobility, not the interference itself.

stem: On the molars, which inclines make these red protrusive marks?
choices: Distal inclines of the maxillary palatal cusps against mesial inclines of the mandibular cusps
Mesial inclines of the maxillary cusps against distal inclines of the mandibular cusps
Facial inclines of the maxillary palatal cusps against lingual inclines of the mandibular buccal cusps
Lingual inclines of the maxillary buccal cusps against facial inclines of the mandibular buccal cusps
ex: Posterior teeth that fail to separate in protrusion contact on the distal inclines of the maxillary teeth and the mesial inclines of the mandibular teeth: the mandible moves forward, so on a maxillary tooth the protrusive pathway runs mesial. Tipped teeth like his #18 are the classic source ("tipped teeth give protrusive interferences"). The reverse pairing would need the mandible to move back, and the palatal-cusp and buccal-cusp pairings are the non-working and working contacts. The red streaks sit on the palatal cusps, so the question is which incline of them: these sit on the distal slopes and run straight front to back (mesiodistally), the protrusive direction. A non-working mark sits on the facial incline of the palatal cusp (the slope facing the central groove) and crosses the cusp at an angle (mesiopalatally on an upper tooth).
pbox: #19 was extracted years ago and never replaced; #18 has tipped mesially into the space
He slides straight forward to edge to edge; see the red marks
why: In protrusion the lower cusps run mesially, so the distal inclines of the palatal cusps (where the red sits) meet mandibular mesial inclines.
This reverses the pairing; it would need the mandible to move back.
Same palatal cusps, wrong incline: that is the non-working contact, on the slope facing the central groove, and its streak would cross the cusp at an angle, while these run straight front to back.
That is a working-side contact.

stem: Which inclines make the red non-working mark on #3?
choices: The facial incline of #3's palatal cusp against the lingual incline of a buccal cusp of #30
The lingual incline of #3's buccal cusp against the facial incline of a buccal cusp of #30
The distal inclines of #3's cusps against the mesial inclines of #30's cusps
The mesial inclines of #3's cusps against the distal inclines of #30's cusps
ex: The help sheet: for the right molars in a left movement (right side non-working), the contact is between the facial incline of the maxillary palatal cusp and the lingual incline of the mandibular buccal cusp. That is the red mark on the inner incline of #3's mesiolingual cusp. The lingual incline of the maxillary buccal cusp against the facial incline of the mandibular buccal cusp is a working-side contact (a right movement), and distal maxillary against mesial mandibular inclines is protrusive.
pbox: "#3 aches when I chew on the LEFT side, and it feels a little loose"
#3 mobility class I (was 0); see the articulating paper
why: Right side non-working in a left move: the facial incline of the maxillary palatal cusp meets the lingual incline of the mandibular buccal cusp.
That pairing is a working-side contact, in a right move.
Distal maxillary inclines against mesial mandibular inclines is the protrusive pairing.
That pairing would need the mandible to move backward; it isn't a non-working contact.

stem: What do you adjust before you seat it for good?
choices: Lighten it until shimstock drags through on light closure but holds on a clench; remove the excursive mark
Nothing: shimstock holding on all three teeth in both closures is the goal for an implant
Take #30 out of contact entirely, in MIP and excursions, so the implant can never be overloaded
Keep the excursive contact on #30 so it shares the working load with the canine
ex: An implant has no PDL: under about 10 lb it moves about 2-3 µm apically against a tooth's 28 µm. So a posterior implant crown is very light in casual closure and equal in maximum intercuspation: on a light closure shimstock (about 12 µm) holds on the neighbors and pulls through the implant with some resistance; on a clench the teeth drop into their PDL and it holds on all of them. Here it holds on the implant at a light closure, so the crown is too heavy, and posterior implants should avoid contact in excursions. No contact at all lets the opposing tooth supererupt.
pbox: Delivering a screw-retained implant crown on #30
See the shimstock test and the radiograph
why: An implant has no PDL, so it should be light on casual closure, equal on a clench, and out of excursions.
Shimstock holding on the implant at light closure means the crown is too heavy, not that it's right.
No contact at all lets the opposing tooth supererupt; the goal is light, not none.
Posterior implants should avoid contact in excursions; the excursive mark has to go.

stem: Why should the implant crown be lighter than #29 and #31 on a light closure?
choices: With no PDL it moves about 2-3 µm; a tooth moves about 28 µm
Titanium is harder than enamel, so it would wear the opposing teeth
Implants supererupt faster than teeth unless they are kept light
It has more proprioception than a tooth, so it feels pressure first
ex: An implant is a titanium root locked in bone with no periodontal ligament, so it moves far less than a tooth (about 2-3 µm against about 28 µm). On a light closure the natural teeth haven't yet dropped into their PDL, so an implant built to equal contact would take the load alone; on a clench the teeth drop in and all of them hold shimstock. The natural teeth have the proprioception, implants can't erupt (the opposing tooth can, which is why it still needs contact on a clench), and the reason is movement, not material.
pbox: Delivering a screw-retained implant crown on #30
See the shimstock test and the radiograph
why: No PDL: the implant barely moves (2-3 µm vs 28 µm), so equal contact would load it alone on a light closure.
The reason is how little it moves, not how hard the material is.
Implants can't erupt; it is the opposing tooth that supererupts without contact.
The natural teeth have the proprioception; the implant has none.

stem: Normally, what opens space between the posterior teeth as a patient protrudes?
choices: The condyles drop down the eminence (Christensen's phenomenon)
The disc rotates forward over the condyle head (Bennett movement)
The posterior teeth intrude into their periodontal ligament
The incisors intrude slightly, letting the molars drop apart
ex: Christensen's phenomenon is the space that opens between the posterior teeth in protrusion as the condyle drops down the articular eminence; the anterior guidance adds to it when the patient has it. Bennett movement is the sideways shift of the mandible toward the working side in a lateral movement, nothing to do with protrusion, and teeth move only microns in their PDL, far too little to open that space.
pbox: #19 was extracted years ago and never replaced; #18 has tipped mesially into the space

stem: How should the #6 implant crown behave in a right lateral excursion?

stem: How should the #6 implant crown touch in MIP compared with #5 and #7?

stem: He wants the anterior teeth rebuilt. What sequence does Dr. Givan use?

stem: What went wrong, and what should the record have been?

The PVS set too slowly in the mouth; switch to a full-arch plaster of Paris record instead
