Zirconia shrinks on firing unless the articulator has been calibrated
Zirconia crowns can only be designed digitally, so the mounting is ignored
The hinge forces the lab to leave every zirconia crown out of occlusion
ex: The hinge doesn't follow the patient's paths, so the crown hits in excursions and has to be ground; zirconia "doesn't adjust easily" or polish well, and grinding loses anatomic form.
why: The hinge doesn't follow the patient's paths, so eccentric contacts are ground, and zirconia adjusts and polishes poorly.
Calibration doesn't control firing shrinkage; the problem is the mismatched paths.
Zirconia crowns are made on mounted casts too; the mounting still matters.
The crown isn't left out of occlusion; it is usually high in excursions.

likely.t: Articulator size: best value when it is similar in size to the patient; a small hinge costs chair time

stem: What does a partial-arch articulator not allow?
choices: Checking the mounting cross-arch, or copying the other side
Mounting the casts in MICP
Hand articulation of the casts
Mounting by a lab that works without a facebow or mounting stand
ex: With only part of the arch you can't check the mounting across the arch or copy the occlusal form from the other side, so crowns often don't match it.
why: With only part of the arch you can't check the mounting across the arch or copy the other side.
They mount in MICP; that is the one position they handle.
Partial-arch casts can still be hand-articulated.
The limitation is cross-arch, not facebow use.

stem: When can a non-adjustable articulator still build a crown that roughly matches the patient's movement?
choices: When its condyles are about 4 inches apart and the cast is oriented to them
When its hinge sits directly behind the second molar, close to the teeth
When the casts are mounted with a thick interocclusal record to open the bite
When it is a partial-arch articulator glued to the back of the cast
ex: An articulator about the size of a person (for example the Hanau-Mate) with the cast in roughly the right place follows paths close to the patient's. A hinge behind the second molar never will.
why: An articulator the size of a person, with the cast oriented to its condyles, builds a crown that roughly follows the patient.
A hinge behind the second molar can never replicate the patient's arcs.
A thick record adds error on a non-adjustable articulator.
Partial-arch articulators glued to casts are the ones that don't match the patient.

likely.t: Articulator size: best value when it is similar in size to the patient; a small hinge costs chair time

stem: To mount casts without a facebow, the articulator should have an intercondylar distance of about:
choices: 110 mm (4 inches)
60 mm (2.5 inches)
150 mm (6 inches)
80 mm (3 inches)
ex: About 110 mm, 4 inches: the size of a person. Used with a universal mounting stand, it puts the casts in the Bonwill position.
why: About 110 mm, 4 inches: roughly the distance between a person's condyles.
Far smaller than a person; a small articulator magnifies the closing-arc error.
Wider than a person's condyles.
Smaller than the 110 mm the procedure calls for.

likely.t: Articulator size: best value when it is similar in size to the patient; a small hinge costs chair time

stem: Casts mounted on a universal mounting stand end up in which position, where average settings can be used without patient records?
choices: The Bonwill position
The terminal hinge position
Centric relation
The neutral zone
ex: The mounting stand places the maxillary cast in the Bonwill position (the 4-inch triangle), where the average protrusive angle, immediate side shift and progressive side shift work.
why: The mounting stand places the casts in the Bonwill position, where average settings work.
The terminal hinge position is where the condyles rotate in CR, not where the stand places the cast.
CR is a joint position, not where a mounting stand places the maxillary cast.
The neutral zone is the space where tongue and lip forces balance.

stem: Sagittal condylar inclination (condylar guidance) is:
choices: The angle at which the condyle descends the articular eminence in the sagittal plane
The angle of the orbiting condyle's inward path in the horizontal plane
The tilt of the occlusal plane relative to Frankfort horizontal
The distance the working condyle shifts sideways right at the start of a lateral move
ex: SCI is the descent down the eminence, seen from the side. The inward path is the Bennett angle; the sideways jump is the immediate side shift.
why: The condyle's descent down the eminence in the sagittal plane is the SCI.
The inward path in the horizontal plane is the Bennett angle.
The plane's tilt is captured by the facebow, not the SCI.
The sideways jump at the start of a move is the immediate side shift.

stem: What does the SCI setting control on a semi-adjustable articulator?
choices: Posterior disclusion with little anterior guidance; cusp height and fossa depth
The width of the central fossae, which follows the orbiting condyle's inward path
The vertical dimension of occlusion at which the casts are mounted
The groove and ridge positions set by the intercondylar distance
ex: Condylar guidance controls posterior disclusion if there is little or no anterior guidance and affects cusp height and fossa depth. Fossa width is the Bennett angle; groove positions follow the intercondylar distance (fully adjustable).
why: Condylar guidance controls posterior disclusion when anterior guidance is minimal, and cusp height and fossa depth.
Fossa width follows the Bennett angle.
The VDO is set by the records and the incisal pin, not the SCI.
Groove and ridge positions follow the intercondylar distance on a fully adjustable articulator.

likely.t: The Bennett angle is the setting he would leave off first; the SCI matters more

stem: When the SCI is set arbitrarily for fixed restorations, what range is common?
ex: Fixed: 20-30° is common. About 0° is used for neutrocentric dentures.
why: Fixed work: 20-30° is the common arbitrary setting.
About 0° is for neutrocentric dentures, not fixed work.
Steeper than the common arbitrary setting; it risks posterior interferences.
Far steeper than any common arbitrary setting.

stem: For neutrocentric dentures, the SCI is set to about:
ex: Neutrocentric dentures use a flat (about 0°) setting; 20-30° is the common arbitrary setting for fixed work.
why: Neutrocentric dentures use a flat, about 0°, setting.
20° is within the common range for fixed work, not neutrocentric dentures.
30° is the common arbitrary fixed setting.
Steeper than any setting the slides give for dentures.

stem: In the articulator handout, the Bennett angle setting mainly affects which feature of the posterior teeth?
choices: The width of the central fossae
Cusp height
The curve of Wilson
Marginal ridge height
ex: In mediotrusion the orbiting condyle moves inward; the angle of that path sets how wide the central fossae must be. Cusp height follows mainly the SCI. The determinants table from the midterm does pair a greater Bennett movement with shorter cusps, but the articulator handout ties the Bennett angle setting to the width of the central fossae.
why: The orbiting condyle's inward path sets how wide the central fossae must be.
Cusp height follows mainly the SCI; the midterm table pairs a greater Bennett movement with shorter cusps, but the handout ties this setting to fossa width.
The curve of Wilson is a frontal curve of the teeth, not an articulator setting.
Marginal ridges aren't set by the Bennett angle.

likely.t: The Bennett angle is the setting he would leave off first; the SCI matters more

stem: Which articulator adjustment did Dr. Givan say he would leave off first, because the average values are close enough for most general dentistry?
choices: The Bennett angle
Sagittal condylar inclination
The incisal guide pin
The centric latch
ex: "If I was going to leave any feature off of an articulator, I'd probably leave this one": the Bennett angle is less commonly adjusted.
why: He would leave the Bennett angle off first: average values are close enough for most work.
Condylar guidance is one of the two settings that matter most.
The incisal guide pin wasn't the feature he named.
The centric latch holds the condyles in CR; it isn't an average-value setting.

likely.t: The Bennett angle is the setting he would leave off first; the SCI matters more

stem: Immediate lateral mandibular translation is also called:
choices: Immediate side shift
Progressive side shift
The Bennett angle
Condylar guidance
ex: Immediate lateral mandibular translation = immediate side shift (ISS), set on more sophisticated instruments along with the Bennett angle on the medial wall.
why: Immediate lateral mandibular translation is the immediate side shift (ISS).
Progressive side shift is the gradual part of the movement, not the immediate jump.
The Bennett angle is the angle of the inward path, a separate setting.
Condylar guidance is the SCI.

stem: A facebow's reference plane is defined by which three points?
choices: Both auditory canals and one anterior point such as nasion or orbitale
Both condyles found with a hinge-axis locator and the incisive papilla
Both hamular notches and the incisive papilla
Both mental foramina and the chin
ex: Two posterior points (usually the ear canals, estimating the transverse horizontal hinge axis) and one anterior point that varies by system: nasion, orbitale, or a set distance from the maxillary teeth.
why: Two ear canals estimate the hinge axis; one anterior point (nasion, orbitale or a set distance) completes the plane.
Locating the condyles exactly is a kinematic hinge-axis locator, not the reference plane.
Hamular notches and the papilla are denture landmarks, not facebow points.
The mental foramina aren't facebow reference points.

likely.t: The facebow mounts the maxillary cast only, on a three-point reference plane

stem: The reference plane a facebow uses is usually:
choices: Frankfort horizontal
The occlusal plane
The midsagittal plane
The curve of Spee
ex: Typically the Frankfort horizontal plane; some systems use Camper's plane.
why: Usually Frankfort horizontal (some systems use Camper's plane).
The occlusal plane is what the facebow transfers, not its reference plane.
The midsagittal plane isn't the facebow's reference plane.
The curve of Spee is a curve of the teeth, not a reference plane.

likely.t: The facebow mounts the maxillary cast only, on a three-point reference plane

stem: In an indirect facebow mounting, what is attached to the articulator to mount the cast?
choices: Only the transfer assembly, on the lower member of the articulator
The whole ear-bow, clipped onto the condylar elements
The patient's CR record, on the upper member
A universal mounting stand in place of the bite plate
ex: Indirect mounting uses only the transfer assembly (with the bite plate) on the lower member: simpler, and the ear-bow stays in the clinic.
why: Only the transfer assembly goes on the lower member: simpler, and the ear-bow stays in the clinic.
The ear-bow stays in the clinic in an indirect mounting.
The CR record relates the mandibular cast; it isn't part of the facebow mounting.
A mounting stand is the no-facebow method.

stem: A kinematic facebow is one that:
choices: Locates the patient's exact hinge axis
Uses the ear canals as the hinge axis
Records chewing paths with six styli
Is built into an intraoral scanner
ex: A bow that finds the exact hinge axis is kinematic (AHA = PHA). One that uses the ear canals and anatomic averages is arbitrary. Six styli on six tables is a pantograph.
why: A kinematic bow finds the exact hinge axis (AHA = PHA).
Using the ear canals and averages is an arbitrary facebow.
Six styli on six tables is a pantograph.
Scanners capture motion, but a kinematic facebow is the hinge-axis locator.

stem: With the Denar Slidematic facebow, where is the anterior reference point marked?
choices: 43 mm above the incisal edge of the right lateral incisor (#7)
43 mm above the incisal edge of the right central incisor (#8)
At nasion, the bridge of the nose between the eyes
At orbitale, the lowest point on the rim of the orbit
ex: The Slidematic ruler rests on #7's incisal edge and marks a point 43 mm above it (adjacent teeth or the upper lip at rest if #7 is missing). Nasion and orbitale are other systems' anterior points.
why: 43 mm above #7's incisal edge, found with the Slidematic ruler.
It is the lateral incisor, #7, not the central.
Nasion is another system's anterior point.
Orbitale is another system's anterior point.

stem: What does the horizontal level on the Slidematic facebow capture?
choices: The esthetic planes: incisal cant and occlusal-plane tilt
The patient's exact transverse horizontal hinge axis
The sagittal condylar inclination of both condyles at once
The vertical dimension of occlusion at rest
ex: The level parallels the bench top the articulator sits on, so any incisal cant and occlusal-plane tilt come to the articulator where you can see them.
why: The level parallels the bench top, so incisal cant and occlusal-plane tilt reach the articulator.
An arbitrary bow doesn't find the exact axis; that is a kinematic bow.
The SCI is set with a protrusive record or an arbitrary value.
The facebow doesn't record the vertical dimension.

stem: Mounting the maxillary cast without a facebow risks all of the following EXCEPT:
choices: A CR record that can no longer be verified in the mouth
An occlusal cant in the esthetic plane
Protrusive, working and non-working interferences
Cusp heights and groove positions that don't match
ex: Wrong maxillary orientation errs in the esthetic plane (cant), the occlusal plane (interferences), cusp height and cusp and groove positions, and adds chairside adjustment. Verifying a CR record has nothing to do with the facebow.
why: Verifying a CR record has nothing to do with the facebow, so this is the exception.
Wrong maxillary orientation risks an occlusal cant.
An occlusal-plane error risks protrusive, working and non-working interferences.
Cusp height and groove and cusp positions may not match the patient.

likely.t: An arbitrary facebow is close enough (2-5 mm); skipping it risks a cant and mounting errors

stem: In protrusion and laterotrusion, a maxillary cast mounted too far posterior or too high causes:
choices: Premature or heavy contacts on the most anterior teeth
Premature or heavy contacts on the most posterior teeth
No error, as long as the MIP record is accurate
An occlusal cant toward the side of the error
ex: Too posterior or too superior: the most anterior teeth hit early or hard. Too anterior or too inferior: the most posterior teeth.
why: Too posterior or too superior: premature or heavy contacts on the most anterior teeth.
The most posterior teeth are loaded when the cast is too anterior or too inferior.
An MIP record can't correct a wrong maxillary mounting in excursions.
A cant comes from a tilted esthetic plane, not an anteroposterior error.

likely.t: An arbitrary facebow is close enough (2-5 mm); skipping it risks a cant and mounting errors

stem: Why is wax often preferred for a CR record?
choices: It sets instantly with the air-water syringe
It captures fine anatomy better than VPS does
It flexes, so it survives shipping without breaking
It can be used with the teeth in light contact
ex: Wax: immediate set, minimal trimming, repeatable for verification, and because it doesn't capture fine anatomy the cusp tips seat in it well. Its weakness is that it is fragile.
why: Wax sets instantly with the air-water syringe and needs little trimming.
Wax captures less anatomy than VPS, which is why cusp tips seat in it well.
Wax is brittle and fragile, not flexible.
CR records are made without tooth contact.

stem: On a semi-adjustable articulator, at what opening should a CR record be made?
choices: The smallest opening that avoids contact, or the VDO you plan to restore
About 20 mm, still within the pure rotation of the condyles
Any opening at all, because the thickness of a CR record doesn't affect its accuracy
Maximum opening, so the condyles are fully translated
ex: The arbitrary axis means the articulator's arc differs from the patient's, so error grows with the opening. At the vertical you will restore, the arcs meet. Thickness doesn't matter only on a fully adjustable articulator.
why: Minimal opening, or the vertical you will restore at, keeps the arbitrary-axis error small.
20 mm is the rotational range, far too thick for a record.
Thickness doesn't matter only on a fully adjustable articulator with the exact axis.
Records are never taken at maximum opening.

stem: The closure from CO into MIP does what?
choices: Decreases the VDO and positions the mandible anteriorly
Increases the VDO and positions the mandible posteriorly
Keeps the VDO and shifts the mandible to the working side
Seats the condyles further up into the fossae
ex: Sliding from the first seated-joint contact into MIP closes the vertical and brings the mandible forward, with many potential interferences.
why: Sliding from CO to MIP closes the vertical and brings the mandible forward.
The slide goes forward and closes, not back and open.
The slide is up and forward, with a change in vertical.
In MIP the condyles come off their seat; they don't seat further.

stem: Dr. Givan called the MIP record the most common record, and also:
choices: The most misused record
The most accurate record
The record labs won't accept
The hardest record to take
ex: "I will suggest to you it is also the most misused record. It's also the record that gets you in most trouble."
why: "It is also the most misused record" and "the record that gets you in most trouble."
Used properly it can be accurate, but he called it the most misused.
Labs mount with whatever record they are sent.
It is a simple record; the trouble is misuse.

likely.t: The MIP record: most common, most misused; hand articulate whenever you can

stem: According to Dr. Givan, what are the first and second most common causes of lab problems?
choices: A bad impression, then the mounting (usually a misused MIP record)
The mounting, then a bad impression
A bad shade selection, then a bad impression
The technician's skill, then the articulator's calibration
ex: Number one: a bad impression (a margin not captured won't appear on the die). Number two: the mounting, usually from misusing MIP records.
why: Number one is a bad impression; number two is the mounting, usually a misused MIP record.
The order is the other way around: the impression comes first.
Shade wasn't on his list.
He blamed the dentist's impression and mounting, not the technician.

likely.t: The MIP record: most common, most misused; hand articulate whenever you can

stem: What did Dr. Givan call the most important rule for MIP records?
choices: Hand-articulate whenever you can; use a record only when needed
Always send a full-arch VPS record so the lab has every contact
Always use wax, because VPS is never accurate for mounting
Take two records and let the lab choose the one that fits
ex: "If possible, don't use a record. Hand articulate always when you can." If you send the lab a record, they will mount with it.
why: "If possible, don't use a record. Hand articulate always when you can."
Full-arch records are the classic mounting error.
VPS can be very accurate if used with care.
If you send the lab a record, they will mount with it; send none "just in case."

likely.t: The MIP record: most common, most misused; hand articulate whenever you can

stem: Per the slides, the minimum removal time of a VPS bite registration is about:
choices: 1 minute 30 seconds
10 seconds
5 minutes
30 seconds
ex: Working time 30-60 seconds from the start of the mix at 72°F; minimum removal time 1 minute 30 seconds. Hard to keep still that long, which is why wax sets "instantly" by comparison.
why: Minimum removal time is 1 minute 30 seconds (working time 30-60 s).
Wax sets in about a second; VPS takes far longer than 10 s.
Longer than the slides' 1.5 minutes.
30 seconds is about the start of the working time, not removal.

stem: Why does a registration rarely fit the stone casts, even when trimmed?
choices: The material is resilient and records more detail than the stone does
The stone expands while the registration shrinks overnight
The record is taken at a higher VDO than the casts are mounted
Registrations cool on the bench and curl at the edges
ex: Two reasons, regardless of material: resilience, and replication of detail greater than the stone model. Occlusion is in microns; 20 µm off and the crown is out of occlusion.
why: Resilience plus more detail than the stone cast: it rarely fits, even trimmed.
The slides blame resilience and detail, not expansion or shrinkage.
VDO isn't the reason a registration fails to fit.
Curling isn't the issue; resilience and detail are.

likely.t: VPS MIP records go over the prep only, trimmed off cusp tips and soft tissue

stem: What are the disadvantages of waxes such as Aluwax or Delar for MIP records?
choices: They need a water bath and they are brittle
They set slowly and need heavy trimming
They cost more than VPS and stick to stone
They can't be chilled with an air-water syringe
ex: Waxes set instantly with the air-water syringe, need little trimming and cost much less; the drawbacks are the water bath and brittleness (and they can get too thin).
why: Waxes need a water bath and are brittle.
Waxes set instantly and need little trimming.
Waxes are comparatively much cheaper than VPS.
The air-water syringe is exactly how wax is set.

stem: Select every item that is one of the five requirements of interocclusal records.
choices: It must not move teeth or displace soft tissue
It must fit the casts as accurately as it fits the mouth
It must not distort in storage or on the way to the lab
It must cover every occluding surface in the arch
It must be made of a material that sets in under 10 seconds
ex: The five (Dawson): no tooth movement or soft-tissue displacement; verifiable in the mouth; fits the casts as accurately as the mouth; verifiable on the casts; no distortion in storage or transport. Covering every occluding surface is the classic error, and no set time is required.
why: Requirement 1: no tooth movement or soft-tissue displacement.
Requirement 3: it fits the casts as accurately as the mouth.
Requirement 5: no distortion in storage or transport.
Covering every occluding surface is the error to avoid, not a requirement.
No set time is among the five requirements.

stem: If missing teeth don't allow a stable MIP mounting, what should you use?
choices: A record base
A thicker VPS record over every tooth
A pantograph
A kinematic facebow
ex: "If missing teeth does not allow stable mounting, must use a record base." Thickening the VPS only adds error.
why: Too few teeth for a stable mounting: use a record base.
More VPS over more teeth only adds error.
A pantograph records movement; it doesn't stabilize a mounting.
A kinematic facebow finds the hinge axis; it doesn't relate the mandibular cast.

stem: A right lateral record sets which settings on a semi-adjustable articulator?
choices: The left SCI and the left Bennett angle and side shift
The right SCI and the right Bennett angle and side shift
Both SCIs, the same as a protrusive record
Only the incisal guide table
ex: Each lateral record sets the contralateral (orbiting) side: moving right, the left condyle slides down its medial wall, so the left settings are set.
why: Moving right, the left condyle orbits down its medial wall, so the left SCI and medial-wall settings are set.
The working-side (right) condyle mostly rotates; it isn't what a right record sets.
Only a protrusive record sets both SCIs.
Lateral records set condylar settings, not the incisal table.

likely.t: Protrusive records are preferred for the SCI: a lateral record reads steeper

stem: Why are protrusive records preferred over lateral records for setting the SCI?
choices: The lateral SCI is steeper; building at the shallower protrusive SCI keeps crowns discluded
The protrusive SCI is the steeper one, which builds taller and more esthetic posterior cusps
Lateral records can't be taken for a semi-adjustable articulator
Protrusive records take two records, so each side is checked twice
ex: Down the medial wall (lateral record) the angle is steeper than down the eminence (protrusive). Built at the shallower angle, contacts avoided in protrusion also miss in laterotrusion, so the patient gets disclusion.
why: The medial wall is steeper than the eminence; building at the shallower protrusive angle keeps restorations discluded.
The protrusive SCI is the shallower one, not the steeper.
They can be; protrusive is simply preferred.
A protrusive record is one record, not two.

likely.t: Protrusive records are preferred for the SCI: a lateral record reads steeper

stem: Many clinicians set an arbitrary 30° SCI for fixed work. Why does it tend to work?
choices: Most patients' eminences are steeper (often 35-40°), so crowns built at 30° still disclude
Most patients' eminences are flatter (10-20°), so 30° adds disclusion in the mouth
30° matches the angle of Bonwill's equilateral triangle
30° matches the curve of Spee in most adults
ex: Protrusive angles range about 20-60°, commonly 35-40°. An articulator shallower than the patient means more disclusion in the mouth; 30° still leaves decent anatomy (20° makes the cusps too shallow).
why: Patients are usually steeper (20-60°, often 35-40°), so 30° still discludes in the mouth with decent anatomy.
If patients were flatter than the articulator, crowns would hit, not disclude.
Bonwill's triangle is about distances, not this angle.
The curve of Spee isn't the reason for 30°.

stem: If a lateral record is taken at 7-10 mm of condylar movement instead of 3-5 mm, the Bennett angle set is:
choices: Smaller, building narrower fossae and more likely interferences
Larger, building wider fossae and fewer interferences
The same, because the orbiting condyle's path is straight
Larger, building taller posterior cusps
ex: The orbiting condyle's path curves: at 3-5 mm the angle is larger, at 7-10 mm smaller, which narrows the fossae. So make records at 3-5 mm.
why: Taken at 7-10 mm the angle is smaller, narrowing the fossae and inviting interferences.
That is what happens at 3-5 mm: a larger angle and wider fossae.
The orbiting path curves, so where you take it matters.
The Bennett angle affects fossa width, not cusp height.

likely.t: Eccentric records at 3-5 mm: farther out, the Bennett angle reads smaller

stem: What does interchangeability (for example the calibrated Denar 320) allow?
choices: Moving mounted casts between articulators without losing accuracy
Using one facebow with any brand of articulator
Programming the articulator without eccentric records
Mounting the mandibular cast without any record
ex: Calibrated articulators exchange mounted casts accurately: the articulator doesn't travel to the lab, fewer are needed, and less damage happens.
why: Calibrated articulators exchange mounted casts accurately, so yours doesn't travel to the lab.
Interchangeability is about mounted casts, not facebows.
Programming still needs records or averages.
The mandibular cast is still related with a record or by hand.

stem: Which setting is found on a fully adjustable articulator but not on a semi-adjustable one?
choices: The intercondylar distance
Sagittal condylar inclination
The Bennett angle
The incisal guide table
ex: Fully adjustable articulators add the intercondylar distance, curved paths and the rotating condyle's movement. SCI and the Bennett angle are the semi-adjustable articulator's two common settings.
why: Intercondylar distance is set on fully adjustable instruments; semi-adjustable ones use about 4 inches.
SCI is one of the semi-adjustable articulator's two common settings.
The Bennett angle is the other common semi-adjustable setting.
Semi-adjustable articulators have incisal guide tables too.

stem: Changing the intercondylar distance on a fully adjustable articulator affects:
choices: The paths of the opposing cusps, so groove and ridge positions
The vertical dimension of occlusion at which the casts are mounted
Only the esthetic plane
The SCI on the working side
ex: Not everyone is 4 inches; the distance changes the paths of the opposing cusps across the tooth, and so the groove and ridge positions.
why: It changes the eccentric paths of opposing cusps, so groove and ridge positions.
The VDO isn't set by the intercondylar distance.
It affects function, not only esthetics.
The SCI is a separate setting.

stem: How is the exact hinge axis found for a kinematic facebow?
choices: Hinge the jaw in CR until the stylus only rotates
Seat the bow's earpieces in both auditory canals and level the bow
Mark a point 43 mm above the lateral incisor
Trace protrusive and lateral paths on six recording tables
ex: A hinge-axis locator: the upper bow holds a grid, the lower a stylus; when the stylus rotates without arcing it sits on the axis, which was once tattooed on the skin. Tracing protrusive and lateral paths on six recording tables is the pantograph, the next step: it records how the jaw moves (the "timing"), not where the hinge axis is.
why: The stylus is adjusted until it only rotates as the mandible hinges in CR: that point is the axis.
Ear canals give an arbitrary axis, not the exact one.
43 mm above #7 is the Slidematic's anterior reference point.
Six tables record movement with a pantograph.

stem: What does a pantograph capture that positional records can't?
choices: The timing of mandibular movement along each path
The patient's exact hinge axis, marked on the skin
The esthetic plane and any cant
The MIP contacts of the teeth
ex: Positional records capture end points; the pantograph traces how the jaw gets there (protrusive and right and left laterotrusive) so a fully adjustable articulator can be tuned to reproduce it.
why: It records how the jaw moves along each path: the timing positional records can't show.
The hinge axis is found with a kinematic locator first.
The esthetic plane is a facebow's job.
MIP contacts come from the casts, not the pantograph.

stem: Why does a pantograph use a central bearing device?
choices: To keep the teeth apart so they can't influence the recorded motion
To hold the six recording tables level during movement
To mark the hinge axis on the patient's skin
To measure the intercondylar distance
ex: The central bearing device separates the teeth, so the tracings show joint- and muscle-guided motion, not tooth guidance.
why: Separating the teeth keeps tooth guidance out of the tracings.
The tables are on the bows; the bearing device separates the teeth.
Marking the axis is the hinge-axis locator's job.
Intercondylar distance is set on the articulator.

stem: Why doesn't the thickness of a CR record affect accuracy on a fully adjustable articulator?
choices: The exact hinge axis is captured, so both open and close on the same arc
Fully adjustable articulators are always mounted in MIP, never in centric relation
The pantograph tracing corrects for the record's thickness
Records for fully adjustable articulators are always under 1 mm
ex: With a kinematic facebow, AHA = PHA, so the terminal hinge arc is the same; on a semi-adjustable the arcs differ and thicker records add error.
why: AHA = PHA with a kinematic bow, so the terminal hinge arcs match.
Fully adjustable articulators are mounted in CR.
The pantograph records movement, not record thickness.
No such limit; thickness simply doesn't matter there.

stem: A patient with strong anterior guidance needs a single crown on #20. What articulator is enough?
choices: A simpler one: the anterior guidance will disclude the crown

stem: Put the steps for setting a semi-adjustable articulator from a protrusive record in order.

Seat the record on the upper cast and the lower cast into it
See the gap: the condylar elements don't touch the fossae
Adjust each SCI until its element touches the superior fossa
