It permanently reprograms the central pattern generator
It ends nocturnal bruxism once the interferences are gone
ex: Occlusal work, such as a splint, "will help provide an environment of healing" that helps resolve other disorders. Being a helpful adjunct does not make occlusion part of the cause, and bruxism is centrally mediated.
why: His 2026 phrasing: occlusal work helps provide an environment of healing.
Most TMDs have nothing to do with occlusion, so it doesn't remove their cause.
The central pattern generator isn't reprogrammed by occlusal treatment.
Bruxism is centrally mediated; a splint stops it only temporarily.

stem: Chewing, swallowing and speaking are regulated by:
choices: The brainstem (central pattern generator, engrams)
The motor cortex alone, by conscious control
The periodontal ligament directly
The lateral pterygoid muscle spindle
ex: Normal function is regulated by the brainstem's central pattern generator (engrams), influenced by peripheral sensory and nociceptive input and by CNS effects such as the limbic system.
why: The brainstem's central pattern generator (engrams) regulates them.
Function is largely subconscious, not run by conscious cortical control.
The PDL gives sensory feedback that influences function; it doesn't regulate it.
Muscle spindles sense length and velocity; they don't run the pattern.

stem: Which is a systemic event, rather than a local one, in the functional disturbance model?
choices: Emotional stress
A high crown
Bruxism
A burn from hot pizza
ex: Systemic events are emotions and stress. A high crown, tissue trauma, strain, bruxism and constant pain input are local events.
why: Emotions and stress are the systemic events.
A high crown is a local event.
Bruxism is listed as a local event.
Tissue trauma, such as a burn, is a local event.

stem: Which is listed as a systemic factor affecting physiologic tolerance?
choices: Genetics, gender, diet, acute or chronic disease
The position the occlusion gives the mandible
An unstable orthopedic relationship of the mandible
A high crown placed last week
ex: Systemic tolerance factors: genetics, gender, diet, acute or chronic disease. The occlusion and an unstable orthopedic relationship are local tolerance factors; a high crown is an event.
why: Genetics, gender, diet and disease are the systemic tolerance factors.
How the occlusion positions the mandible is a local tolerance factor.
An unstable orthopedic relationship is a local tolerance factor.
A high crown is an event, not a tolerance factor.

stem: A patient says, "My bite never bothered me in 30 years, then last Tuesday the pain started." In the model, what most likely changed?
choices: The event or the tolerance, so the total now exceeds the tolerance
Nothing: symptoms need a malocclusion that is new
The occlusion itself must have changed on the day the pain started
The central pattern generator stopped working
ex: Each element of the model (function, event, tolerance) can change, and events tolerated one day may not be another. That is the typical TMD story: fine until one day it isn't, often without a known cause. It does not require a new malocclusion.
why: Any element can change; an event tolerated before may now exceed the tolerance.
Symptoms can start without a new malocclusion: tolerance or events change.
The occlusion needn't change; the tolerance often does.
Normal function continues; it's the balance of events and tolerance that tipped.

likely.t: The functional disturbance model and the five etiologies

stem: Which is NOT on the slides' list of signs and symptoms when the masticatory system's tolerance is exceeded?
choices: Gingival recession
Pulpitis
Ear pain
Tooth mobility
ex: The list: pulpitis, tooth wear or fracture, tooth mobility, masticatory muscle pain, TMJ pain, ear pain and headache pain. Occlusal trauma rarely affects the gingiva and mucosa.
why: Gingival recession isn't on the list; trauma rarely affects the gingiva.
Pulpitis is sign a.
Ear pain is sign f.
Tooth mobility is sign c.

stem: Which is NOT one of the five etiologies of functional disturbances?
choices: Periodontal infection
Trauma
Deep pain input
Parafunctional activities
ex: The five: mandibular stability, trauma, emotional stress, deep pain input and parafunctional activities. Infection causes most periodontal bone loss, but it isn't on this list.
why: Infection causes most periodontal bone loss but isn't one of the five.
Trauma is etiology 2.
Deep pain input is etiology 4.
Parafunctional activities are etiology 5.

likely.t: The functional disturbance model and the five etiologies

stem: Mandibular stability regards:
choices: The simultaneous fit of the teeth and both joints against the skull
The fit of the teeth alone in MIP
The condyles alone seated in centric relation
How firmly the teeth resist horizontal mobility under a 500 g test force
ex: Mandibular stability is the simultaneous fit of the teeth (occlusal stability) and both joints (orthopedic stability) against the skull. Either one alone is only half of it.
why: Mandibular stability is teeth and both joints fitting the skull together.
The teeth alone are occlusal stability, only half of it.
The joints alone are orthopedic stability, only half of it.
Mobility is about trauma, not mandibular stability.

stem: Which sign did Pullinger and Seligman note more often in TMD patients?
choices: A CO to MIP slide greater than 2 mm
A deep vertical overlap greater than 2 mm
Canine guidance on both sides
Three or more missing anterior teeth
ex: Their signs: skeletal anterior open bite, a CO-MIP slide over 2 mm, horizontal overjet over 4 mm, and five or more missing posterior teeth. These are also found in non-TMD patients.
why: A CO-MIP slide over 2 mm is one of their four signs.
Their sign is horizontal overjet over 4 mm, not deep vertical overlap.
Canine guidance is a goal, not one of their signs.
Their sign is five or more missing posterior teeth.

stem: What did Pullinger and Seligman conclude about occlusion and TMD?
choices: Occlusion is not the most important factor; multiple co-factors were more common
Occlusion causes most TMDs, so prophylactic equilibration should be used to prevent them
The four signs are found only in TMD patients
A CO-MIP slide is the single cause of intracapsular disorders
ex: Because the same signs appear in the non-TMD population, they concluded occlusion is not the most important factor in TMDs; multiple co-factors were more common.
why: The signs appear in non-TMD patients too, so occlusion isn't the most important factor.
They concluded the opposite, and prophylactic equilibration isn't supported.
The signs were also found in the non-TMD population.
They found multiple co-factors more common than any single occlusal cause.

stem: In the review of 57 epidemiologic studies (Table 7-2), how many found no relationship between occlusion and TMD?
ex: 22 found no relationship and 35 found occlusion related to TMD symptoms, but the conditions varied widely, a relationship doesn't imply cause, and the studies usually didn't specify the type of TMD.
why: 22 found no relationship.
35 found occlusion related to symptoms, the other part of the 57.
10% is the share with MIP coincident with CR, not a study count.
57 is the total number of studies reviewed.

stem: Why does the dental literature give weak evidence about occlusion and TMD, according to Dr. Givan?
choices: Studies rarely specify which TMD, so patient groups are mixed
Studies only enroll patients who have no symptoms
Occlusion can't be measured on mounted casts
TMDs are too rare to study in groups
ex: The literature "rarely breaks down exactly which TMD" it studied: joint and muscle patients are bundled together, so causes can't be separated. TMDs are common, not rare.
why: Studies rarely say which TMD they studied, so groups are mixed.
The problem is mixed TMD groups, not only asymptomatic patients.
Occlusion can be measured; the problem is the diagnostic categories.
TMDs are common; the problem is mixing different ones.

stem: Joints fully seated and teeth fully in contact (MIP) give, respectively:
choices: Orthopedic stability and occlusal stability
Occlusal stability and orthopedic stability
Orthopedic instability and occlusal stability
Mandibular stability and dental instability
ex: Joints fully seated = orthopedic stability; teeth fully in contact (MIP) = occlusal stability. Together they are the ideal of mandibular stability, and they lead to the treatment goals.
why: Seated joints are orthopedic stability; full contact in MIP is occlusal stability.
This reverses them: the joints are orthopedic, the teeth occlusal.
Seated joints are orthopedic stability, not instability.
Both together make mandibular stability; MIP contact is occlusal stability.

stem: In the treatment goals for the musculoskeletal stable position, the condyles rest:
choices: In their most superior-anterior position against the slopes of the eminences
In their most posterior-superior position in the fossae
In their most inferior-anterior position at the crest of the eminence
Wherever the teeth put them in MIP
ex: Goal 1: condyles in their most superior-anterior position against the posterior slopes of the articular eminences (centric relation). The posterior-superior "retruded" version is the older idea of CR.
why: Goal 1: most superior-anterior against the slopes of the eminences.
Posterior-superior is the older, retruded idea of CR.
The crest of the eminence is where the condyle goes in protrusion, not CR.
That describes MIP, which takes the condyles off their seat in about 90%.

stem: In the alert feeding position, the treatment goals call for:
choices: Posterior contacts more prominent than anterior contacts
Anterior contacts more prominent than posterior contacts
No posterior contacts, only canine guidance
Equal contacts on every tooth, front and back
ex: Goal 5: with the head forward and down (alert feeding posture), the posterior tooth contacts are more prominent than the anterior. Goal 4 is the eccentric one: anterior teeth disclude the posterior.
why: Goal 5: posterior contacts more prominent with the head forward and down.
That reverses goal 5.
Canine guidance applies to eccentric movement (goal 4), not the feeding posture.
Goal 5 asks for heavier posterior contacts, not equal ones.

stem: Orthopedic instability is defined as:
choices: With the teeth in MIP, one or both condyles not stable with the disc and fossa
With the joints seated, the teeth unable to reach any contact at all on closure
A tooth with progressive mobility under occlusal load
A splint that doesn't cover all the teeth in the arch
ex: Orthopedic instability: when the teeth are brought into MIP, one (or both) condyles are not in a stable relationship with the disc and fossa. A stable occlusion with unstable joints may lead to an intracapsular disorder.
why: The definition: teeth in MIP, one or both condyles unstable with the disc and fossa.
With the joints seated the teeth do reach a first contact; that is occlusal instability.
Progressive mobility is traumatic mobility, from the trauma section.
Partial coverage is a splint design question.

likely.t: Orthopedic instability: ~10% coincident, > 3 mm raises risk, loading (bruxism) adds to it

stem: An unstable relationship of the condyle to the fossa may lead to which kind of TMD?
choices: An intracapsular disorder
Protective co-contraction
Myofascial pain with trigger points
A growth disorder
ex: An unstable condyle-fossa relationship may lead to an intracapsular disorder, inside the joint capsule. Protective co-contraction is the muscle response to an acute occlusal change, such as a high crown.
why: An unstable condyle-fossa relationship may lead to an intracapsular disorder.
Protective co-contraction is a muscle response to an acute contact change.
Myofascial pain is a specific muscle TMD with trigger points.
Growth disorders are their own Bell's category.

stem: Which condylar misposition (from seated, with the teeth in MIP) presents an increased risk?
choices: More than 3 mm
1-2 mm
Under 1 mm
Any misposition at all
ex: A misposition of 1-2 mm is not likely to create a problem; more than 3 mm presents increased risk (some say 4 mm). Increased risk doesn't mean the patient will have a problem.
why: Over 3 mm presents increased risk (some say 4).
1-2 mm is not likely to create a problem.
Under 1 mm is well within the tolerated range.
Small mispositions of 1-2 mm are not likely to matter.

likely.t: Orthopedic instability: ~10% coincident, > 3 mm raises risk, loading (bruxism) adds to it

stem: Besides the degree of discrepancy, what is the other risk factor for orthopedic instability causing a problem?
choices: The amount of loading, so patients who brux have greater risk
The patient's Angle class
The number of restorations in the mouth
Whether the patient has canine guidance or group function
ex: The two risk factors: the degree of discrepancy and the amount of loading. Bruxers load their joints heavily, so they have greater risk. Orthopedic instability needs loading forces to destabilize.
why: Loading is the second risk factor; bruxers have greater risk.
Angle class isn't one of the two risk factors.
The number of restorations isn't listed as a risk factor.
Guidance type isn't one of the two risk factors.

likely.t: Orthopedic instability: ~10% coincident, > 3 mm raises risk, loading (bruxism) adds to it

stem: What do the slides say about open bite and Angle Class II as causes of TMD?
choices: Reports show more TMDs with them, but the literature doesn't support it well
They are proven causes, so they should be corrected to prevent TMD
They are protective against intracapsular disorders
They matter only in children with primary teeth
ex: Increased incidence of TMDs with open bite or Angle Class II has been reported, "but not well supported by literature." Malocclusion may only become important when considering joint position.
why: Increased incidence has been reported but isn't well supported by the literature.
They aren't proven causes, and correcting them to prevent TMD isn't supported.
Nothing says they protect the joint.
The slide is about adults' malocclusion and joint position, not primary teeth.

stem: In Dr. Givan's resident-era patient, what had led to her pain?
choices: Years of restorations built to MIP, away from orthopedic stability
A single high crown, placed the week before she first came to the clinic
Nocturnal bruxism started by a mediotrusive contact
A partial-coverage splint that let her molars supererupt
ex: Restored over the years without anyone checking whether the condyles were seated, she was kept in dental stability while moving farther out of orthopedic stability, until she couldn't tolerate it. A splint let the condyles seat (an open bite appeared), then provisionals for over a year and final restorations.
why: Years of restorations to MIP moved her farther from orthopedic stability.
Her story was gradual, over many dentists and years, not one crown.
Bruxism isn't started by contacts; her problem was orthopedic instability.
She was treated with a full-coverage splint; partial coverage wasn't the story.

stem: Where does the protective reflex opening after unexpectedly biting something hard occur?
choices: In the trigeminal motor nucleus, subconsciously
In the primary motor cortex, consciously
In the lateral pterygoid muscle itself
In the periodontal ligament, without the CNS
ex: Reflex responses are rapid, involuntary movements; this one is subconscious and occurs in the trigeminal motor nucleus. It is complex: opening means shutting down many muscles and activating many others.
why: Subconscious, in the trigeminal motor nucleus.
It is involuntary, not a conscious cortical act.
The muscle responds, but the reflex is organized in the brainstem.
The PDL senses the contact; the reflex needs the CNS.

stem: According to EMG studies, what happens when mediotrusive contacts are eliminated?
choices: The masseter and temporalis are not activated by a mediotrusive movement
The lateral pterygoid stops working in protrusion
The suprahyoid muscles can no longer open the jaw
Elevator muscle activity rises, because the posterior teeth lose their support
ex: With mediotrusive contacts eliminated, the masseter and temporalis aren't activated in that movement. That supports canine guidance, which keeps the posterior teeth apart in excursions.
why: Without mediotrusive contacts, the masseter and temporalis aren't activated.
The lateral pterygoid's role in protrusion isn't what these studies showed.
Suprahyoid opening isn't affected by removing mediotrusive contacts.
Activity falls, not rises, without those posterior contacts.

likely.t: Muscles vs joints: movement problems in the muscles, loading problems in the joints

stem: The Manns study divided a full-coverage maxillary splint into anterior, premolar and molar blocks. Which theory did later studies confirm?
choices: A lack of posterior contact fails to activate muscle contraction
Anterior tooth contact inhibits muscle contraction
Premolar contact alone gives full elevator activity
Tooth contact has no effect on elevator activity
ex: Two theories came from it: anterior contact inhibits contraction, or a lack of posterior contact fails to activate it. The second was confirmed: adding the molar contacts brought the activity to full.
why: Lack of posterior contact fails to activate contraction: confirmed by later studies.
Anterior inhibition was the other theory; it wasn't the one confirmed.
Adding the molar contacts was what brought activity to full.
Contact clearly changed elevator activity in the study.

likely.t: Muscles vs joints: movement problems in the muscles, loading problems in the joints

stem: Which describes ortho-function rather than parafunction?
choices: Protective reflexes are present and posterior contact stimulates the elevators
Muscle hyperactivity raises the level of tonus, giving muscle fatigue and strain
Clenching and grinding during sleep
Muscles fire without feedback from tooth contacts
ex: Ortho-function (normal function): elevation, depression, laterotrusion; protective reflexes present; tooth contacts affect specific muscle groups. Parafunction (clenching, bruxism, habits) raises tonus and isn't driven by tooth contacts.
why: Ortho-function has protective reflexes, and posterior contact stimulates the elevators.
Hyperactivity raising tonus is parafunction.
Clenching and grinding in sleep are parafunction.
Firing without tooth-contact feedback is what happens in parafunction.

stem: A patient guards her jaw movement after a crown is left high. This TMD type is:
choices: Protective muscle co-contraction
An intracapsular disorder
Myofascial pain with trigger points
Chronic mandibular hypomobility
ex: Protective muscle co-contraction: restricted or guarded movement from co-contraction of the muscles to avoid pain from the initial event (the high contact). The altered movement then leads to muscle soreness.
why: Protective co-contraction: guarded movement to avoid pain from the high contact.
An intracapsular disorder is inside the joint, from orthopedic instability.
Myofascial pain is a specific muscle TMD with trigger points.
Hypomobility (ankylosis, contracture) is a chronic Bell's category.

likely.t: Introducing an interference (the high crown) causes protective co-contraction

stem: How did Dr. Givan describe protective co-contraction itself?
choices: A normal, healthy avoidance response with nothing pathologic about it
A centrally mediated disorder like bruxism
A joint disorder that results from long-standing orthopedic instability
A sign that the patient will develop myofascial pain
ex: "There's nothing pathologic about it": it is an avoidance behavior. The trouble is that moving in ways we normally don't leads to localized muscle soreness (myalgia).
why: "Nothing pathologic about it": a normal avoidance response.
Bruxism is centrally mediated; co-contraction is a response to a contact.
It is a muscle response, not a joint disorder.
It can cause soreness, but he didn't say it leads to myofascial pain.

likely.t: Introducing an interference (the high crown) causes protective co-contraction

stem: Posterior mediotrusive and laterotrusive contacts are found:
choices: Equally in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients
Mostly in symptomatic patients
Only in patients with a CO-MIP slide over 2 mm
Mostly in patients with intracapsular disorders
ex: Both kinds are equally noted in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients, "a very important point." It's the CO-MIP slide over 2 mm and interferences to maximum closure that are more common in symptomatic patients.
why: Equally noted in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients.
They aren't concentrated in symptomatic patients; that's the key point.
They are found regardless of the size of any slide.
They are found equally in patients with and without symptoms.

likely.t: Existing interferences: equal in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients; prophylactic equilibration not supported

stem: How does the incidence of a CO-MIP slide compare between symptomatic and asymptomatic patients?
choices: Under 2 mm is equal; over 2 mm is more common in symptomatic patients
Any slide at all is more common in symptomatic patients
Over 2 mm is equal; under 2 mm is more common in symptomatic patients
A slide is never found in asymptomatic patients
ex: Under 2 mm: equal incidence. Over 2 mm: increased incidence in symptomatic patients. Incidence still doesn't prove causality.
why: Under 2 mm equal; over 2 mm more common in symptomatic patients.
Slides under 2 mm are equally common in both groups.
This reverses the 2 mm threshold.
Slides are common in healthy patients too.

likely.t: Existing interferences: equal in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients; prophylactic equilibration not supported

stem: A patient with no symptoms has a mediotrusive contact on #3 that has been there for years. What does current practice support?
choices: Leave it: equilibrating to prevent TMD is not supported
Equilibrate it now, before it causes a TMD
Replace #3 with a crown that removes the contact
Place a partial-coverage splint to disclude it
ex: Eliminating existing interferences doesn't seem to alter TMD symptoms, and equilibrating for prevention is not supported. The rule is to avoid introducing a new mediotrusive contact in a restoration.
why: Leave it: equilibrating to prevent TMD isn't supported.
Prophylactic equilibration isn't supported, and removing old interferences doesn't change symptoms.
A crown to remove a harmless contact is irreversible treatment without indication.
A partial splint risks supereruption and isn't indicated without symptoms.

likely.t: Existing interferences: equal in symptomatic and asymptomatic patients; prophylactic equilibration not supported

stem: Why should you avoid building a mediotrusive contact into a new crown, even though existing ones may be left alone?
choices: Introducing one is a sudden change that can cause pain or dysfunction
A new mediotrusive contact is what starts nocturnal bruxism in most patients
Existing contacts are always removed later anyway
A mediotrusive contact makes the crown debond
ex: Introducing an interference can lead to pain or dysfunction: "too sudden of a change for a patient." Slow changes over a lifetime are usually tolerated. Bruxism is centrally mediated, not started by contacts.
why: Introducing an interference is a sudden change that can lead to pain or dysfunction.
Bruxism is centrally mediated; contacts don't start it.
Existing contacts are usually left alone, not removed.
Debonding isn't the reason he gave.

likely.t: Introducing an interference (the high crown) causes protective co-contraction

stem: What "better question" did the slides pose about occlusion and functional disturbances?
choices: Does CNS posturing of the mandible forward of MIP increase risk as a co-factor?
Does every Angle Class II malocclusion lead to an intracapsular disorder within ten years?
Do partial splints prevent intracapsular disorders?
Does group function cause more TMD than canine guidance?
ex: The precise effect of occlusal stability isn't established ("sometimes related and sometimes not!"). The better question: does CNS posturing of the mandible anteriorly or anterolaterally to MIP increase risk as a co-factor for muscle and joint disorders?
why: The better question: does CNS posturing forward of MIP increase risk as a co-factor?
Nothing on the slides predicts TMD from any malocclusion in a time frame.
Partial splints aren't the subject of the better question.
Guidance type isn't the better question on the slide.

stem: By the general statements on the slides, problems bringing the teeth together (mandibular movement) are often manifested in:
choices: The muscles
The joints
The periodontal ligament
The pulp
ex: Problems bringing the teeth into the intercuspal position are answered by the muscles; once the teeth are in occlusion, problems with applying force are answered in the joints. Both have exceptions.
why: Problems bringing the teeth together are answered by the muscles.
Joints answer problems with force once the teeth are in occlusion.
The PDL isn't one of the two general statements.
The pulp isn't one of the two general statements.

likely.t: Muscles vs joints: movement problems in the muscles, loading problems in the joints

stem: Occlusal therapy is:
choices: A general term for any treatment that alters a patient's occlusal condition
Only irreversible treatments, such as equilibration, crowns and orthodontics
Only splint therapy for TMD patients
Treatment of the TM joint with surgery
ex: Occlusal therapy is any treatment that alters the occlusal condition, reversible (non-invasive, temporary) or irreversible (invasive, permanent).
why: Any treatment that alters the occlusal condition, reversible or irreversible.
Occlusal therapy includes reversible treatments too.
Splints are only one occlusal therapy.
Joint surgery is only one of the irreversible options.

stem: Which reversible treatment for a functional disturbance changes the occlusal stability?
choices: A flat plane stabilization splint
Physical therapy, self-directed or professionally assisted
Pharmacotherapy
Counseling
ex: Of the reversible treatments (education, physical therapy, pharmacotherapy, counseling, the flat plane stabilization splint), only the splint changes the occlusal stability.
why: The flat plane stabilization splint is the reversible treatment that changes occlusal stability.
Physical therapy is reversible but doesn't change the occlusion.
Medication doesn't change the occlusion.
Counseling doesn't change the occlusion.

stem: Which is NOT one of the uses of splint therapy listed on the slides?
choices: Curing nocturnal bruxism
Muscle pain
Protecting teeth and restorations
Part of trial therapy
ex: Splint therapy: muscle pain, protect teeth and restorations, alleviate joint pain, part of trial therapy. It protects the teeth from bruxism but doesn't cure it (bruxism is centrally mediated).
why: A splint doesn't cure bruxism; it protects the teeth while bruxism continues.
Muscle pain is a listed use.
Protecting teeth and restorations is a listed use.
Trial therapy is a listed use.

stem: How does a stabilizing splint differ from a repositioning splint?
choices: Stabilizing seats the joints; repositioning holds a chosen non-centric position
Stabilizing covers only some of the teeth; repositioning always covers all of them
Stabilizing is mandibular; repositioning is maxillary
Stabilizing is worn by day; repositioning only at night
ex: A stabilizing splint provides dental stability with the joints seated in an orthopedically stable relationship. A repositioning splint is used in disc displacements, sleep apnea and similar cases where a specific non-centric mandibular position is desired.
why: Stabilizing seats the joints; repositioning holds a chosen non-centric position.
Coverage (full or partial) is a separate choice from stabilizing or repositioning.
Either kind can be maxillary or mandibular.
Day or night wear depends on the arch, not on stabilizing vs repositioning.

likely.t: Splints: stabilizing vs repositioning, maxillary vs mandibular, full coverage

stem: A maxillary stabilization splint has:
choices: A posterior flat plane with an anterior ramp
Cusp indentations for each opposing tooth
Coverage of the anterior teeth only
A ramp behind the lower incisors
ex: Maxillary splint: a posterior flat plane (no indentations or elevations, so no eccentric contacts) with an anterior ramp that discludes the posterior teeth. Indentations would create eccentric contacts.
why: A posterior flat plane with an anterior ramp.
Indentations would create eccentric contacts; the posterior plane is flat.
Anterior-only coverage is a partial splint, not the maxillary stabilization splint.
The ramp behind the lower incisors describes the mandibular splint.

likely.t: Splints: stabilizing vs repositioning, maxillary vs mandibular, full coverage

stem: Which relationship is a maxillary splint ideally suited for?
choices: Class II division 1, with excessive horizontal overlap
Class III, edge to edge
Class II division 2, with deep vertical overlap
Class I with canine guidance
ex: Maxillary splints can be used in Class I, II and even III, and are ideally suited for Class II division 1 (excessive horizontal overlap): it is easier to get anterior contacts on the ramp.
why: Ideally suited for Class II division 1: excessive horizontal overlap.
It can be used in Class III, but Class II division 1 is the ideal fit.
Division 2 has a deep bite, not the excessive overjet the slide names.
It works in Class I, but that isn't the ideal named.

stem: What is the main risk of a partial-coverage splint worn a lot?
choices: Covered teeth may intrude and uncovered teeth may extrude
The condyles are held too far forward of centric relation all night
It can't disclude the posterior teeth
It needs a facebow to make
ex: Partial coverage may cause covered teeth to intrude and non-covered teeth to extrude (supereruption), and it may not be as effective; full coverage is recommended in almost all situations.
why: Covered teeth may intrude and uncovered teeth extrude.
Joint position depends on the splint's design, not on partial coverage.
Anterior-only splints do disclude the posterior teeth.
A facebow has nothing to do with the coverage risk.

likely.t: Splints: stabilizing vs repositioning, maxillary vs mandibular, full coverage

stem: For a patient with a functional disturbance, irreversible occlusal treatment is indicated only when:
choices: Evidence suggests the mandibular instability is the primary cause
The patient has any malocclusion other than a Class I molar relationship
A splint has relieved the symptoms for one week
The patient asks for a permanent solution
ex: Irreversible occlusal treatment is only indicated when sufficient evidence suggests the primary etiologic factor is the mandibular instability (the occlusal condition). You can't ungrind a tooth.
why: Only when evidence suggests the primary cause is the mandibular instability.
Most malocclusions are tolerated; class alone isn't an indication.
A week of splint relief doesn't prove occlusion is the primary cause.
The decision rests on evidence about the cause, not on the request alone.

likely.t: Conservative first: reversible and irreversible treatments have similar success (50-90%)

stem: When irreversible occlusal therapy is chosen, the type is determined by:
choices: The severity of the malocclusion, doing the least that meets the goal
The cost of the materials and of the laboratory fees for the restorations
The patient's age only
Whether the patient bruxes
ex: Perform the least amount of dental alteration that fulfills the treatment goal, and let the severity of the malocclusion decide the type: grinding, then fixed prosthetics and minor orthodontics, then major orthodontics and surgery.
why: The severity of the malocclusion decides, doing the least that meets the goal.
Material cost isn't how the type is chosen.
Age alone doesn't decide the type of therapy.
Bruxism is managed with a splint; it doesn't set the type of occlusal therapy.

stem: Selective grinding (equilibration) should:
choices: Reshape enamel only, avoiding exposed dentin and iatrogenic sensitivity
Reduce cusps well into dentin when needed, to flatten the whole occlusion
Be done prophylactically to prevent TMD
Remove existing mediotrusive contacts in every patient
ex: Selective grinding is minor reshaping of enamel surfaces; avoid exposing dentin and creating iatrogenic sensitivity. If it would reach dentin, a restorative approach is used instead.
why: Enamel only; avoid exposing dentin and iatrogenic sensitivity.
Going into dentin is where a restorative approach replaces grinding.
Prophylactic equilibration isn't supported.
Existing mediotrusive contacts are usually left alone.

stem: By the rule of thirds, a discrepancy in the middle third of the tooth is usually treated with:
choices: Minor orthodontics and fixed prosthetics
Selective grinding
Major orthodontics and orthognathic surgery
A partial-coverage splint
ex: First third: selective grinding. Middle third: minor orthodontics and fixed prosthetics (where most deviations fall). Beyond: major orthodontics, orthognathic surgery and prosthetics. Mark the contacts with the condyles in the desired position.
why: Middle third: minor orthodontics and fixed prosthetics.
Selective grinding is for the first third.
Major orthodontics and surgery are for discrepancies beyond the middle third.
A partial splint isn't on the rule of thirds.

stem: How do the long-term success rates of reversible and irreversible treatments for functional disturbances compare?
choices: They are similar, 50-90%
Irreversible about 90%, reversible about 50%
Reversible about 90%, irreversible about 10%
Neither has been measured
ex: Long-term success is similar for both, 50-90%. That is why conservative treatment is the first attempt.
why: Both report similar long-term success, 50-90%.
Irreversible treatment isn't more successful; the rates are similar.
Reversible treatment isn't far better; the rates are similar.
Both have been measured: 50-90% each.

likely.t: Conservative first: reversible and irreversible treatments have similar success (50-90%)

stem: Because conservative and non-conservative treatments report similar success, the treatment philosophy is:
choices: Try conservative treatment first; go further only if it fails
Start with irreversible treatment to save time
Choose by which is cheapest for the lab
Combine every reversible and irreversible option at once
ex: Conservative treatment is the first attempt; non-conservative treatment is attempted if conservative approaches fail. Symptoms, the dentition, systemic health, esthetics and finances also affect the choice.
why: Conservative first; non-conservative only if it fails.
Similar success means the conservative option comes first.
Lab cost isn't the basis of the philosophy.
Treatment is stepwise, not everything at once.

likely.t: Conservative first: reversible and irreversible treatments have similar success (50-90%)

stem: Which is NOT one of the reasons given for weak evidence on treating functional disturbances?
choices: Splints are too expensive to study
A lack of double-blind clinical trials
Disagreement on the TMD diagnostic categories
Some causal factors, such as emotional stress, are hard to control
ex: The three reasons: a lack of scientific evidence (the standard is the double-blind trial), a lack of agreement on diagnostic categories, and causal factors that are difficult to control or eliminate. Cost isn't one; splints are inexpensive.
why: Cost isn't a listed reason; splints are inexpensive.
A lack of double-blind clinical trials is reason 1.
Disagreement on diagnostic categories is reason 2.
Hard-to-control causes such as stress is reason 3.

stem: Of the four population groups, which did Dr. Givan call the "red light," where guidance is hardest?
choices: TMD symptomatic and needing a lot of dental treatment
TMD asymptomatic, needing no dental treatment
TMD asymptomatic, needing dental treatment
TMD symptomatic, needing no dental treatment
ex: Most patients are TMD asymptomatic, with or without dental needs (the hygiene patient, and the bulk of practice). The hardest are symptomatic patients who also need a lot of dental treatment.
why: Symptomatic and needing a lot of dental treatment: the hardest group.
This is the basic hygiene patient, the easiest group.
Asymptomatic patients needing treatment are the bulk of practice.
Symptomatic patients without dental needs aren't the red light he described.

stem: "A force is only traumatic when it produces trauma." Which is NOT one of the five factors that characterize a force?
choices: Velocity
Magnitude
Direction
Distribution
ex: The five: magnitude, frequency, duration, direction and distribution (how many teeth resist it, as in posterior bite collapse).
why: Velocity isn't one of the five factors.
Magnitude is factor 1.
Direction is factor 4.
Distribution (how many teeth resist it) is factor 5.

stem: Which direction of force did Dr. Givan say the teeth handle poorly?
choices: Horizontal
Vertical, down the long axis
Apical
Axial on the centric cusps
ex: "We're very good about vertical forces, not so good about horizontally directed forces." That is why bruxism, a horizontal force, is so damaging.
why: Horizontal forces are handled poorly.
Vertical forces down the long axis are handled well.
Apical (axial) force is what the PDL is built for.
Axial forces on centric cusps are the goal of ideal occlusion.

stem: Bruxism is an example of which type of trauma?
choices: Microtrauma: small repetitive forces over time
Macrotrauma: a sudden force with structural change
Orthopedic trauma
Iatrogenic trauma from a high crown
ex: Microtrauma is small repetitive forces over a period of time (bruxism); macrotrauma is a sudden force resulting in structural alterations, such as an auto accident.
why: Bruxism is microtrauma: small repetitive forces over time.
Macrotrauma is a sudden force, such as an auto accident.
Orthopedic trauma is a broken jaw.
A high crown is an acute event, not the trauma type named for bruxism.

stem: Where does occlusal trauma usually show up?
choices: The attachment apparatus (PDL and adjacent structures)
The gingiva and alveolar mucosa around the traumatized teeth
The enamel rods only
The marginal gingiva first
ex: The attachment apparatus is the usual site; the gingiva and mucosa are rarely affected. Whether bone loss may be reversible depends on the connective tissue attachment, which is affected by inflammation, not occlusion.
why: The attachment apparatus is the usual site.
The gingiva and mucosa are rarely affected.
Enamel can wear, but the usual site of occlusal trauma is the attachment.
The gingiva is rarely the site of occlusal trauma.

stem: Which is listed as a histologic change, rather than a clinical finding, of occlusal trauma?
choices: Cemental changes
Tooth migration
Tenderness to pressure
Widening of the PDL
ex: Histologic: injury to the PDL, bone resorption, cemental changes, vascular injury, pulpal hyperemia (?). Clinical: mobility, migration, attrition, widening of the PDL, tenderness, pulpal pain, TMJ flattening (controversial).
why: Cemental changes are histologic.
Tooth migration is a clinical finding.
Tenderness to pressure is a clinical finding.
Widening of the PDL is a clinical (radiographic) finding.

stem: The actual initial vertical movement of a healthy tooth under load is about:
choices: 28 µm
2-3 µm
150 µm
1 mm
ex: About 28 µm, the same for anterior and posterior teeth, though no vertical mobility is clinically observable. An implant moves 2-3 µm under 10 lb; 150 µm is the horizontal physiologic limit.
why: About 28 µm, the same front and back.
2-3 µm is an implant under 10 lb.
150 µm is the horizontal physiologic limit.
1 mm is Miller class 2 horizontal movement.

likely.t: Tooth mobility: 28 µm, 150 µm limit, adapted vs traumatic, Miller's index

stem: After vertical loading, how long does a tooth take for full recovery?
choices: Almost 4 hours
About 7 seconds
About 1 minute
About 2 days
ex: The immediate rebound is about 7 µm, but full recovery takes almost 4 hours.
why: Full recovery takes almost 4 hours.
The immediate rebound is about 7 µm, not 7 seconds.
Full recovery is much slower than a minute.
It recovers within hours, not days.

stem: An implant's vertical movement under a 10-lb force is about 2-3 µm. Why does it move at all?
choices: Viscoelastic strain of the bony interface
A thin periodontal ligament around the fixture
Flexing of the abutment screw
Rebound of the cortical plate after 4 hours
ex: The movement is due to the viscoelastic strain of the bony interface; an implant has no PDL.
why: Viscoelastic strain of the bony interface.
An implant has no periodontal ligament.
Screw flexing isn't the reason given.
The 4-hour recovery is a natural tooth's.

stem: What is considered the limit of physiologic horizontal tooth mobility?
choices: 150 µm
28 µm
56 µm
1 mm
ex: A 500 g force moves a tooth horizontally 56 to 108 µm; 150 µm is the limit of physiologic horizontal mobility. Beyond that it is abnormal or pathologic.
why: 150 µm is the physiologic limit.
28 µm is the vertical movement of a tooth.
56 µm is the low end of the normal range under 500 g.
1 mm is Miller class 2.

likely.t: Tooth mobility: 28 µm, 150 µm limit, adapted vs traumatic, Miller's index

stem: Which tooth is expected to have more horizontal mobility?
choices: A single-rooted tooth
A multi-rooted tooth
An osseointegrated implant
Every tooth has the same
ex: Single-rooted teeth have more mobility than multi-rooted. Horizontal mobility also depends on PDL width, root attachment area, alveolar elasticity and the tooth's function.
why: Single-rooted teeth are more mobile.
Multi-rooted teeth have more attachment, so they move less.
Implants move least of all.
Root number and area change mobility.

stem: Which is an indication for splinting teeth?
choices: Traumatic mobility that is increasing
Adapted mobility that has been stable for years
Physiologic mobility under 150 µm
Mobility that is greatest in the morning
ex: Traumatic mobility (progressive, when the tissues' tolerance is exceeded) is the indication for splinting: more surface area to resist the force. Adapted mobility doesn't need it.
why: Increasing (traumatic) mobility is the indication for splinting.
Stable adapted mobility is monitored, not splinted.
Mobility under 150 µm is physiologic.
Morning mobility is normal daily variation.

stem: On Miller's Mobility Index (1938), a score of 2 means:
choices: Any horizontal movement up to 1 mm
Barely distinguishable tooth movement
More than 1 mm, or depressed or rotated
No detectable movement
ex: 0 = no detectable movement; 1 = barely distinguishable; 2 = any horizontal movement up to 1 mm; 3 = more than 1 mm or depressed or rotated. The tooth is held between two instruments and moved back and forth. (Dr. Abou-Arraj's L10 slide grades it differently: 1 = up to 1 mm, 2 = more than 1 mm, 3 = horizontal and vertical.)
why: 2 = any horizontal movement up to 1 mm.
1 = barely distinguishable movement.
3 = more than 1 mm, or depressed or rotated.
0 = no detectable movement.

likely.t: Tooth mobility: 28 µm, 150 µm limit, adapted vs traumatic, Miller's index

stem: Why do patients with tooth wear usually seek treatment?
choices: For esthetic concerns; pain is usually not a symptom
Because of severe pain from exposed dentin
Because the teeth become mobile
Because their TMJ starts clicking
ex: Pain is usually not a symptom of wear (it is too slow); patients usually seek treatment for esthetics, often too late for an easy fix.
why: Esthetics; pain is usually not a symptom.
Wear is too slow to cause severe pain as a rule.
Mobility is a different outcome of force.
Clicking is a joint sign, not why wear patients come in.

stem: Which teeth are often the first to wear (early signs)?
choices: Canines and incisors involved in anterior guidance
Second molars on the non-working side
Maxillary premolars at the CEJ
Mandibular incisors from bulimia
ex: Canines and incisors involved in anterior guidance are often first to wear. Best to treat before wear extends to multiple teeth.
why: The canines and incisors in anterior guidance wear first.
Non-working molars aren't the early sign named.
Maxillary premolars at the CEJ are where NCCLs are most common.
Bulimia spares the mandibular incisors.

stem: For a severely worn tooth, crown lengthening is often not indicated if:
choices: 3 mm of tooth structure is coronal to the papilla
The tooth has Miller class 1 mobility
The wear is from erosion rather than attrition
The patient is over 60
ex: General rule: if 3 mm of tooth structure is coronal to the papilla, crown lengthening is often not indicated. Severe wear may otherwise need crown lengthening, endodontics or orthodontic extrusion first.
why: 3 mm coronal to the papilla: crown lengthening often not indicated.
Mobility doesn't decide crown lengthening in this rule.
The rule is about tooth height, not the type of wear.
Age isn't part of the rule.

stem: A composite restoration standing above the surrounding worn tooth (a "proud restoration") points to:
choices: Erosion
Attrition
Abfraction
Physiologic wear
ex: Erosion (chemically assisted wear) dissolves tooth but not the restoration, leaving it proud; you also see dull facets and cupping, as dentin wears faster than enamel. Attrition wears both together.
why: Erosion dissolves tooth but not the restoration, leaving it proud.
Attrition wears tooth and restoration together.
Abfraction is a cervical notch.
Physiologic wear is age-appropriate wear, not the sign of acid.

likely.t: Mechanisms of wear and the erosion patterns (GERD, bulimia)

stem: Cupping of a wear facet means:
choices: Dentin is wearing faster than enamel, typical of erosion
Enamel and dentin are at the same height, typical of attrition
A V-shaped notch at the CEJ
A rounded saucer from toothbrushing
ex: Cupping (dentin wear > enamel wear) is an erosion sign. In attrition enamel and dentin in the facet are at the same height.
why: Dentin wearing faster than enamel: an erosion sign.
Same height enamel and dentin is attrition.
A V-shaped notch at the CEJ is a cervical lesion.
A rounded saucer is a cervical lesion form.

stem: When wear mechanisms act together, what does the presence of acid do?
choices: It accelerates mechanical wear
It slows attrition by softening the enamel
It stops abrasion from toothbrushing
It has no effect on other mechanisms
ex: Mechanisms frequently act simultaneously, and the presence of acid accelerates mechanical wear.
why: Acid accelerates mechanical wear.
Acid speeds attrition, it doesn't slow it.
Acid speeds abrasion too.
Mechanisms interact; acid makes the others worse.

stem: The classic erosion pattern of GERD is on:
choices: The lingual of all maxillary teeth to the second molars and the occlusals of the mandibular molars
The facial surfaces of the maxillary and mandibular premolars and canines at the CEJ, on both sides
The incisal edges of the mandibular incisors only
The buccal surfaces of the mandibular molars only
ex: GERD: lingual of all maxillary teeth to the 2nd molars and the occlusal surfaces of the mandibular molars, often asymmetrical, worse on the side the patient sleeps on.
why: Lingual of all maxillary teeth to the 2nd molars and the mandibular molar occlusals.
Facial of maxillary premolars at the CEJ is the NCCL site.
Mandibular incisors aren't the GERD site.
The GERD pattern is lingual and occlusal, not mandibular buccal.

likely.t: Mechanisms of wear and the erosion patterns (GERD, bulimia)

stem: Why is GERD erosion often asymmetrical?
choices: The side they prefer to sleep on gets more of the refluxed acid
The working side is where the patient chews most of their acidic food
The tongue protects one side only
The parotid duct opens on one side only
ex: In sleep, refluxed acid rolls off the tongue onto the lingual surfaces, and the side the patient sleeps on gets more of it (on the back, both sides).
why: The preferred sleeping side gets more acid.
Chewing side isn't the reason; it happens in sleep.
The tongue carries the acid onto the lingual surfaces.
Salivary ducts aren't the reason given.

stem: A "screwdriver" appearance of the front teeth comes from:
choices: Biting citrus fruit and sucking the juice through the teeth
Pooling soda in the back of the mouth
Holding chlorinated water while swimming
Horizontal toothbrushing
ex: Citrus fruit abuse type 1: bite fruit and suck juice through the teeth, eroding the front teeth to a screwdriver shape. Type 2 (chewing on the molars) looks like beverage pooling.
why: Citrus type 1: biting fruit and sucking the juice through the teeth.
Pooling soda gives severe wear with high caries.
Chlorine erosion is from swimming, not a screwdriver shape.
Horizontal brushing is abrasion at the cervical area.

stem: Generalized erosion on all teeth with a satin appearance and islands of exposed dentin fits which habit?
choices: Swishing soda and holding it in the vestibule to fizz
Pooling soda in the back of the mouth to cool
Biting lemons on the molars
Sleeping on one side with reflux
ex: Carbonated beverage pattern 1 (swish, hold in the vestibule, swallow): generalized satin erosion with dentin islands. Pattern 2 (pooling in the back) is very severe with high caries.
why: Swishing and holding soda in the vestibule: generalized satin erosion with dentin islands.
Pooling in the back is very severe with high caries.
Chewing citrus on the molars gives more posterior wear.
Reflux erodes the maxillary linguals and mandibular molar occlusals.

stem: Which is listed as a less common cause of erosion?
choices: Swimming in chlorinated water
Toothbrushing with whitening paste
Clenching during the day
Nail biting
ex: Less common: drug abuse (aspirin, meth), swimming (chlorine erosion) and occupational exposure (battery and galvanizing workers). Toothbrushing is abrasion; clenching and nail biting are loads.
why: Swimming (chlorine erosion) is a less common cause.
Toothbrushing causes abrasion, not erosion.
Clenching is a load, not an acid.
Nail biting is a load linked to cervical lesions, not erosion.

stem: Noncarious cervical lesions are most common on:
choices: The facial surfaces of maxillary premolars
The lingual surfaces of mandibular molars
The incisal edges of maxillary incisors
The occlusal surfaces of mandibular molars
ex: NCCLs are found throughout the mouth, most often on the facial of maxillary premolars; lingual lesions occur but are rarely severe.
why: Facial of maxillary premolars is most common.
Lingual lesions are rarely severe.
Incisal edges aren't cervical.
Occlusal surfaces aren't cervical.

likely.t: Abfraction and noncarious cervical lesions: unproven clinically, multifactorial

stem: When are noncarious cervical lesions usually restored with resin composite?
choices: When needed: progression, sensitivity, esthetics or food collection
As soon as any lesion is found, before it can progress or become sensitive
Only after orthodontic treatment
Never; they are always left alone
ex: Treatment is typically delayed until it becomes necessary: lesion progression, impact on quality of life (sensitivity), poor esthetics or food collection. Caries is often absent; silver diamine fluoride can arrest it.
why: Restore when needed: progression, sensitivity, esthetics or food collection.
Treatment is typically delayed until it becomes necessary.
Orthodontics isn't the trigger for restoring.
They are restored when they become a problem.

stem: What is the status of abfraction as a cause of cervical lesions?
choices: Supported in vitro, but clinically neither validated nor rejected
Proven as the primary mechanism in clinical trials
Rejected because lesions only occur on the lingual
Proven to be caused by horizontal toothbrushing alone
ex: Abfraction (tensile fatigue flexing the cervical area under load, with "stress corrosion") is supported by in vitro studies, but clinical documentation has not validated or rejected it, so it isn't a primary mechanism of wear.
why: Supported in vitro; clinically neither validated nor rejected.
It hasn't been proven clinically.
Lesions are most common on the facial.
Brushing is one factor; the etiology is multifactorial.

likely.t: Abfraction and noncarious cervical lesions: unproven clinically, multifactorial

stem: Which loads are described as more damaging to mineralized tissue in relation to NCCLs?
choices: The sustained loads of clenching and nail biting
The dynamic, shifting loads of bruxism
The loads of normal chewing
The loads of swallowing
ex: Clenching, nail biting and a diagnosis of TMD are significantly associated with NCCLs, and the sustained loads of clenching and nail biting are more damaging than the dynamic (shifting) loads of bruxism.
why: The sustained loads of clenching and nail biting are more damaging.
The slide says bruxism's dynamic loads are less damaging.
Normal chewing isn't named as the damaging load.
Swallowing loads aren't named.

likely.t: Abfraction and noncarious cervical lesions: unproven clinically, multifactorial

stem: How does emotional stress raise muscle tonicity, per the slides?
choices: Gamma efferents stimulate intrafusal fibers of the muscle spindles, sensitizing the muscle
Periodontal ligament receptors fire on every tooth contact and activate the elevator muscles
The lateral pterygoid pulls the disc forward
Cortisol relaxes the extrafusal fibers
ex: The emotional centers act through the hypothalamus, reticular system and limbic system; gamma efferents stimulate intrafusal fibers of the muscle spindles to contract, "sensitizing" the muscle and raising tonicity, often in the head and neck.
why: Gamma efferents to the intrafusal fibers sensitize the muscle.
That is the posterior-contact feedback of normal function, not stress.
Disc movement isn't how stress raises tonus.
The slides describe sensitizing, not relaxing.

stem: A patient has limited opening with a painful pulpitis on #31. After the tooth is extracted, the opening returns to normal. This illustrates:
choices: Deep pain input as an etiology
Orthopedic instability
Protective reflex opening
Microtrauma from bruxism
ex: Deep pain input is often overlooked: limited opening with odontogenic pain that returns to normal once the pulpal problem is resolved. Remote pain, such as cervical pain, can also affect the masticatory system.
why: Deep pain input: the opening returns once the odontogenic pain is gone.
Orthopedic instability doesn't resolve with an extraction.
Reflex opening is the brief response to a hard bite.
Microtrauma is repetitive force, such as bruxism.

stem: Which findings are common in patients who clench?
choices: A history of fractured, chipped or splayed teeth, and tori or exostoses
Scalloped tongue borders only
A screwdriver shape of the incisors
Erosion on the lingual surfaces of all the maxillary teeth to the second molars
ex: Clenching patients often present with a history of fractured, chipped, broken or splayed teeth, and tori or exostoses are common. The scalloped tongue comes from nighttime tongue compression.
why: Fractured, chipped or splayed teeth and tori or exostoses.
The scalloped tongue comes from nighttime tongue compression.
The screwdriver shape is citrus sucking.
Maxillary lingual erosion is GERD or bulimia.

stem: Holding a violin under the chin is listed as which kind of parafunctional habit?
choices: A daytime occupational-related habit
A nocturnal habit
A form of bruxism
A protective reflex
ex: Occupational-related daytime habits include biting pencils, pens or nails and holding objects under the chin (a telephone or a violin).
why: Holding a violin under the chin is an occupational daytime habit.
It happens while awake, so it isn't nocturnal.
Bruxism is rhythmic grinding during sleep.
A protective reflex is an involuntary opening.

stem: A scalloped lateral border of the tongue is a clinical sign of:
choices: Pushing the tongue against the teeth during sleep
Bulimia nervosa, from repeated contact with acid during purging
A high crown
Chlorine erosion
ex: Clinical signs of parafunction include cheek biting and a scalloped tongue from the pressure of pushing it against the teeth during sleep (tongue compression).
why: Tongue pressure against the teeth during sleep.
Bulimia erodes the maxillary anteriors.
A high crown gives protective co-contraction.
Chlorine erodes enamel; it doesn't scallop the tongue.

stem: Bruxism is associated with:
choices: A change from a deeper to a lighter phase of sleep
The deepest phase of non-REM sleep only
REM sleep, about 80% of the night
Waking up fully
ex: Bruxism is associated with a change from a deeper to a lighter phase (arousal phases). Sleep is about 80% non-REM (physical rest) and 20% REM (psychic rest). Flashing lights, sound or touch can induce an event.
why: A change from deeper to lighter sleep (arousal).
It starts at the shift toward lighter sleep, not in deep sleep only.
REM is about 20% of the night; non-REM is 80%.
It happens in sleep, at arousal, without full waking.

stem: Aside from changes of sleep phase, bruxism has a relationship to:
choices: Oxygen saturation, with an association to sleep apnea
Blood glucose after the evening meal
The patient's Angle class
The number of missing posterior teeth
ex: Bruxism relates to O2 saturation (and an association with sleep apnea), an interesting line of research today.
why: Oxygen saturation, with an association to sleep apnea.
Glucose isn't on the slide.
Angle class isn't related to bruxism.
Missing teeth were a Pullinger sign for TMD, not a bruxism link.

stem: Compared with normal function, bruxism forces are (Table 7-3):
choices: Several times greater and horizontally directed
About the same and vertically directed
Smaller but more frequent
Greater but always down the long axis
ex: Bruxism forces are often 3-5 times those of normal function and horizontal rather than along the long axis; the mandible can be in any position, and protective reflexes are absent in sleep.

They are much greater and horizontal.
They are greater, not smaller.
They are horizontal, not along the long axis.

stem: What is the primary treatment for bruxism, and its goal?
choices: A stabilization splint, so the patient bruxes against it and preserves the teeth
Equilibration to remove the contacts that start it
A partial-coverage anterior splint to stop the grinding for good
Crowns on every worn tooth before anything else

why: A stabilization splint: brux against it and preserve the teeth.
Contacts don't start bruxism, so equilibration won't stop it.
Partial coverage risks supereruption, and no splint stops it for good.
Crowning worn teeth first just exposes the crowns to the bruxism.

likely.t: Bruxism is centrally mediated, not started by occlusion; the splint protects the teeth

stem: After a stabilization splint is placed, what usually happens to the bruxism?
choices: It stops for a while, then returns
It stops permanently
It gets worse immediately
It moves to the daytime
ex: Splint placement results in a temporary cessation (a temporary muscle discoordination), and after time the bruxism returns, because it is centrally mediated.
why: It stops for a while, then returns.
It is centrally mediated, so it isn't stopped for good.
Placement gives a temporary cessation, not a worsening.
The slides don't describe it moving to the daytime.

likely.t: Bruxism is centrally mediated, not started by occlusion; the splint protects the teeth

stem: What did Rugh's data show?
choices: Nocturnal masseter activity rose with stressful life events and fell on vacation
Nocturnal masseter activity stayed the same every night, regardless of life events
Removing interferences ended nocturnal muscle activity
Children brux more on vacation
ex: Rugh tracked masseter EMG over days against events (job interview, fight with a parent, quitting a job, vacation in Hawaii): activity followed stress, and stress, pain and nocturnal muscle activity were well correlated.
why: Masseter activity followed stressful events and fell on vacation.
Activity changed with stress.
Rugh's data were about stress, not interferences.
Rugh's data were in adults' life events, not children.

stem: A parent is worried about a 6-year-old who grinds loudly at night. Chewing is normal. What should you tell them?
choices: It is common and often benign; monitor it
Make a maxillary stabilization splint now
Equilibrate the primary teeth
It shows an intracapsular disorder
ex: Bruxism in children is common and not considered associated with symptoms; the developing dentition affects occlusal stability. Inform parents it is often benign and advise monitoring; evaluate if masticatory function is affected.
why: Common and often benign: inform and monitor.
A splint isn't needed when function is normal.
Equilibrating primary teeth isn't indicated.
It is a developing dentition, not a joint disorder.

stem: What is the most likely explanation for her symptoms?
choices: Protective muscle co-contraction from the high crown
An intracapsular disorder from orthopedic instability
Nocturnal bruxism started by the new crown
Myofascial pain from emotional stress
ex: A crown that hits first in MIP, then guarded movement and sore elevators on that side within days: protective co-contraction, a muscle-origin TMD caused by an acute occlusal change. No joint signs, and bruxism isn't started by contacts.
pbox: "My jaw muscles on the right ache, and I chew carefully on the left"
#30 contacts first in MIP; opening guarded and slow; right masseter tender to palpation
No noises; no pain on loading
why: A high crown, then guarded movement and sore muscles: protective co-contraction.
No joint signs, and the change was acute and occlusal.
Bruxism isn't started by contacts.
Stress can contribute, but the timing points to the crown.

likely.t: Introducing an interference (the high crown) causes protective co-contraction

stem: What should be done first?
choices: Adjust the crown to remove the premature contact
Make a full-mouth equilibration of every interference
Start orthognathic evaluation
Place a partial-coverage anterior splint for six months

pbox: "My jaw muscles on the right ache, and I chew carefully on the left"
#30 contacts first in MIP; opening guarded and slow; right masseter tender to palpation
No noises; no pain on loading
why: Remove the premature contact you introduced.
Equilibrating the rest of the mouth isn't supported.
Surgery isn't indicated for an acute high contact.
A partial splint risks supereruption and doesn't fix the cause.

likely.t: Introducing an interference (the high crown) causes protective co-contraction

stem: His wear pattern is most consistent with:
choices: Attrition
Erosion
Abrasion
Abfraction
ex: Shiny facets with sharp edges that match the opposing teeth and sit only at the contacts, enamel and dentin at the same height: attrition, the tooth-to-tooth wear of bruxism.
pbox: Partner hears him grinding at night; wakes with tired jaws; two incisal chips this year
Shiny facets with sharp edges that match the opposing teeth, only where they contact; enamel and dentin level in the facets
Scalloped lateral borders of the tongue; mandibular tori
why: Matching, shiny, sharp-edged facets at the contacts: attrition.
Erosion facets are dull and cupped.
Abrasion needs a third body, such as a toothbrush.
Abfraction is a cervical notch.

stem: Which appliance fits him best?
choices: A full-coverage maxillary stabilization splint, worn at night
A partial-coverage anterior bite plate worn day and night
A mandibular repositioning splint holding the jaw forward
No appliance; equilibrate the canines instead
ex: Night grinding with heavy clenching: a full-coverage maxillary splint (flat posterior plane, anterior ramp) is sturdy, stable and for nighttime. Partial coverage risks supereruption; a repositioning splint is for disc displacement or apnea.
pbox: Partner hears him grinding at night; wakes with tired jaws; two incisal chips this year
Shiny facets with sharp edges that match the opposing teeth, only where they contact; enamel and dentin level in the facets
Scalloped lateral borders of the tongue; mandibular tori
why: Full-coverage maxillary splint for night grinding.
Partial coverage risks supereruption.
Repositioning splints are for disc displacement or apnea.
Equilibration won't stop centrally mediated bruxism.

stem: He asks whether adjusting his bite will stop the grinding. What is the best answer?
choices: No: bruxism starts in the brain, so the splint protects the teeth instead
Yes: removing the mediotrusive contacts will stop it for good
