stem: Why is a complete denture occlusion usually built and adjusted on an articulator rather than in the mouth?
choices: The tissue compresses under each contact, so the denture moves
An edentulous patient can't open wide enough for the teeth to be adjusted in the mouth
Articulating paper won't mark on the plastic of denture teeth
Centric relation can't be found once all the teeth are gone
ex: The Realeff (Hanau): every time the teeth hit, the tissue under the base compresses and the denture moves. Hanau saw that the occlusion can't be created in the mouth. CR is actually fairly easy to find in denture patients.
why: The Realeff: the tissue sinks under each contact, so the denture moves and misleads you.
Opening isn't the problem; the moving denture is.
Paper marks denture teeth; the marks are just unreliable because the denture tips.
CR is fairly easy to find in denture patients.

likely.t: Build and check the occlusion on an articulator: Hanau's Realeff

stem: After the maxillary posterior teeth are lost, the ridge resorbs:
choices: Upward and toward the midline
Downward and away from the midline
Upward and outward
Downward and forward
ex: Maxillary anterior: upward and inward; maxillary posterior: upward and toward the midline. The maxilla gets smaller. Downward and outward is the mandibular posterior; downward and forward the mandibular anterior.
why: Maxillary posterior bone resorbs upward and toward the midline.
Downward is the mandible; the maxilla goes up and in.
The maxilla resorbs inward, not outward.
Downward and forward is the mandibular anterior.

likely.t: Resorption patterns, crossbite and pseudo-Class III

stem: At the level where the teeth used to be, how does the outline of the edentulous mandibular arch compare with the dentate arch?
choices: Larger, because the mandible resorbs downward and outward
Smaller, because the mandible resorbs upward and inward
The same size, because only the ridge height changes
Narrower in front but wider at the molars
ex: Less bone, but a bigger arch: the mandible resorbs downward and forward in front and downward and outward behind, so the ridge that is left sits outside where the teeth were, and the arch becomes larger than the dentate jaw at tooth level, the opposite of the maxilla. That is how resorption creates a pseudo-Class III.
why: The mandible loses bone but resorbs down and out, so at tooth level its arch ends up larger.
Less bone doesn't make the mandibular arch smaller: upward and inward describes the maxilla, which gets smaller.
Width changes too: down and out makes the mandible larger.
The mandibular anterior goes down and forward, so it isn't narrower in front.

likely.t: Resorption patterns, crossbite and pseudo-Class III

stem: After the teeth are lost, the tongue tends to:
choices: Hypertrophy, filling the space and mostly troubling the lower denture
Atrophy, leaving more room for the lower denture
Retract, so it no longer touches the lingual flange
Lose its muscle tone, so it can't help hold the denture
ex: "Nature abhors a vacuum": the tongue grows into the space where teeth used to be, which is a challenge mostly for the mandibular denture.
why: The tongue hypertrophies into the space where the teeth were, mostly troubling the lower denture.
It grows, not shrinks, after tooth loss.
It fills the space and presses on the denture; it doesn't retract.
It isn't losing tone; its size is the problem.

likely.t: All removable is movable: what resists tipping, the tongue, interarch space

stem: Why is a patient whose teeth were extracted recently, with plenty of bone, often harder to treat with dentures?
choices: There may not be enough interarch space for the base and teeth
The firm new ridges can't take any support until they have resorbed
The tongue hasn't yet grown into the extraction spaces
Centric relation can't be recorded until the sockets heal
ex: A denture needs room for its base and teeth; with lots of bone, limited interarch space makes it far more difficult. More bone does help stability, but space is the problem.
why: Plenty of bone can leave too little interarch space for the base and teeth.
Firm ridges with plenty of bone help; space is the problem.
The tongue grows over time; that isn't why recent extractions are hard.
CR can be recorded; the space for the denture is the issue.

likely.t: All removable is movable: what resists tipping, the tongue, interarch space

stem: Support, retention and stability each name a force a complete denture resists. Which force does support resist?
choices: Vertical force toward the tissues
Vertical dislodgement away from the tissues
Horizontal force
Rotation around the incisal edges
ex: Support resists the vertical force of closing and compressing the dentures together, pressing them toward the tissues. Retention resists vertical dislodgement away from the tissues; stability resists horizontal force.
why: Support resists vertical force toward the tissues.
Vertical dislodgement away from the tissues is retention.
Horizontal force is stability.
Rotation isn't one of the three definitions; support is vertical force toward the tissues.

likely.t: Support, stability and retention: what each resists, and stability matters most

stem: Which property matters most for a complete denture, because when it fails biting hurts and patients can't eat?
choices: Stability
Retention
Support
Esthetics
ex: "Of all the things that we need to address, stability is the most important." Poor retention bothers patients but doesn't hurt; implants are fabulous at stability.
why: Stability is the most important: sliding sideways hurts and stops patients eating.
Retention bothers patients, but it doesn't hurt.
Support matters, but stability is the one he ranked first.
Esthetics isn't one of the three; stability is the most important of them.

likely.t: Support, stability and retention: what each resists, and stability matters most

stem: Which areas are good at taking support for complete dentures?
choices: The buccal shelf and retromolar pad below, and the palate above
The crest of the anterior ridges and the premaxilla
The floor of the mouth and the lingual frenum
The labial vestibule and the inner surface of the lip
ex: The primary support areas: the buccal shelf and the retromolar pad in the mandible, the palate in the maxilla. The ridges themselves aren't good at taking support, and the premaxilla takes force poorly once the teeth are gone.
why: The buccal shelf and retromolar pad below and the palate above are the primary support areas.
The ridges aren't good at taking support, and the premaxilla takes force poorly after tooth loss.
The floor of the mouth is movable tissue, not a support area.
The vestibule and lip are movable tissues beyond the peripheral border.

stem: Why are the anterior denture teeth usually kept out of contact in centric occlusion?
choices: The premaxilla takes force poorly once the teeth are gone
Anterior denture teeth are made of weaker acrylic
Anterior contact is needed only for the facebow record
The incisors must stay free to set the vertical dimension
ex: In both balanced and non-balanced setups the contacts are usually only posterior, to protect the premaxilla, which doesn't take forces well after tooth loss; anterior contact also tips the denture. The anteriors are for appearance.
why: The premaxilla takes force poorly once the teeth are gone, so contacts stay posterior.
Material isn't the reason; anterior denture teeth are the same materials.
A facebow doesn't need anterior contact.
Vertical dimension is set with the rims, not by leaving the incisors free.

stem: Why is centric relation fairly easy to find in most denture patients?
choices: When the elevator muscles contract, they seat the joints
The resorbed ridges guide the mandible straight back
The denture teeth hold the condyles in their fossae
Edentulous patients lose the ability to protrude
ex: With no teeth guiding the jaw elsewhere, muscle contraction seats the condyles, so CR is pretty easy. Most patients don't posture forward, though some skeletal Class IIs will.
why: Contracting elevators seat the condyles, with no teeth guiding the jaw elsewhere.
Ridges don't guide the mandible; the muscles seat the joints.
Denture teeth don't hold the condyles; muscle contraction seats them.
They can still protrude; most simply don't posture forward.

likely.t: Centric occlusion, not MIP, in a denture; CR is easy to find

stem: Balanced occlusion is defined as:
choices: Bilateral, simultaneous contact of anterior and posterior teeth in centric and eccentric positions
Contact of the posterior teeth in centric occlusion with separation in every eccentric position
Working-side contact on the canines, with the non-working side free of contact
Contact of the maxillary lingual cusps only, with no anterior contact in any position
ex: Balance keeps the teeth touching on both sides, front and back, in centric and eccentric positions. Contact in centric only is non-balanced; working-side canine contact is canine guidance for natural teeth; lingual cusps only describes lingualized occlusion.
why: Balance: both sides, anterior and posterior, touching at once in centric and eccentric positions.
Contact in centric only is non-balanced occlusion.
Working-side canine contact is canine guidance for natural teeth.
Lingual cusps only, with no anterior contact, describes lingualized occlusion.

likely.t: Balanced vs non-balanced: contacts, anterior contact, teeth, articulator (his table)

stem: Non-balanced denture occlusion is defined as:
choices: Flat teeth on a plane parallel to the foundation, with no guidance or curve
Anatomic teeth set on a compensating curve so they stay in contact in every excursion
Semi-anatomic teeth set in protrusive balance, with the anterior teeth guiding
Lingualized teeth set with a compensating curve for left-right balance
ex: Flat (zero-degree) teeth in an anteroposterior plane parallel to the ridges, no guidance, no compensating curve: contact in centric only. A compensating curve and contact in excursions are tools of balance.
why: Non-balanced: flat teeth on a plane parallel to the ridges, no guidance, no compensating curve.
Teeth kept in contact in excursions on a compensating curve is balanced occlusion.
Protrusive balance with guiding anteriors is a balanced setup with anatomic teeth.
A compensating curve for left-right balance is balanced lingualized occlusion.

likely.t: Balanced vs non-balanced: contacts, anterior contact, teeth, articulator (his table)

stem: Why is the articulator's condylar guidance set to zero when building a non-balanced denture?
choices: The patient's own condylar guidance then separates the teeth
It programs the articulator to match the patient's protrusive path exactly
It keeps the posterior teeth in contact in every eccentric movement
It lets the anterior teeth guide the mandible in protrusion
ex: Build the denture as if the condyles moved flat; in the mouth the patient's eminence makes the condyles drop, so any condylar guidance they have helps disclude the prosthesis. Matching the patient is what a balanced denture needs.
why: Built at zero, the denture separates as the patient's real (never zero) guidance drops the condyles.
Matching the patient's path is what a balanced denture needs, not a non-balanced one.
Keeping contact in excursions is balance; zero guidance is used to lose it.
Non-balanced dentures have no anterior contact or guidance.

likely.t: Balanced vs non-balanced: contacts, anterior contact, teeth, articulator (his table)

stem: In a non-balanced setup, why may the mandibular second molars be left off?
choices: The ascending ramus starts to rise there, so a flat plane can't be kept
Second molars would carry too much of the vertical support
The retromolar pad has to stay uncovered by the denture base
Second molars make the denture too long for the articulator
ex: The flat plane can't follow the rising ramus, so the last molar is often omitted. The retromolar pad is a support area the base covers.
why: The ramus rises behind the first molar, so a flat plane can't continue there.
Support comes from the buccal shelf and pad, not from leaving teeth off.
The retromolar pad is a support area the base covers.
Articulator size isn't the reason; the rising ramus is.

likely.t: Non-balanced is neutrocentric: neutralize the inclines, centralize the forces

stem: While a bolus of food is between the denture teeth, bilateral balance:
choices: Doesn't exist, and the denture can easily tip
Holds the denture most firmly against the tissues while chewing
Moves to the anterior teeth
Increases as the patient bites harder
ex: With food between the teeth there is no balance at all; the teeth come together only as the food breaks down. That reasoning is behind the non-balanced approach and behind how denture patients are taught to chew.
why: With food between the teeth there's no balance, and the denture can tip.
Balance needs tooth contact, and a bolus keeps the teeth apart.
The anterior teeth don't take over; incising food tips the denture.
Biting harder on a bolus increases tipping, not balance.

stem: Which advice helps a new denture wearer keep the dentures from tipping while eating?
choices: Put food on both sides and chew as vertically as possible on the premolars
Incise food with the central incisors so the posterior teeth stay free
Chew on one side so the other side can seal the denture
Take large bites so the bolus seats the dentures firmly
ex: Patients are trained to put food on both sides, chew vertically, avoid big bites and chew on the premolars: "the incisors are for smiling, but the posterior teeth allow you to chew." Biting into a sandwich tips the back down and flips the lower denture up.
why: Both sides, chewing vertically, on the premolars: how denture patients avoid tipping.
Incising with the front teeth tips the back down and flips the lower denture up.
Chewing on one side tips the denture; food goes on both sides.
Big bites tip dentures; patients learn to avoid them.

stem: Why is lingualized occlusion so popular?
choices: The teeth are much easier to arrange, and it can be set balanced or non-balanced
It is the only scheme that lets the anterior teeth touch in protrusion without tipping
It gives the most esthetic posterior teeth of any scheme
Its fewer contacts make the teeth wear more slowly
ex: It is easier to set and works either way, so it fits almost any patient; most of the school's dentures are lingualized. It doesn't provide anterior contact, anatomic balanced teeth are the most esthetic, and fewer contacts make wear show sooner.
why: It is much easier to arrange and works balanced or non-balanced.
Lingualized doesn't provide anterior contact; anatomic balanced teeth can.
Anatomic teeth in balance give the best esthetics.
Fewer contacts make wear show sooner, not slower.

likely.t: Lingualized occlusion: easy to set, balanced or not, no anterior contact

stem: When a lingualized denture is set in balance, anterior contact in protrusion is:
choices: Not provided, because the denture can't be kept from tipping front to back
Required, so the anterior teeth guide the patient forward and seat the denture
Provided on the canines only
Provided whenever the teeth are porcelain
ex: A balanced lingualized setup gives left-right balance with a little plane and compensating curve, but no anterior contact: in class he said never, since the denture can't be kept from tipping front to back, and the slides call it difficult, though it can be compensated. With anatomic teeth the anteriors can touch in protrusion; not here.
why: Balanced lingualized gives left-right balance only; it can't stop front-to-back tipping (the slides: difficult, though it can be compensated).
Anterior guidance tips a denture; lingualized doesn't provide it.
There is no canine contact either.
Tooth material doesn't change the scheme.

likely.t: Lingualized occlusion: easy to set, balanced or not, no anterior contact

stem: What is a disadvantage of lingualized occlusion?
choices: With fewer contacts, wear shows sooner and vertical dimension can be lost
It can't be used when the ridges are badly resorbed
It needs anatomic teeth set on a fully adjustable, fully programmed articulator
It is the hardest scheme for a lab to set
ex: Fewer teeth touching means wear is more prominent and VDO may be lost. It works with all ridge forms, uses semi-anatomic teeth with a long lingual cusp, and is easier to set.
why: Fewer contacts make wear more prominent, and VDO can be lost.
It works with all ridge morphologies, resorbed ones included.
It uses semi-anatomic teeth with a long lingual cusp and is easy to set.
It is easier to set than a full anatomic balance.

stem: Anatomic denture teeth have cusp angles of about:
choices: About 30-33°
About 12-22°
About 45-60°
ex: Anatomic: 30-33° (the handout says 30° or more), with sulci and ridges, looking like teeth. Semi-anatomic: about 12-22° (the 12° and 20° molds). Non-anatomic: 0°.
why: Anatomic teeth have cusp angles of 30-33° (the handout: 30° or more).
About 12-22° is semi-anatomic.
0° is non-anatomic (flat).
45-60° is steeper than any denture tooth form described.

likely.t: Tooth forms (30-33°, 12-22°, 0°), their names, for and against, and choosing for the patient

stem: Which is an advantage of flat (0°) posterior denture teeth?
choices: They put the least lateral force on the denture, so stability is easier
They give the most natural-looking posterior teeth
They penetrate and grind food better than cusped teeth
They let the anterior teeth touch in protrusion
ex: A flat tooth has no horizontal (lateral) forces on the denture, so stability is easier; they also suit any jaw relation, crossbites and poor neuromuscular control, and are simpler to adjust. Anatomic teeth are the most esthetic and chew a little better.
why: No lateral forces on the denture, so stability is easiest to get.
Anatomic teeth give the most natural-looking posteriors.
Cusped teeth penetrate and grind food better, though flat teeth are clinically fine.
Non-balanced flat setups have no anterior contact.

likely.t: Tooth forms (30-33°, 12-22°, 0°), their names, for and against, and choosing for the patient

stem: What does the evidence show about chewing with anatomic versus flat denture teeth?
choices: Anatomic teeth grind better, but flat teeth are just as successful clinically
Flat teeth leave patients unable to maintain their nutrition
There is no difference at all in how well they penetrate food
Anatomic teeth double chewing efficiency, so they should be used for every patient
ex: Anatomic teeth do penetrate and grind better, but flat-plane non-balanced dentures are clinically just as successful and patients keep great nutrition. Chewing ability is one factor of many. The review the slides cite (Abduo, 2013) favors cusped teeth, set balanced or lingualized, mainly for patient acceptance.
why: Anatomic teeth grind a bit better, but flat-plane dentures are clinically just as successful.
Patients with flat teeth maintain great nutrition.
Anatomic teeth do penetrate better; the difference just isn't clinically significant.
The difference is small, and chewing is only one factor of many.

likely.t: Tooth forms (30-33°, 12-22°, 0°), their names, for and against, and choosing for the patient

stem: How are porcelain denture teeth held in the denture base?
choices: Mechanically: pins in the anterior teeth, diatorics in the posterior teeth
By a chemical bond between the porcelain and the base resin
With a silane primer and a resin cement applied after the base is processed
By the tight fit of the posterior palatal seal
ex: Porcelain doesn't bond to the denture base, so the resin flows around pins (anteriors) or into diatorics, holes with undercuts (posteriors). Composite and acrylic teeth bond chemically.
why: Porcelain doesn't bond, so pins (anteriors) and diatorics (posteriors) hold it mechanically.
Porcelain teeth don't bond chemically to the base resin.
They are processed into the base, held by pins or diatorics, not cemented.
The palatal seal is about fit to the tissues, not holding teeth.

likely.t: Denture tooth materials: porcelain, composite and cross-linked resin, acrylic

stem: Why are composite denture teeth the usual choice for good dentures today?
choices: They bond to the base, don't chip, sound softer and resist wear
They cost the least of the three materials and need no special technique
They are held in the base with pins and diatorics
They are harder and denser than denture porcelain
ex: Composite teeth bond chemically to the base, don't chip, are quieter than porcelain's click-clack and come in wear-resistant cross-linked or layered forms. They are not inexpensive; acrylic is the affordable one.
why: They bond to the base, don't chip, are quieter and come wear-resistant: the number one go-to.
Composite teeth are pricey; acrylic is the affordable one, and setting them takes technique.
Pins and diatorics hold porcelain teeth.
Denture porcelain is the denser, harder material.

likely.t: Denture tooth materials: porcelain, composite and cross-linked resin, acrylic

stem: Plain acrylic denture teeth are used mainly for:
choices: Temporary prostheses, because they are affordable but wear and stain
High-end dentures, because they look the most natural
Patients who brux, because they resist wear best
Implant overdentures, because they bond to titanium
ex: Acrylic teeth bond to the acrylic base and are far more affordable, but they wear and can stain, so they are used mainly for interim prostheses.
why: Affordable but wear and stain, so they suit interim prostheses.
High-end dentures use composite or porcelain.
Acrylic wears more than composite.
They bond to the acrylic base, not to titanium.

likely.t: Denture tooth materials: porcelain, composite and cross-linked resin, acrylic

stem: As a patient's denture teeth wear, what happens?
choices: The patient closes farther, losing vertical dimension of occlusion
The dentures become more retentive
The cusp angles become steeper
Centric relation moves forward
ex: Wear lets the patient close down farther, so vertical dimension is lost; that is why wear resistance matters, and why lingualized setups, with fewer contacts, show it sooner.
why: Worn teeth let the patient close farther: lost vertical dimension.
Wear doesn't improve retention.
Wear flattens cusps; it doesn't steepen them.
CR is a joint position; wear doesn't move it.

likely.t: Denture tooth materials: porcelain, composite and cross-linked resin, acrylic

stem: On a mold chart, what decision sets the mandibular anterior mold and the posterior teeth for each occlusal scheme?
choices: The maxillary anterior mold chosen for the patient
The mandibular posterior mold chosen for the ridge
The shade chosen to match the complexion
The condylar guidance set on the articulator
ex: "The denture occlusion is entirely based upon whatever selection we make to pick out that anterior maxillary mold." The chart lists the mandibular anterior and the posterior molds engineered to articulate with it.
why: The maxillary anterior mold sets everything else engineered to articulate with it.
The mandibular posterior mold follows from the maxillary anterior choice.
Shade doesn't determine the molds.
Condylar guidance is an articulator setting, not on the mold chart.

likely.t: The maxillary anterior mold sets the rest, and it's chosen on esthetics

stem: The maxillary anterior mold is chosen mostly on:
choices: Esthetics
Occlusion
The condylar guidance
The posterior cusp angle
ex: Usually more on esthetics than occlusion: the canine positions, the wax rim, personality (soft or bold) and shape (square, tapering, ovoid). The occlusion comes from the posterior teeth engineered to go with it.
why: The anterior mold is chosen more on esthetics than occlusion.
Occlusion comes from the posterior teeth engineered to match the anterior mold.
Condylar guidance doesn't pick an anterior mold.
Cusp angle is a posterior-tooth choice, made by scheme.

likely.t: The maxillary anterior mold sets the rest, and it's chosen on esthetics

stem: Making the central incisor about 1/16 of the bizygomatic width (Berry's ratio) is:
choices: Not scientifically valid, but it tends to look natural
A validated predictor of natural incisor width
The way the occlusal plane is set on the wax rim
How the condylar guidance is estimated without a record
ex: Asked whether it is scientifically valid: "absolutely not." Does it tend to work? "Yeah, it actually does": that proportion looks natural. The same goes for the ala-to-ala measure.
why: Not scientifically valid, but the proportion tends to look natural.
It has no scientific merit; it just tends to look good.
The occlusal plane comes from the shaped wax rim.
Condylar guidance comes from a protrusive record or is set by scheme.

likely.t: The maxillary anterior mold sets the rest, and it's chosen on esthetics

stem: A wax rim shaped in the mouth tells you each of these EXCEPT:
choices: The condylar guidance
The lip support
Where the incisal edges go
The occlusal plane
ex: The wax rim shows the lip support, the position and length of the incisal edges, the midline and canines, and its shape becomes the occlusal plane. Condylar guidance comes from a protrusive record (or is set to zero for non-balanced).
why: Condylar guidance comes from a protrusive record, not the wax rim.
The rim pushes the lips out to the right support.
The rim's edge marks where the incisal edges go and how long the teeth are.
The rim's shape becomes the occlusal plane.

stem: Each is a factor in choosing the posterior tooth form EXCEPT:
choices: Whether the patient's temperament is bold or soft
The patient's neuromuscular control and experience with dentures
The interarch distance
The jaw relation: Class I, II or III
ex: Posterior teeth depend on the scheme and on neuromuscular control, arch (ridge) morphology, jaw relations, interarch distance, arch length and denture experience. Soft and bold describe anterior molds.
why: Bold or soft describes anterior molds (temperament), not posterior tooth form.
Neuromuscular control and denture experience help decide the posterior form.
Interarch distance is a big factor in posterior tooth choice.
Jaw relations (Class I, II, III) affect posterior tooth choice.

stem: In a balanced denture, the plane of occlusion is made steeper. To keep the posterior teeth in contact, you would:
choices: Use flatter cusps or a flatter compensating curve
Steepen the compensating curve to match the new plane
Use taller cusps
Lower the patient's condylar guidance
ex: Thielemann's formula (the Review lecture's Thielmann): balance = (condylar guidance × anterior guidance) / (cusp angle × compensating curve × plane of occlusion). Raise the plane, and the cusp angle or the compensating curve must come down to keep the balance. The patient's condylar guidance can't be changed.
why: A steeper plane means flatter cusps or a flatter curve to keep the balance (Thielemann's proportions).
A steeper curve plus a steeper plane would overshoot the balance.
Taller cusps work the wrong way when the plane is steepened.
The patient's condylar guidance can't be changed.

likely.t: Hanau and Thielemann: the five determinants, which are fixed and which vary

stem: How do the five determinants of occlusion apply to natural teeth compared with dentures?
choices: The same factors are used to keep natural teeth apart, not together
They don't apply to natural teeth at all
They are used to build balancing contacts on natural teeth
Only the condylar guidance applies to natural teeth
ex: Hanau's relationships were first used for their original purpose, keeping denture teeth together. For the dentate patient we turn them around to keep the teeth apart (posterior disclusion): the same tool, used differently.
why: Same factors, reversed: keep natural teeth apart (disclusion) instead of together.
They apply to natural teeth too, used in reverse.
Balancing contacts are interferences on natural teeth.
All five factors apply, condylar guidance among them.

likely.t: Hanau and Thielemann: the five determinants, which are fixed and which vary

stem: A removable partial denture replaces two missing teeth in an otherwise healthy arch. The occlusion is planned:
choices: Like the dentate patient: canine guidance or group function, with posterior disclusion
Like a complete denture, with bilateral balance in every excursion
With flat teeth and no guidance, so the prosthesis never contacts in excursions
With balancing contacts on the non-working side to stabilize the clasps
ex: The more natural teeth remain, the more the teeth are in charge and the more you plan dentate occlusion. The more teeth that are lost, the more you plan like a complete denture, for stability.
why: Many natural teeth remain, so the teeth are in charge: plan dentate occlusion.
Complete-denture balance is for when most teeth are lost.
Flat teeth with no guidance is a complete-denture scheme.
Non-working contacts are interferences on natural teeth.

likely.t: Partial dentures: the more natural teeth remain, the more dentate the occlusion

stem: Her chief complaint is mainly a problem of:
choices: Stability
Retention
Support
Esthetics
ex: A denture that slides around and hurts when she chews is failing to resist horizontal force: stability, the most important of the three. Retention problems (lifting off) bother patients but don't hurt.
pbox: "My lower denture slides around when I chew, and it hurts"
Skeletal Class I before her teeth were extracted
Mandibular ridge severely resorbed and now outside the maxillary ridge in the back; flabby anterior maxillary tissue
Mild hand tremor; struggles to hold the lower denture in with her tongue and cheeks
why: A denture that slides and hurts when she chews is failing at stability.
Retention problems (lifting off) bother patients but don't hurt.
Support is resistance to vertical force toward the tissues; her complaint is sideways sliding.
Her complaint is function and pain, not appearance.

likely.t: Support, stability and retention: what each resists, and stability matters most

stem: How is her jaw relationship best described now?
choices: Pseudo-Class III, from resorption
Skeletal Class II
True skeletal Class III
Skeletal Class I, as it was before her extractions
ex: She was skeletal Class I; the mandible resorbing outward and the maxilla inward has put the mandibular ridge outside the maxillary one: a pseudo-Class III. A true skeletal Class III would have been there before the teeth were lost.
pbox: "My lower denture slides around when I chew, and it hurts"
Skeletal Class I before her teeth were extracted
Mandibular ridge severely resorbed and now outside the maxillary ridge in the back; flabby anterior maxillary tissue
Mild hand tremor; struggles to hold the lower denture in with her tongue and cheeks
why: A Class I patient whose mandible resorbed out and maxilla in is a pseudo-Class III.
Class II would put the mandible back; hers sits outside the maxilla.
A true skeletal Class III exists before tooth loss; hers came from resorption.
Her ridge relationship has changed from Class I.

likely.t: Resorption patterns, crossbite and pseudo-Class III

stem: Which occlusal scheme suits her new dentures best?
choices: Non-balanced, with flat posterior teeth
Bilateral balance with anatomic posterior teeth
Lingualized and balanced, on a compensating curve
Canine guidance with posterior disclusion
ex: Severe resorption, flabby tissue, a crossbite relationship and poor neuromuscular control all point to non-balanced flat teeth: the least lateral force, easy in any jaw relation and crossbite. Balance, lingualized or not, suits good ridges, firm tissue and good control, and canine guidance is for natural teeth.
pbox: "My lower denture slides around when I chew, and it hurts"
Skeletal Class I before her teeth were extracted
Mandibular ridge severely resorbed and now outside the maxillary ridge in the back; flabby anterior maxillary tissue
Mild hand tremor; struggles to hold the lower denture in with her tongue and cheeks
